abstract: We describe pulse - stream firing integrated circuits that imple(cid:173) ment asynchronous analog neural networks. Synaptic weights are stored dynamically, and weighting uses time-division of the neural pulses from a signalling neuron to a receiving neuron. MOS transistors in their "ON" state act as variable resistors to control a capacitive discharge, and time-division is thus achieved by a small synapse circuit cell. The VLSI chip set design uses 2.5J.1.m CMOS technology.
originalAbstract: We describe pulse - stream firing integrated circuits that imple(cid:173) ment asynchronous analog neural networks. Synaptic weights are stored dynamically, and weighting uses time-division of the neural pulses from a signalling neuron to a receiving neuron. MOS transistors in their "ON" state act as variable resistors to control a capacitive discharge, and time-division is thus achieved by a small synapse circuit cell. paragraphs: This paper describes integrated circuits for asynchronous analog neural networks in which neurons communicate through streams of pulses. The implementation must represent connection strengths and apply them to signals traveling between neurons. It does this using dynamically stored synaptic weights and a time-division mechanism for weighting the pulses.

The central circuit idea uses MOS transistors in their conducting state as variable resistors. These resistors control the discharge of a capacitor, providing the electrical mechanism for time division. Through this arrangement, a small synapse circuit cell controls how the pulse signal from a sending neuron influences a receiving neuron.

The chip-set design uses 2.5-micrometer CMOS technology. Its contribution is a concrete hardware organization joining pulse-based communication, analog operation, and programmable connection strengths. The small synapse cell is especially relevant because it provides the weighting function at the point where neurons connect. The paper thus explains how timing and capacitor discharge can implement synaptic weighting within an integrated asynchronous neural-network design.
summary.tldr: An asynchronous analog chip design weights neural pulse streams through compact synapse circuits that control capacitor-discharge timing.

title: Programmable Analog Pulse-Firing Neural Networks

abstract: Recurrent Cascade-Correlation CRCC) is a recurrent version of the Cascade(cid:173) Correlation learning architecture of Fah I man and Lebiere [Fahlman, 1990]. RCC can learn from examples to map a sequence of inputs into a desired sequence of outputs. New hidden units with recurrent connections are added to the network as needed during training. In effect, the network builds up a finite-state machine tailored specifically for the current problem. RCC retains the advantages of Cascade-Correlation: fast learning, good generalization, automatic construction of a near-minimal multi-layered network, and incremental training. 1 THE ARCHITECTURE Cascade-Correlation [Fahlman, 1990] is a supervised learning architecture that builds a near-minimal multi-layer network topology in the course of training. Initially the network contains only inputs, output units, and the connections between them. This single layer of connections is trained (using the Quickprop algorithm [Fahlman, 1988]) to minimize the error. When no further improvement is seen in the level of error, the network's performance is evaluated. If the error is small enough, we stop. Otherwise we add a new hidden unit to the network in an attempt to reduce the residual error. To create a new hidden unit, we begin with a pool of candidate units, each of which receives weighted connections from the network's inputs and from any hidden units already present in the net. The outputs of these candidate units are not yet connected into the active network. Multiple passes through the training set are run, and each candidate unit adjusts its incoming weights to maximize the correlation between its output and the residual error in the active net. When the correlation scores stop improving, we choose the best candidate, freeze its incoming weights, and add it to the network. This process is called "tenure." After tenure,

paragraphs: Recurrent Cascade-Correlation is an architecture for learning a desired output sequence from an input sequence. It extends Cascade-Correlation by adding hidden units with recurrent connections during training. These connections support sequence-dependent computation, while the growing architecture lets the network develop the internal structure needed for the particular problem.

The supplied description explains the underlying construction process. Training begins with connections between inputs and outputs. When progress stalls and error remains too high, candidate hidden units are trained to correlate with the remaining error. The best candidate is added to the active network, with its incoming weights frozen. This makes network growth responsive to what the current model still fails to capture.

In the recurrent version, the authors describe the resulting system as effectively building a task-specific finite-state machine. They report retaining fast learning, good generalization, incremental training, and automatic construction of a near-minimal multilayer network. The approach matters because learning determines both the sequence mapping and much of the machinery used to represent it.
summary.tldr: Recurrent Cascade-Correlation grows recurrent hidden units during training to construct a compact network tailored to a sequence-learning problem.

title: The Recurrent Cascade-Correlation Architecture

abstract: We analyze in detail the performance of a Hamming network clas(cid:173) sifying inputs that are distorted versions of one of its m stored memory patterns. The activation function of the memory neurons in the original Hamming network is replaced by a simple threshold function. The resulting Threshold Hamming Network (THN) cor(cid:173) rectly classifies the input pattern, with probability approaching 1, using only O(mln m) connections, in a single iteration. The THN drastically reduces the time and space complexity of Hamming Net(cid:173) work classifiers.
originalAbstract: We analyze in detail the performance of a Hamming network clas(cid:173) sifying inputs that are distorted versions of one of its m stored memory patterns. The activation function of the memory neurons in the original Hamming network is replaced by a simple threshold function. The resulting Threshold Hamming Network (THN) cor(cid:173) rectly classifies the input pattern, with probability approaching 1, using only O(mln m) connections, in a single iteration. paragraphs: The paper analyzes a network that classifies an input as a distorted version of one of its stored memory patterns. The task is to identify the appropriate stored pattern despite changes in the input. It begins with the Hamming network and modifies how its memory neurons become active.

The proposed Threshold Hamming Network replaces the original activation function with a simple threshold function. The analysis shows that the resulting network can perform classification in a single iteration. With m stored patterns, it uses a number of connections that scales as O(m ln m), relating the required network resources to the number of memories.

The probability of correct classification approaches one under the analyzed setting. Together, the probability result, connection count, and single-iteration operation describe both reliability and efficiency. The authors characterize the change as a drastic reduction in the time and space complexity of Hamming-network classifiers. The significance is that a simpler activation rule supports a substantially more economical classification architecture.
summary.tldr: Threshold Hamming Networks classify distorted memories in one iteration with O(m ln m) connections and correctness probability approaching one.

title: Single-Iteration Threshold Hamming Networks

paragraphs: This paper studies the classification capacity of multilayer perceptrons whose first hidden layer contains threshold logic units. It considers dichotomies, or assignments of input points to two classes, and gives a counting result for point configurations that occur with positive probability under random selection. The aim is to connect network structure with the number of classifications it can represent.

The analysis also yields a connectivity requirement when the number of points exceeds the product of input dimension and first-layer width. In that setting, the stated result requires every first-layer unit to connect to all inputs. The resulting maximal capacities, in Cover's sense, are twice the input dimension per hidden unit and two input patterns per synaptic weight.

The abstract states that single-hidden-layer networks attain both capacities, which match the corresponding single-neuron values. Comparing these results with estimates of VC dimension reveals a difference between capacity notions: for sufficiently large input dimension and hidden-layer width, VC dimension exceeds Cover's capacity. Thus, the theoretical measure chosen affects how network classification capacity is characterized.
summary.tldr: A counting theorem relates multilayer classification capacity to connectivity and shows that VC dimension can exceed Cover's capacity.

title: Counting function theorem for multi-layer networks

paragraphs: The paper compares more than ten prominent models of orientation and ocular dominance columns in visual cortex. Some models describe the spatial patterns themselves, while others explain how those patterns develop through activity. Evaluating both kinds together helps separate a model’s descriptive success from its proposed account of formation.

The authors implement the models on parallel computers, explore their parameter settings extensively, and compare predictions quantitatively with optical measurements from macaque visual cortex. This makes the comparison broader than checking whether one selected output looks convincing. It examines how well the proposed mechanisms account for measured cortical organization across explored settings.

Many apparently different models turn out to share underlying principles and consequently produce similar predictions. Certain pattern models and developmental correlation-based learning models disagree with the measurements. Among the models investigated, competitive Hebbian approaches and Swindale’s model provide the closest agreement. The finding favors those approaches within the comparison while also showing that differences in model presentation need not imply differences in explanatory behavior.
summary.tldr: A quantitative comparison of cortical-column models finds shared principles and identifies competitive Hebbian models and Swindale’s model as the best matches tested.

title: A Critical Comparison of Models for Orientation and Ocular Dominance Columns in the Striate Cortex

abstract: We present an algorithm for fast stochastic gradient descent that uses a nonlinear adaptive momentum scheme to optimize the late time convergence rate. The algorithm makes effective use of curvature information, requires only O(n) storage and computation, and delivers convergence rates close to the theoretical optimum. We demonstrate the technique on linear and large nonlinear backprop networks.
originalAbstract: We present an algorithm for fast stochastic gradient descent that uses a nonlinear adaptive momentum scheme to optimize the late time convergence rate. The algorithm makes effective use of curvature information, requires only O(n) storage and computation, and delivers convergence rates close to the theoretical optimum. We demonstrate the technique on linear and large nonlinear backprop networks.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a stochastic gradient descent algorithm aimed at improving convergence late in optimization. Its main mechanism is a nonlinear adaptive momentum scheme. Momentum carries information from previous updates into subsequent ones, and here that mechanism adapts to make effective use of the objective's curvature.

Curvature describes how the slope of the objective changes as the parameters move. Using this information can help determine how updates should behave as optimization progresses. The proposed algorithm incorporates it while requiring only O(n) storage and computation, so both costs grow linearly with the number of parameters rather than requiring a full pairwise description of curvature.

The authors report convergence rates close to the theoretical optimum and demonstrate the technique on linear networks and large nonlinear networks trained by backpropagation. The contribution combines a targeted improvement in late-stage convergence with a modest computational requirement. This matters because the benefit of a more informed update rule must be considered alongside its cost: the reported method seeks faster progress without making each update prohibitively expensive.
summary.tldr: Adaptive momentum uses curvature information to approach optimal late-stage stochastic convergence with linear storage and computation.

title: Using Curvature Information for Fast Stochastic Search

abstract: We discuss a strategy for polychotomous classification that involves estimating class probabilities for each pair of classes, and then cou(cid:173) pling the estimates together. The coupling model is similar to the Bradley-Terry method for paired comparisons. We study the na(cid:173) ture of the class probability estimates that arise, and examine the performance of the procedure in simulated datasets. The classifiers used include linear discriminants and nearest neighbors: applica(cid:173) tion to support vector machines is also briefly described.
originalAbstract: We discuss a strategy for polychotomous classification that involves estimating class probabilities for each pair of classes, and then cou(cid:173) pling the estimates together. The coupling model is similar to the Bradley-Terry method for paired comparisons. We study the na(cid:173) ture of the class probability estimates that arise, and examine the performance of the procedure in simulated datasets. The classifiers used include linear discriminants and nearest neighbors: applica(cid:173) tion to support vector machines is also briefly described.

paragraphs: The paper considers classification problems with more than two possible classes. Its strategy first estimates class probabilities separately for every pair of classes. Each estimate addresses a smaller question about two alternatives, but the final prediction still needs to describe the full set of possible classes in a coherent way.

Pairwise coupling provides the connection between these local estimates and the overall classification problem. The proposed coupling model resembles the Bradley–Terry approach to paired comparisons. Rather than leaving the pairwise outputs as separate decisions, it combines them into class probability estimates. The authors study the nature of those resulting probabilities as part of understanding what the procedure produces.

The method is examined on simulated datasets using linear discriminants and nearest-neighbor classifiers, and its application to support vector machines is briefly discussed. This range shows how the coupling step can be considered separately from the choice of pairwise classifier. The central contribution is a probabilistic route from two-class estimates to a multiclass result.
summary.tldr: Pairwise coupling combines probabilities from two-class comparisons into probability estimates for a multiclass problem.

title: Classification by Pairwise Coupling

abstract: While the understanding of the functional role of different classes of neurons in the awake primary visual cortex has been extensively studied since the time of Hubel and Wiesel (Hubel and Wiesel, 1962), our understanding of the feature selectivity and functional role of neurons in the primary auditory cortex is much farther from com(cid:173) plete. Moving bars have long been recognized as an optimal stimulus for many visual cortical neurons, and this finding has recently been confirmed and extended in detail using reverse correlation methods (Jones and Palmer, 1987; Reid and Alonso, 1995; Reid et al., 1991; llingach et al., 1997). In this study, we recorded from neurons in the primary auditory cortex of the awake primate, and used a novel re(cid:173) verse correlation technique to compute receptive fields (or preferred stimuli), encompassing both multiple frequency components and on(cid:173) going time. These spectrotemporal receptive fields make clear that neurons in the primary auditory cortex, as in the primary visual cor(cid:173) tex, typically show considerable structure in their feature processing properties, often including multiple excitatory and inhibitory regions in their receptive fields. These neurons can be sensitive to stimulus edges in frequency composition or in time, and sensitive to stimulus transitions such as changes in frequency. These neurons also show strong responses and selectivity to continuous frequency modulated stimuli analogous to visual drifting gratings.

paragraphs: This study asks which patterns of sound individual neurons in the primary auditory cortex prefer. The researchers recorded neural activity in awake primates and used a new reverse-correlation technique to estimate receptive fields. These descriptions combine sound frequency with time, allowing a neuron's preferred stimulus to include an evolving pattern across multiple frequencies.

The resulting receptive fields often contain several excitatory and inhibitory regions. In plain language, different parts of a sound pattern can promote or suppress a response. This structure reveals selectivity for more than the presence of a single frequency: neurons can respond to boundaries in frequency composition, boundaries in time, and transitions such as changes in frequency.

The neurons also respond strongly and selectively to continuously frequency-modulated sounds, which the authors compare with drifting visual gratings. Together, the findings reveal organized feature processing in auditory cortex with parallels to visual cortex. The methodological contribution is a way to make those preferences visible across both frequency and ongoing time.
summary.tldr: Reverse correlation reveals structured auditory cortical preferences for sound patterns spanning frequency and time.

title: Characterizing Neurons in the Primary Auditory Cortex of the Awake Primate Using Reverse Correlation

abstract: Many belief networks have been proposed that are composed of binary units. However, for tasks such as object and speech recog(cid:173) nition which produce real-valued data, binary network models are usually inadequate. Independent component analysis (ICA) learns a model from real data, but the descriptive power of this model is severly limited. We begin by describing the independent factor analysis (IFA) technique, which overcomes some of the limitations of ICA. We then create a multilayer network by cascading single(cid:173) layer IFA models. At each level, the IFA network extracts real(cid:173) valued latent variables that are non-linear functions of the input data with a highly adaptive functional form, resulting in a hier(cid:173) archical distributed representation of these data. Whereas exact maximum-likelihood learning of the network is intractable, we de(cid:173) rive an algorithm that maximizes a lower bound on the likelihood, based on a variational approach.

However, for tasks such as object and speech recog(cid:173) nition which produce real-valued data, binary network models are usually inadequate. Independent component analysis (ICA) learns a model from real data, but the descriptive power of this model is severly limited. We begin by describing the independent factor analysis (IFA) technique, which overcomes some of the limitations of ICA. We then create a multilayer network by cascading single(cid:173) layer IFA models. At each level, the IFA network extracts real(cid:173) valued latent variables that are non-linear functions of the input data with a highly adaptive functional form, resulting in a hier(cid:173) archical distributed representation of these data. Whereas exact maximum-likelihood learning of the network is intractable, we de(cid:173) rive an algorithm that maximizes a lower bound on the likelihood, based on a variational approach.

paragraphs: The paper develops a hierarchical probabilistic model for real-valued data, motivated by tasks such as object and speech recognition. The authors argue that binary-unit belief networks are usually inadequate for these data and that independent component analysis has limited descriptive power. They begin with independent factor analysis, or IFA, which addresses some of ICA's limitations.

The hierarchy is constructed by cascading single-layer IFA models. Each level extracts real-valued latent variables that are nonlinear functions of its input, with highly adaptable functional forms. Passing these representations through successive levels produces a hierarchical distributed representation. The contribution is thus a way to build multiple levels of real-valued structure from the single-layer IFA model.

Exact maximum-likelihood learning for the resulting network is intractable. The authors derive a variational learning algorithm that instead maximizes a lower bound on likelihood. This supplies a tractable optimization target tied to the probabilistic model. The distinction matters: the algorithm optimizes the stated bound, while the richer multilayer representation makes direct exact likelihood optimization computationally unavailable.
summary.tldr: Cascaded independent factor analyzers learn hierarchical real-valued representations through a variational lower bound on likelihood.

title: Learning a Hierarchical Belief Network of Independent Factor Analyzers

abstract: We consider the hypothesis that systems learning aspects of visual per- ception may beneﬁt from the use of suitably designed developmental pro- gressions during training. Four models were trained to estimate motion velocities in sequences of visual images. Three of the models were “de- velopmental models” in the sense that the nature of their input changed during the course of training. They received a relatively impoverished visual input early in training, and the quality of this input improved as training progressed. One model used a coarse-to-multiscale develop- mental progression (i.e. it received coarse-scale motion features early in training and ﬁner-scale features were added to its input as training progressed), another model used a ﬁne-to-multiscale progression, and the third model used a random progression. The ﬁnal model was non- developmental in the sense that the nature of its input remained the same throughout the training period. The simulation results show that the coarse-to-multiscale model performed best. Hypotheses are offered to account for this model’s superior performance. We conclude that suit- ably designed developmental sequences can be useful to systems learn- ing to estimate motion velocities. The idea that visual development can aid visual learning is a viable hypothesis in need of further study.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether changing the visual input available during training can help a system learn to estimate motion velocity. It compares four models trained on image sequences. Three receive limited input initially and progressively richer input later, allowing the authors to investigate developmental progressions as part of the learning process.

The progressions differ in how visual features become available. One starts with coarse motion features and later adds finer ones; another starts with fine features and expands toward multiple scales; a third uses a random progression. The fourth model receives the same kind of input throughout training, providing a nondevelopmental comparison.

In the simulations, the coarse-to-multiscale model performs best. The authors offer hypotheses for its advantage and conclude that suitably designed developmental sequences can help motion-velocity learning. The qualification matters: the result favors a particular progression among those tested, rather than showing that any changing input schedule is beneficial. The broader idea that visual development aids learning remains a viable hypothesis requiring further study.
summary.tldr: A coarse-to-multiscale training progression performs best among four motion-learning models, supporting further study of developmental input schedules.

title: Visual Development Aids the Acquisition of Motion Velocity Sensitivities

abstract: We present an analysis of concentration-of-expectation phenomena in layered Bayesian networks that use generalized linear models as the local conditional probabilities. This framework encompasses a wide variety of probability distributions, including both discrete and continuous random variables. We utilize ideas from large deviation analysis and the delta method to devise and evaluate a class of approximate inference algo- rithms for layered Bayesian networks that have superior asymptotic error bounds and very fast computation time.
originalAbstract: We present an analysis of concentration-of-expectation phenomena in layered Bayesian networks that use generalized linear models as the local conditional probabilities. This framework encompasses a wide variety of probability distributions, including both discrete and continuous random variables. We utilize ideas from large deviation analysis and the delta method to devise and evaluate a class of approximate inference algo- rithms for layered Bayesian networks that have superior asymptotic error bounds and very fast computation time.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes approximate inference in layered Bayesian networks. In the networks considered, generalized linear models specify the local conditional probabilities. This defines the scope of the analysis while allowing a broad range of probability distributions, including models with discrete variables and models with continuous variables.

The authors examine concentration-of-expectation phenomena and use ideas from large deviation analysis and the delta method to construct inference approximations. These mathematical tools support both the design of the algorithms and the evaluation of their errors. The approximation procedure is therefore tied to an analysis of how accurately it represents the probabilistic calculations of the network.

The resulting class of algorithms is reported to combine very fast computation with superior asymptotic error bounds. The qualification matters: asymptotic bounds describe error behavior in a limiting regime, rather than promising the same error for every individual network. The contribution is an analytically supported route to fast inference across the broad distributional family covered by the stated layered-network formulation.
summary.tldr: Concentration analysis yields fast approximate inference algorithms with improved asymptotic error bounds for a class of layered Bayesian networks.

title: On the Concentration of Expectation and Approximate Inference in Layered Networks

abstract: In this paper we argue that the choice of the SVM cost parameter can be critical. We then derive an algorithm that can fit the entire path of SVM solutions for every value of the cost parameter, with essentially the same computational cost as fitting one SVM model.
originalAbstract: In this paper we argue that the choice of the SVM cost parameter can be critical. We then derive an algorithm that can fit the entire path of SVM solutions for every value of the cost parameter, with essentially the same computational cost as fitting one SVM model.

paragraphs: An SVM's cost parameter affects which fitted solution is obtained, and this paper argues that choosing it can be critical. Studying that choice therefore involves understanding how the solution changes as the parameter varies. The paper makes this family of solutions the central computational object.

The authors derive an algorithm that fits the entire regularization path, covering every value of the cost parameter. A path represents the relationship between parameter settings and their associated SVM solutions. Computing it provides access to the full family of fits, extending the scope of a single training procedure beyond one selected setting.

The striking stated result is that this full-path calculation has essentially the same computational cost as fitting one SVM model. That claim makes comprehensive exploration of parameter-dependent solutions computationally appealing. The algorithm addresses the cost of obtaining the available fits; the abstract's motivation remains that the parameter choice matters. Its contribution is an efficient way to expose the full range of solutions relevant to that choice.
summary.tldr: The paper derives an algorithm for the full SVM regularization path at essentially the computational cost of fitting a single SVM.

title: The Entire Regularization Path for the Support Vector Machine

abstract: We discuss a method for obtaining a subject’s a priori beliefs from his/her behavior in a psychophysics context, under the assumption that the behavior is (nearly) optimal from a Bayesian perspective. The method is nonparametric in the sense that we do not assume that the prior belongs to any ﬁxed class of distributions (e.g., Gaussian). Despite this increased generality, the method is relatively simple to implement, being based in the simplest case on a linear programming algorithm, and more generally on a straightforward maximum likelihood or maximum a posteriori formulation, which turns out to be a convex optimization problem (with no non-global local maxima) in many important cases. In addition, we develop methods for analyzing the uncertainty of these esti- mates. We demonstrate the accuracy of the method in a simple simulated coin-ﬂipping setting; in particular, the method is able to precisely track the evolution of the subject’s posterior distribution as more and more data are observed. We close by brieﬂy discussing an interesting connection to recent models of neural population coding.

Despite this increased generality, the method is relatively simple to implement, being based in the simplest case on a linear programming algorithm, and more generally on a straightforward maximum likelihood or maximum a posteriori formulation, which turns out to be a convex optimization problem (with no non-global local maxima) in many important cases. In addition, we develop methods for analyzing the uncertainty of these esti- mates. We demonstrate the accuracy of the method in a simple simulated coin-ﬂipping setting; in particular, the method is able to precisely track the evolution of the subject’s posterior distribution as more and more data are observed. We close by brieﬂy discussing an interesting connection to recent models of neural population coding.

paragraphs: This paper asks how a person's prior beliefs can be recovered from behavior in a psychophysics task. The approach assumes the behavior is optimal, or nearly optimal, from a Bayesian perspective. It then reasons backward from the observed behavior to the probability distribution that could have guided it.

The method is nonparametric: the prior need not belong to a predetermined family such as Gaussian distributions. Despite that flexibility, the simplest formulation uses linear programming. More general versions use maximum likelihood or maximum a posteriori estimation, and many important cases yield convex optimization problems without nonglobal local maxima. The authors also develop ways to quantify uncertainty in the recovered beliefs.

A simulated coin-flipping example demonstrates accurate inference, including precise tracking of the subject's evolving posterior as observations accumulate. The paper also briefly connects the approach to neural population coding models. Its main contribution is a computationally manageable method for estimating flexible belief distributions, with the behavioral interpretation resting on the stated assumption of near-Bayesian optimality.
summary.tldr: Assuming near-Bayesian-optimal behavior, the method infers flexible prior beliefs and quantifies uncertainty through tractable optimization.

title: Nonparametric inference of prior probabilities from Bayes-optimal behavior

abstract: Reliably recovering 3D human pose from monocular video requires constraints that bias the estimates towards typical human poses and motions. We define priors for people tracking using a Laplacian Eigenmaps Latent Variable Model (LELVM). LELVM is a probabilistic dimensionality reduction model that naturally combines the advantages of latent variable models---definining a multimodal probability density for latent and observed variables, and globally differentiable nonlinear mappings for reconstruction and dimensionality reduction---with those of spectral manifold learning methods---no local optima, ability to unfold highly nonlinear manifolds, and good practical scaling to latent spaces of high dimension. LELVM is computationally efficient, simple to learn from sparse training data, and compatible with standard probabilistic trackers such as particle filters. We analyze the performance of a LELVM-based probabilistic sigma point mixture tracker in several real and synthetic human motion sequences and demonstrate that LELVM provides sufficient constraints for robust operation in the presence of missing, noisy and ambiguous image measurements.

paragraphs: Recovering three-dimensional human pose from a single camera requires constraints that favor plausible poses and motions. This paper supplies those constraints through a Laplacian Eigenmaps Latent Variable Model. The model learns a probabilistic representation that can serve as a prior during tracking, helping interpret image measurements that may support several possible poses.

The model combines latent-variable modeling with spectral manifold learning. It represents multimodal probability densities and provides globally differentiable nonlinear mappings for reconstruction and dimensionality reduction. Its spectral component contributes learning without local optima, the ability to unfold highly nonlinear manifolds, and practical scaling to latent spaces with many dimensions.

The authors describe the model as computationally efficient, learnable from sparse training data, and compatible with standard probabilistic trackers such as particle filters. They evaluate a probabilistic sigma-point mixture tracker using the model on real and synthetic human-motion sequences. In those evaluations, the learned constraints are sufficient for robust tracking despite missing, noisy, and ambiguous image measurements, connecting the representation's properties to practical tracking behavior.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic Laplacian Eigenmaps model supplies pose constraints that support robust human tracking under difficult image measurements.

title: People Tracking with the Laplacian Eigenmaps Latent Variable Model

abstract: Under natural viewing conditions, human observers shift their gaze to allocate processing resources to subsets of the visual input. Many computational models have aimed at predicting such voluntary attentional shifts. Although the importance of high level stimulus properties (higher order statistics, semantics) stands undisputed, most models are based on low-level features of the input alone. In this study we recorded eye-movements of human observers while they viewed photographs of natural scenes. About two thirds of the stimuli contained at least one person. We demonstrate that a combined model of face detection and low-level saliency clearly outperforms a low-level model in predicting locations humans fixate. This is reflected in our finding fact that observes, even when not instructed to look for anything particular, fixate on a face with a probability of over 80% within their first two fixations (500ms). Remarkably, the model's predictive performance in images that do not contain faces is not impaired by spurious face detector responses, which is suggestive of a bottom-up mechanism for face detection. In summary, we provide a novel computational approach which combines high level object knowledge (in our case: face locations) with low-level features to successfully predict the allocation of attentional resources.

paragraphs: People direct their gaze toward selected parts of a scene, allocating visual processing to those locations. Many computational predictions of gaze rely on low-level image properties. This paper tests whether adding knowledge about faces improves those predictions, combining a face detector with a low-level saliency model.

The authors record eye movements while observers view natural-scene photographs, about two thirds of which contain at least one person. The combined model clearly outperforms the low-level model at predicting fixation locations. Observers also fixate on a face with probability above 80% within their first two fixations, roughly 500 milliseconds, even without instructions to search for anything specific.

On images without faces, false responses from the face detector do not impair the combined model's predictive performance. The authors interpret this as suggestive of a bottom-up face-detection mechanism. Overall, the study shows that incorporating face locations can improve gaze prediction, linking object-level information to where visual attention is allocated in the evaluated natural scenes.
summary.tldr: Combining face detection with low-level saliency improves predictions of human gaze in natural scenes.

title: Predicting human gaze using low-level saliency combined with face detection

abstract: Uncertainty is omnipresent when we perceive or interact with our environment, and the Bayesian framework provides computational methods for dealing with it. Mathematical models for Bayesian decision making typically require datastructures that are hard to implement in neural networks. This article shows that even the simplest and experimentally best supported type of synaptic plasticity, Hebbian learning, in combination with a sparse, redundant neural code, can in principle learn to infer optimal Bayesian decisions. We present a concrete Hebbian learning rule operating on log-probability ratios. Modulated by reward-signals, this Hebbian plasticity rule also provides a new perspective for understanding how Bayesian inference could support fast reinforcement learning in the brain. In particular we show that recent experimental results by Yang and Shadlen [1] on reinforcement learning of probabilistic inference in primates can be modeled in this way.

paragraphs: Bayesian decision-making provides a way to act under uncertainty, but its mathematical representations can be difficult to implement in neural networks. This paper asks whether a simple, biologically supported form of synaptic change could nevertheless learn optimal Bayesian decisions. Its proposed construction combines Hebbian learning with a sparse and redundant neural representation.

The authors give a concrete learning rule that operates on log-probability ratios. This connects synaptic adaptation to the quantities used in probabilistic decisions. Their central result is an in-principle demonstration: with the specified representation and learning mechanism, simple plasticity can support learning to make Bayesian-optimal choices.

The rule can also be modulated by reward signals, providing a possible account of how Bayesian inference supports rapid reinforcement learning in the brain. The authors show that it can model previously reported primate experiments on learning probabilistic inference. The contribution is a concrete connection between neural plasticity and probabilistic decision-making, while retaining the distinction between a possible mechanism and proof of the mechanism used by the brain.
summary.tldr: Hebbian plasticity with a sparse, redundant neural code can in principle learn Bayesian-optimal decisions and model reward-guided probabilistic learning.

title: Hebbian Learning of Bayes Optimal Decisions

abstract: We propose a Bayesian nonparametric approach to relating multiple time series via a set of latent, dynamical behaviors. Using a beta process prior, we allow data-driven selection of the size of this set, as well as the pattern with which behaviors are shared among time series. Via the Indian buffet process representation of the beta process predictive distributions, we develop an exact Markov chain Monte Carlo inference method. In particular, our approach uses the sum-product algorithm to efficiently compute Metropolis-Hastings acceptance probabilities, and explores new dynamical behaviors via birth/death proposals. We validate our sampling algorithm using several synthetic datasets, and also demonstrate promising unsupervised segmentation of visual motion capture data.

paragraphs: Multiple time series can contain related patterns of dynamic behavior without all using the same patterns. This paper models those relationships through a collection of hidden dynamical behaviors. A beta-process prior lets the data guide both the size of that collection and the pattern of sharing across the individual time series.

The authors develop an exact Markov chain Monte Carlo inference method using the Indian buffet process representation of the beta process's predictive distributions. The sampler explores additions and removals of behaviors through birth and death proposals. It uses the sum-product algorithm to compute Metropolis-Hastings acceptance probabilities efficiently, making this structural exploration part of the inference procedure.

Synthetic datasets are used to validate the sampling algorithm. An application to visual motion-capture data also shows promising unsupervised segmentation. The contribution links learning recurring dynamics with learning which sequences share them, so the model can discover a common behavioral vocabulary while allowing each time series to use its own subset.
summary.tldr: A beta-process model learns a data-driven collection of dynamical behaviors and how they are shared across time series.

title: Sharing Features among Dynamical Systems with Beta Processes

abstract: We present a model that describes the structure in the responses of different brain areas to a set of stimuli in terms of stimulus categories" (clusters of stimuli) and "functional units" (clusters of voxels). We assume that voxels within a unit respond similarly to all stimuli from the same category, and design a nonparametric hierarchical model to capture inter-subject variability among the units. The model explicitly captures the relationship between brain activations and fMRI time courses. A variational inference algorithm derived based on the model can learn categories, units, and a set of unit-category activation probabilities from data. When applied to data from an fMRI study of object recognition, the method finds meaningful and consistent clusterings of stimuli into categories and voxels into units."

The model explicitly captures the relationship between brain activations and fMRI time courses. A variational inference algorithm derived based on the model can learn categories, units, and a set of unit-category activation probabilities from data. When applied to data from an fMRI study of object recognition, the method finds meaningful and consistent clusterings of stimuli into categories and voxels into units."

paragraphs: This paper studies brain responses by grouping both the things people see and the brain locations that respond to them. Stimulus groups become categories, while groups of voxels become functional units. Learning both groupings provides a way to describe how patterns of brain activity relate to structure among the presented stimuli.

The central assumption is that voxels belonging to the same functional unit respond similarly to stimuli within a category. A nonparametric hierarchical model captures variation in these units across individuals. It also explicitly connects brain activations to the time courses measured by fMRI, making the observed signals part of the account of category-dependent responses.

The authors derive a variational inference algorithm that learns stimulus categories, functional units, and activation probabilities for each unit-category pairing. Applied to an object-recognition fMRI study, the method finds meaningful and consistent groupings of both stimuli and voxels. The result supports jointly organizing the stimulus and brain sides of the data while accommodating differences between subjects.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical model jointly discovers stimulus categories and functional brain units while accounting for variation across individuals.

title: Categories and Functional Units: An Infinite Hierarchical Model for Brain Activations

abstract: Accurate and detailed models of the progression of neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's (AD) are crucially important for reliable early diagnosis and the determination and deployment of effective treatments. In this paper, we introduce the ALPACA (Alzheimer's disease Probabilistic Cascades) model, a generative model linking latent Alzheimer's progression dynamics to observable biomarker data. In contrast with previous works which model disease progression as a fixed ordering of events, we explicitly model the variability over such orderings among patients which is more realistic, particularly for highly detailed disease progression models. We describe efficient learning algorithms for ALPACA and discuss promising experimental results on a real cohort of Alzheimer's patients from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative.
originalAbstract: Accurate and detailed models of the progression of neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's (AD) are crucially important for reliable early diagnosis and the determination and deployment of effective treatments. In this paper, we introduce the ALPACA (Alzheimer's disease Probabilistic Cascades) model, a generative model linking latent Alzheimer's progression dynamics to observable biomarker data. In contrast with previous works which model disease progression as a fixed ordering of events, we explicitly model the variability over such orderings among patients which is more realistic, particularly for highly detailed disease progression models. We describe efficient learning algorithms for ALPACA and discuss promising experimental results on a real cohort of Alzheimer's patients from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative.

paragraphs: The paper introduces ALPACA, a generative model connecting unobserved Alzheimer's disease progression to measurable biomarkers. The motivation is that detailed progression models could support earlier diagnosis and the development and deployment of effective treatments. ALPACA provides a probabilistic framework for relating those underlying disease dynamics to observed patient data.

Its central modeling choice is to allow the ordering of progression events to vary among patients. Earlier approaches described progression through a fixed event sequence. Representing variability across sequences allows the model to capture patient differences explicitly, which the authors argue is particularly relevant when progression is described in considerable detail.

The paper also presents efficient learning algorithms and reports promising experimental results using an Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative patient cohort. These results support investigating variable-order event cascades as a model of progression. The stated finding is promising performance on patient data; the abstract presents improved diagnosis and treatment as motivations for accurate progression models.
summary.tldr: ALPACA models patient-to-patient variation in Alzheimer's progression event order and links those hidden dynamics to observed biomarkers.

title: Probabilistic Event Cascades for Alzheimer's disease

abstract: Although human object recognition is supposedly robust to viewpoint, much research on human perception indicates that there is a preferred or “canonical” view of objects. This phenomenon was discovered more than 30 years ago but the canonical view of only a small number of categories has been validated experimentally. Moreover, the explanation for why humans prefer the canonical view over other views remains elusive. In this paper we ask: Can we use Internet image collections to learn more about canonical views? We start by manually finding the most common view in the results returned by Internet search engines when queried with the objects used in psychophysical experiments. Our results clearly show that the most likely view in the search engine corresponds to the same view preferred by human subjects in experiments. We also present a simple method to find the most likely view in an image collection and apply it to hundreds of categories. Using the new data we have collected we present strong evidence against the two most prominent formal theories of canonical views and provide novel constraints for new theories.

paragraphs: People can recognize objects from different viewpoints, yet they often prefer a particular view of an object. The paper investigates whether Internet image collections can help study these canonical views. This offers a way to extend an area where experimental validation had covered only a small number of object categories and the reasons for viewpoint preferences remained unclear.

The authors first manually identify the most common views in search-engine images for objects already used in human perception experiments. They find that the most frequent search-result view matches the view preferred by human participants. This correspondence provides evidence that the distribution of views in those collections is informative about the preferences measured experimentally.

They then introduce a simple method for finding the most likely view in an image collection and apply it to hundreds of categories. Using the expanded collection of observations, they present strong evidence against the two leading formal theories of canonical views. The work contributes both a broader source of evidence and constraints that future explanations of viewpoint preference should address.
summary.tldr: Common viewpoints in Internet images match tested human preferences and provide broader evidence challenging prominent theories of canonical views.

title: Learning about Canonical Views from Internet Image Collections

abstract: We propose a novel Bayesian approach to solve stochastic optimization problems that involve ﬁnding extrema of noisy, nonlinear functions. Previous work has focused on representing possible functions explicitly, which leads to a two-step procedure of ﬁrst, doing inference over the function space and second, ﬁnding the extrema of these functions. Here we skip the representation step and directly model the distribution over extrema. To this end, we devise a non-parametric conjugate prior where the natural parameter corresponds to a given kernel function and the sufﬁcient statistic is composed of the observed function values. The resulting posterior distribution directly captures the uncertainty over the maximum of the unknown function.

Previous work has focused on representing possible functions explicitly, which leads to a two-step procedure of ﬁrst, doing inference over the function space and second, ﬁnding the extrema of these functions. Here we skip the representation step and directly model the distribution over extrema. To this end, we devise a non-parametric conjugate prior where the natural parameter corresponds to a given kernel function and the sufﬁcient statistic is composed of the observed function values. paragraphs: Finding the best input to a noisy nonlinear function requires reasoning about an optimum that cannot be observed directly. The paper proposes a Bayesian approach that represents uncertainty about the maximizing argument itself. This places the unknown location of the optimum at the center of the statistical model.

The approach differs from a procedure that first represents possible functions and then finds an optimum for each one. Instead, it models a distribution over extrema directly. To make this possible, the authors construct a nonparametric conjugate prior. Its natural parameter corresponds to a kernel function, and its sufficient statistic is built from the observed function values.

The resulting posterior expresses uncertainty about the unknown function's optimum without the intermediate function-representation step. The significance is a change in what Bayesian inference targets: the quantity needed for optimization is modeled directly. The stated contribution is this prior-and-posterior construction for stochastic optimization, which connects noisy function observations to uncertainty over the maximizing argument.
summary.tldr: The paper constructs a Bayesian model that directly tracks uncertainty over a noisy function's maximizing argument.

title: A Nonparametric Conjugate Prior Distribution for the Maximizing Argument of a Noisy Function

abstract: Dropout and other feature noising schemes control overfitting by artificially corrupting the training data. For generalized linear models, dropout performs a form of adaptive regularization. Using this viewpoint, we show that the dropout regularizer is first-order equivalent to an $\LII$ regularizer applied after scaling the features by an estimate of the inverse diagonal Fisher information matrix. We also establish a connection to AdaGrad, an online learner, and find that a close relative of AdaGrad operates by repeatedly solving linear dropout-regularized problems. By casting dropout as regularization, we develop a natural semi-supervised algorithm that uses unlabeled data to create a better adaptive regularizer. We apply this idea to document classification tasks, and show that it consistently boosts the performance of dropout training, improving on state-of-the-art results on the IMDB reviews dataset.

paragraphs: Dropout controls overfitting by artificially corrupting training features. This paper explains its effect in generalized linear models through adaptive regularization: the corruption induces a penalty whose behavior depends on the data. That perspective turns a training procedure based on noise into something that can be studied through the optimization objective it produces.

The authors show a first-order equivalence between the dropout regularizer and an L2 regularizer after a feature scaling based on an estimate of inverse diagonal Fisher information. The first-order qualification matters because this is an approximation-level relationship. They also connect the analysis to AdaGrad, showing that a close relative repeatedly solves linear problems regularized by dropout.

The regularization view then motivates a semi-supervised algorithm. Unlabeled examples help construct a better adaptive regularizer, so data without labels can influence how the labeled learning problem is constrained. On document classification tasks, the authors report consistent improvements over dropout training and an improvement over the stated state of the art on the IMDB reviews dataset.
summary.tldr: Viewing dropout as adaptive regularization in generalized linear models leads to a semi-supervised method that improves reported document classification results.

title: Dropout Training as Adaptive Regularization

abstract: Discriminative methods for learning structured models have enabled wide-spread use of very rich feature representations. However, the computational cost of feature extraction is prohibitive for large-scale or time-sensitive applications, often dominating the cost of inference in the models. Significant efforts have been devoted to sparsity-based model selection to decrease this cost. Such feature selection methods control computation statically and miss the opportunity to fine-tune feature extraction to each input at run-time. We address the key challenge of learning to control fine-grained feature extraction adaptively, exploiting non-homogeneity of the data. We propose an architecture that uses a rich feedback loop between extraction and prediction. The run-time control policy is learned using efficient value-function approximation, which adaptively determines the value of information of features at the level of individual variables for each input. We demonstrate significant speedups over state-of-the-art methods on two challenging datasets. For articulated pose estimation in video, we achieve a more accurate state-of-the-art model that is simultaneously 4$\times$ faster while using only a small fraction of possible features, with similar results on an OCR task.

paragraphs: Structured prediction models can use rich features, but computing those features may cost more than making the prediction itself. Selecting a fixed subset reduces computation uniformly across inputs. This paper instead learns how to decide which features are worth extracting for each particular input and each individual variable within its structured output.

The proposed architecture creates a feedback loop between feature extraction and prediction. A learned runtime policy uses efficient value-function approximation to estimate the value of additional information. This allows feature choices to respond to differences among inputs, making computational effort adaptive rather than deciding all feature use before the input arrives.

Experiments on articulated pose estimation in video and optical character recognition demonstrate substantial speedups over the compared state-of-the-art methods. For pose estimation, the authors report a model that is more accurate and four times faster while using only a small fraction of the available features. Similar results are reported for recognition. These findings show that adaptive feature acquisition can improve the practical accuracy-and-computation tradeoff in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: A learned policy adaptively selects features during structured prediction, achieving a more accurate pose-estimation model that is four times faster in the reported evaluation.

title: Learning Adaptive Value of Information for Structured Prediction

abstract: We define a fairness solution criterion for multi-agent decision-making problems, where agents have local interests. This new criterion aims to maximize the worst performance of agents with consideration on the overall performance. We develop a simple linear programming approach and a more scalable game-theoretic approach for computing an optimal fairness policy. This game-theoretic approach formulates this fairness optimization as a two-player, zero-sum game and employs an iterative algorithm for finding a Nash equilibrium, corresponding to an optimal fairness policy. We scale up this approach by exploiting problem structure and value function approximation. Our experiments on resource allocation problems show that this fairness criterion provides a more favorable solution than the utilitarian criterion, and that our game-theoretic approach is significantly faster than linear programming.

This new criterion aims to maximize the worst performance of agents with consideration on the overall performance. We develop a simple linear programming approach and a more scalable game-theoretic approach for computing an optimal fairness policy. This game-theoretic approach formulates this fairness optimization as a two-player, zero-sum game and employs an iterative algorithm for finding a Nash equilibrium, corresponding to an optimal fairness policy. We scale up this approach by exploiting problem structure and value function approximation. Our experiments on resource allocation problems show that this fairness criterion provides a more favorable solution than the utilitarian criterion, and that our game-theoretic approach is significantly faster than linear programming.

paragraphs: When several agents have their own interests, a policy that achieves strong total performance can still leave some agents doing poorly. This paper defines a fairness criterion for sequential decision-making that aims to improve the worst agent performance while also considering overall performance. It makes the distribution of outcomes among agents part of the optimization objective.

The authors give two methods for computing an optimal fairness policy. One uses linear programming. The other recasts the optimization as a two-player zero-sum game and iteratively searches for a Nash equilibrium corresponding to an optimal fairness policy. Exploiting problem structure and approximating value functions makes the game-based approach more scalable.

Experiments on resource allocation problems find that the proposed criterion produces a more favorable solution than the utilitarian criterion under the study's evaluation. They also show that the game-theoretic method is significantly faster than linear programming. The results connect a specific notion of fairness to a practical computational approach, rather than treating fairness solely as a property assessed after choosing a policy.
summary.tldr: A fairness objective considers worst-agent and overall performance, with a game-theoretic solver that is faster than linear programming in resource allocation experiments.

title: Fairness in Multi-Agent Sequential Decision-Making

abstract: The use of M-estimators in generalized linear regression models in high dimensional settings requires risk minimization with hard L_0 constraints. Of the known methods, the class of projected gradient descent (also known as iterative hard thresholding (IHT)) methods is known to offer the fastest and most scalable solutions. However, the current state-of-the-art is only able to analyze these methods in extremely restrictive settings which do not hold in high dimensional statistical models. In this work we bridge this gap by providing the first analysis for IHT-style methods in the high dimensional statistical setting. Our bounds are tight and match known minimax lower bounds. Our results rely on a general analysis framework that enables us to analyze several popular hard thresholding style algorithms (such as HTP, CoSaMP, SP) in the high dimensional regression setting. Finally, we extend our analysis to the problem of low-rank matrix recovery.

In this work we bridge this gap by providing the first analysis for IHT-style methods in the high dimensional statistical setting. Our bounds are tight and match known minimax lower bounds. Our results rely on a general analysis framework that enables us to analyze several popular hard thresholding style algorithms (such as HTP, CoSaMP, SP) in the high dimensional regression setting. paragraphs: The paper studies high-dimensional regression with a hard limit on the number of nonzero parameters. Such a sparsity constraint makes estimation challenging because the method must select which parameters remain active while minimizing a loss. Iterative hard thresholding, also described as projected gradient descent, offers fast and scalable algorithms for this task.

The central contribution is theoretical. Earlier analyses required restrictive settings that did not hold in the high-dimensional statistical models considered here. The authors provide an analysis for IHT-style methods in this setting, with tight error bounds matching known minimax lower bounds. This connects the algorithms’ computational appeal to statistically optimal accuracy in the analyzed problems.

A general framework supports the analysis of several related algorithms, including HTP, CoSaMP, and SP, rather than addressing only one update rule. The authors also extend the analysis to low-rank matrix recovery, where the desired structure is a matrix with few independent directions. The work thus supplies shared theoretical tools for efficient procedures that enforce structural constraints directly during estimation.
summary.tldr: A general analysis gives hard-thresholding algorithms minimax-matching error bounds in high-dimensional estimation and extends to low-rank recovery.

title: On Iterative Hard Thresholding Methods for High-dimensional M-Estimation

abstract: We study an idealised sequential resource allocation problem. In each time step the learner chooses an allocation of several resource types between a number of tasks. Assigning more resources to a task increases the probability that it is completed. The problem is challenging because the alignment of the tasks to the resource types is unknown and the feedback is noisy. Our main contribution is the new setting and an algorithm with nearly-optimal regret analysis. Along the way we draw connections to the problem of minimising regret for stochastic linear bandits with heteroscedastic noise. We also present some new results for stochastic linear bandits on the hypercube that significantly out-performs existing work, especially in the sparse case.

Giving a task more resources increases its chance of completion. The learner must make these decisions without knowing how well each resource type aligns with each task, and the resulting feedback is noisy.

The main contribution is both this learning setting and an algorithm with a nearly optimal regret analysis. Regret measures the cost of decisions made while the learner is still discovering how to allocate resources effectively. The guarantee therefore addresses the cumulative consequences of learning through allocation, rather than only the quality of a final allocation.

The analysis connects the problem to stochastic linear bandits with heteroscedastic noise, meaning that observation noise need not have uniform variance. The authors also obtain new results for stochastic linear bandits on the hypercube, reporting substantial improvements over existing work, especially in sparse cases. These connections make the contribution relevant both to the resource-allocation formulation and to the associated bandit problems.
summary.tldr: A sequential multi-resource allocation model yields a nearly regret-optimal algorithm and improved results for related stochastic linear bandit problems.

title: Linear Multi-Resource Allocation with Semi-Bandit Feedback

abstract: To make sense of the world our brains must analyze high-dimensional datasets streamed by our sensory organs. Because such analysis begins with dimensionality reduction, modelling early sensory processing requires biologically plausible online dimensionality reduction algorithms. Recently, we derived such an algorithm, termed similarity matching, from a Multidimensional Scaling (MDS) objective function. However, in the existing algorithm, the number of output dimensions is set a priori by the number of output neurons and cannot be changed. Because the number of informative dimensions in sensory inputs is variable there is a need for adaptive dimensionality reduction. Here, we derive biologically plausible dimensionality reduction algorithms which adapt the number of output dimensions to the eigenspectrum of the input covariance matrix. We formulate three objective functions which, in the offline setting, are optimized by the projections of the input dataset onto its principal subspace scaled by the eigenvalues of the output covariance matrix. In turn, the output eigenvalues are computed as i) soft-thresholded, ii) hard-thresholded, iii) equalized thresholded eigenvalues of the input covariance matrix. In the online setting, we derive the three corresponding adaptive algorithms and map them onto the dynamics of neuronal activity in networks with biologically plausible local learning rules. Remarkably, in the last two networks, neurons are divided into two classes which we identify with principal neurons and interneurons in biological circuits.

This paper asks how a neural network could adjust the dimensionality of its representation as that information changes. It extends an earlier similarity-matching approach whose output dimensionality was fixed in advance by the number of output neurons.

The authors formulate three optimization objectives that connect this adaptation to the input covariance matrix: a description of how input variations occur together. In the offline setting, their solutions project data onto its principal subspace. In two of the resulting networks, neurons separate into classes identified with principal neurons and interneurons. The contribution is an objective-based account of adaptive dimensionality reduction that also yields plausible neural implementations.
summary.tldr: Three optimization objectives yield biologically plausible neural algorithms that adapt output dimensionality to the statistical structure of incoming data.

title: A Normative Theory of Adaptive Dimensionality Reduction in Neural Networks

abstract: For statistical learning in high dimension, sparse regularizations have proven useful to boost both computational and statistical efficiency. In some contexts, it is natural to handle more refined structures than pure sparsity, such as for instance group sparsity. Sparse-Group Lasso has recently been introduced in the context of linear regression to enforce sparsity both at the feature and at the group level. We propose the first (provably) safe screening rules for Sparse-Group Lasso, i.e., rules that allow to discard early in the solver features/groups that are inactive at optimal solution. Thanks to efficient dual gap computations relying on the geometric properties of $\epsilon$-norm, safe screening rules for Sparse-Group Lasso lead to significant gains in term of computing time for our coordinate descent implementation.

paragraphs: Sparse-Group Lasso is a linear regression method that encourages sparsity at two levels: individual features and groups of features. This is useful when variables have a meaningful group structure and the desired solution should select among both groups and their members. Computing that solution can still be demanding in high-dimensional problems.

The paper introduces provably safe screening rules that identify features or groups that will be inactive in the optimal solution. A solver can discard these components early, reducing the amount of work remaining. Safety is the crucial property: the screening rules certify inactivity at the optimum, making early removal compatible with solving the original optimization problem.

The rules rely on efficient dual-gap calculations using geometric properties of the epsilon-norm. The authors incorporate them into a coordinate descent implementation and report significant reductions in computing time. The contribution therefore improves how Sparse-Group Lasso is solved by using mathematical certificates to eliminate unnecessary computation while retaining its feature-level and group-level selection behavior.
summary.tldr: Provably safe screening removes inactive features and groups early, substantially accelerating the authors’ Sparse-Group Lasso solver.

title: GAP Safe Screening Rules for Sparse-Group Lasso

abstract: Understanding how humans perceive the likability of high-dimensional objects'' such as faces is an important problem in both cognitive science and AI/ML. Existing models generally assume these preferences to be fixed. However, psychologists have found human assessment of facial attractiveness to be context-dependent. Specifically, the classical Beauty-in-Averageness (BiA) effect, whereby a blended face is judged to be more attractive than the originals, is significantly diminished or reversed when the original faces are recognizable, or when the blend is mixed-race/mixed-gender and the attractiveness judgment is preceded by a race/gender categorization, respectively. This "Ugliness-in-Averageness" (UiA) effect has previously been explained via a qualitative disfluency account, which posits that the negative affect associated with the difficult race or gender categorization is inadvertently interpreted by the brain as a dislike for the face itself. In contrast, we hypothesize that human preference for an object is increased when it incurs lower encoding cost, in particular when its perceived {\it statistical typicality} is high, in consonance with Barlow's seminal efficient coding hypothesis.'' This statistical coding cost account explains both BiA, where facial blends generally have higher likelihood than ``parent faces'', and UiA, when the preceding context or task restricts face representation to a task-relevant subset of features, thus redefining statistical typicality and encoding cost within that subspace. We use simulations to show that our model provides a parsimonious, statistically grounded, and quantitative account of both BiA and UiA. We validate our model using experimental data from a gender categorization task. We also propose a novel experiment, based on model predictions, that will be able to arbitrate between the disfluency account and our statistical coding cost account of attractiveness.

paragraphs: Blending faces often makes the result appear more attractive, but this preference depends on context. Recognizing the original faces can weaken the effect, while categorizing race or gender before judging certain blends can reverse it. The paper seeks a statistical explanation for why averaging can produce different attractiveness judgments.

The authors hypothesize that people prefer objects requiring less encoding effort, particularly those perceived as statistically typical. A blend can appear attractive because it is more likely under the relevant face distribution. A preceding task can change which features enter the representation, however, changing what counts as typical within that restricted feature space. The same coding-cost principle can therefore account for both increased and decreased attractiveness.

Simulations provide a quantitative account of these opposing effects, and the authors validate the model with data from a gender categorization task. They also propose an experiment to distinguish their account from an explanation based on difficult categorization producing negative feelings. That experiment is a proposed test, while the presented evidence supports the statistical account as a model of contextual preference.
summary.tldr: A statistical coding-cost model explains how context can make blended faces seem either more or less attractive.

title: Beauty-in-averageness and its contextual modulations: A Bayesian statistical account

abstract: Analyzing the structure and function of proteins is a key part of understanding biology at the molecular and cellular level. In addition, a major engineering challenge is to design new proteins in a principled and methodical way. Current computational modeling methods for protein design are slow and often require human oversight and intervention. Here, we apply Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to the task of generating protein structures, toward application in fast de novo protein design. We encode protein structures in terms of pairwise distances between alpha-carbons on the protein backbone, which eliminates the need for the generative model to learn translational and rotational symmetries. We then introduce a convex formulation of corruption-robust 3D structure recovery to fold the protein structures from generated pairwise distance maps, and solve these problems using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers. We test the effectiveness of our models by predicting completions of corrupted protein structures and show that the method is capable of quickly producing structurally plausible solutions.

paragraphs: Computational protein design can be slow and require substantial human intervention. This paper investigates generative adversarial networks as a route toward quickly generating protein structures. The aim is to support principled design by learning to produce structural representations, with experiments assessing whether the resulting structures are plausible.

The model represents a protein through distances between pairs of alpha-carbon atoms along its backbone. Distances do not change when the entire structure is translated or rotated, so the generator does not need to learn those symmetries. This representation shifts the generation task from directly placing atoms in space to producing a map of their pairwise separations.

To convert generated distance maps into three-dimensional structures, the authors introduce a convex recovery formulation that is robust to corruption and solve it using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers. They evaluate the models by completing corrupted protein structures and report fast production of structurally plausible solutions. The stated evidence concerns structural completion and plausibility, supporting the broader motivation of fast de novo protein design.
summary.tldr: GAN-generated backbone distance maps and robust three-dimensional recovery quickly produce plausible completions of corrupted protein structures.

title: Generative modeling for protein structures

abstract: We present an approach to map utterances in conversation to logical forms, which will be executed on a large-scale knowledge base. To handle enormous ellipsis phenomena in conversation, we introduce dialog memory management to manipulate historical entities, predicates, and logical forms when inferring the logical form of current utterances. Dialog memory management is embodied in a generative model, in which a logical form is interpreted in a top-down manner following a small and flexible grammar. We learn the model from denotations without explicit annotation of logical forms, and evaluate it on a large-scale dataset consisting of 200K dialogs over 12.8M entities. Results verify the benefits of modeling dialog memory, and show that our semantic parsing-based approach outperforms a memory network based encoder-decoder model by a huge margin.
