paragraphs: Conversational questions often leave information unstated because earlier turns already supplied it. This paper addresses that problem by translating each utterance into a logical form that can be executed against a large knowledge base. Understanding a question therefore involves constructing an explicit query while recovering the context needed to make that query meaningful.

The approach maintains dialog memory containing earlier entities, predicates, and logical forms. A generative model uses this history while interpreting the current utterance, building its logical form from the top down according to a small, flexible grammar. Remembering previous query structure alongside the things being discussed gives the model resources for resolving the omissions common in conversation.

Training uses denotations, or the answers produced by logical forms, without requiring explicit annotations of those forms. Evaluation covers 200,000 dialogs involving 12.8 million entities. The reported results support the benefits of dialog memory and show a large advantage over a memory-network encoder-decoder model. The contribution combines contextual conversation handling with executable semantic structure at the scale of a large knowledge base.
summary.tldr: Dialog memory helps a semantic parser turn context-dependent conversational questions into executable knowledge-base queries.

title: Dialog-to-Action: Conversational Question Answering Over a Large-Scale Knowledge Base

abstract: Ridge leverage scores provide a balance between low-rank approximation and regularization, and are ubiquitous in randomized linear algebra and machine learning. Deterministic algorithms are also of interest in the moderately big data regime, because deterministic algorithms provide interpretability to the practitioner by having no failure probability and always returning the same results. We provide provable guarantees for deterministic column sampling using ridge leverage scores. The matrix sketch returned by our algorithm is a column subset of the original matrix, yielding additional interpretability. Like the randomized counterparts, the deterministic algorithm provides $(1+\epsilon)$ error column subset selection, $(1+\epsilon)$ error projection-cost preservation, and an additive-multiplicative spectral bound. We also show that under the assumption of power-law decay of ridge leverage scores, this deterministic algorithm is provably as accurate as randomized algorithms. Lastly, ridge regression is frequently used to regularize ill-posed linear least-squares problems. While ridge regression provides shrinkage for the regression coefficients, many of the coefficients remain small but non-zero. Performing ridge regression with the matrix sketch returned by our algorithm and a particular regularization parameter forces coefficients to zero and has a provable $(1+\epsilon)$ bound on the statistical risk. As such, it is an interesting alternative to elastic net regularization.

paragraphs: Large matrices can be compressed by selecting informative columns. This paper develops a deterministic selection method based on ridge leverage scores, which balance low-rank approximation with regularization. The resulting sketch contains actual columns of the original matrix, aiding interpretation, while deterministic selection produces repeatable results without sampling failure probability.

The authors prove approximation guarantees for column subset selection and preservation of projection costs, both with a factor of one plus epsilon. They also provide an additive-multiplicative spectral bound. Under the additional assumption that ridge leverage scores decay according to a power law, the deterministic method is provably as accurate as randomized algorithms. That comparison explicitly depends on the stated decay assumption.

Using the selected columns and a particular regularization parameter instead forces coefficients to zero while retaining a provable one-plus-epsilon statistical risk bound. This makes the approach an interesting alternative to elastic net regularization, combining column selection with controlled prediction risk.
summary.tldr: Deterministic ridge leverage score sampling yields interpretable matrix sketches with approximation guarantees and supports sparse ridge regression with bounded statistical risk.

title: Ridge Regression and Provable Deterministic Ridge Leverage Score Sampling

abstract: We present two new algorithms, ASYNCADA and HEDGEHOG, for asynchronous sparse online and stochastic optimization. ASYNCADA is, to our knowledge, the first asynchronous stochastic optimization algorithm with finite-time data-dependent convergence guarantees for generic convex constraints. In addition, ASYNCADA: (a) allows for proximal (i.e., composite-objective) updates and adaptive step-sizes; (b) enjoys any-time convergence guarantees without requiring an exact global clock; and (c) when the data is sufficiently sparse, its convergence rate for (non-)smooth, (non-)strongly-convex, and even a limited class of non-convex objectives matches the corresponding serial rate, implying a theoretical “linear speed-up”. The second algorithm, HEDGEHOG, is an asynchronous parallel version of the Exponentiated Gradient (EG) algorithm for optimization over the probability simplex (a.k.a. Hedge in online learning), and, to our knowledge, the first asynchronous algorithm enjoying linear speed-ups under sparsity with non-SGD-style updates. Unlike previous work, ASYNCADA and HEDGEHOG and their convergence and speed-up analyses are not limited to individual coordinate-wise (i.e., “box-shaped”) constraints or smooth and strongly-convex objectives. Underlying both results is a generic analysis framework that is of independent interest, and further applicable to distributed and delayed feedback optimization

paragraphs: Asynchronous optimization lets parallel workers make progress without exact synchronization, but proving useful guarantees becomes harder with richer objectives and constraints. This paper introduces ASYNCADA and HEDGEHOG for sparse online and stochastic optimization. Their analyses extend beyond coordinate-wise box constraints and objectives that are both smooth and strongly convex.

ASYNCADA handles generic convex constraints, proximal updates for composite objectives, and adaptive step sizes. It has finite-time, data-dependent guarantees and anytime convergence guarantees without requiring an exact global clock. With sufficiently sparse data, its convergence rate matches the corresponding serial rate across several objective classes, including a limited nonconvex class, yielding a theoretical linear speedup.

HEDGEHOG is an asynchronous parallel form of Exponentiated Gradient for optimization over the probability simplex. It likewise achieves linear speedups under sparsity, extending this benefit to updates outside the usual stochastic-gradient form. A common analysis framework underlies both algorithms and also applies to distributed optimization and delayed feedback. Sparsity is therefore a stated condition enabling the speedup results across these broader settings.
summary.tldr: ASYNCADA and HEDGEHOG extend asynchronous optimization guarantees to broader constraints and updates, with theoretical linear speedups under sparsity.

title: Think out of the "Box": Generically-Constrained Asynchronous Composite Optimization and Hedging

abstract: When agents interact with a complex environment, they must form and maintain beliefs about the relevant aspects of that environment. We propose a way to efficiently train expressive generative models in complex environments. We show that a predictive algorithm with an expressive generative model can form stable belief-states in visually rich and dynamic 3D environments. More precisely, we show that the learned representation captures the layout of the environment as well as the position and orientation of the agent. Our experiments show that the model substantially improves data-efficiency on a number of reinforcement learning (RL) tasks compared with strong model-free baseline agents. We find that predicting multiple steps into the future (overshooting), in combination with an expressive generative model, is critical for stable representations to emerge. In practice, using expressive generative models in RL is computationally expensive and we propose a scheme to reduce this computational burden, allowing us to build agents that are competitive with model-free baselines.

paragraphs: An agent operating in a complex environment needs a useful internal account of its surroundings. The paper studies how predictive learning with an expressive generative environment model can build such belief states. It focuses on visually rich, dynamic three-dimensional environments, where the representation must retain meaningful spatial information.

The learned representation captures the environment's layout together with the agent's position and orientation. The authors find that predicting several steps ahead, called overshooting, is critical for stable representations when combined with an expressive generative model. This connects the stability of the internal state to a training objective that reaches beyond the immediately following observation.

On several reinforcement learning tasks, the model substantially improves data efficiency relative to strong model-free agents. The authors also address the computational expense of expressive generative modeling with a scheme that reduces the burden and enables agents competitive with model-free baselines. The findings distinguish two practical issues: obtaining useful learning from available experience and making the predictive machinery affordable enough to use. The proposed framework addresses both in the reported environments.
summary.tldr: Expressive generative models trained to predict multiple steps ahead form stable spatial belief states and improve reinforcement learning data efficiency.

title: Shaping Belief States with Generative Environment Models for RL

abstract: In this paper, we study large-scale convex optimization algorithms based on the Newton method applied to regularized generalized self-concordant losses, which include logistic regression and softmax regression. We first prove that our new simple scheme based on a sequence of problems with decreasing regularization parameters is provably globally convergent, that this convergence is linear with a constant factor which scales only logarithmically with the condition number. In the parametric setting, we obtain an algorithm with the same scaling than regular first-order methods but with an improved behavior, in particular in ill-conditioned problems. Second, in the non parametric machine learning setting, we provide an explicit algorithm combining the previous scheme with Nystr\"om projections techniques, and prove that it achieves optimal generalization bounds with a time complexity of order O(n df), a memory complexity of order O(df^2) and no dependence on the condition number, generalizing the results known for least squares regression. Here n is the number of observations and df is the associated degrees of freedom. In particular, this is the first large-scale algorithm to solve logistic and softmax regressions in the non-parametric setting with large condition numbers and theoretical guarantees.

In the parametric setting, we obtain an algorithm with the same scaling than regular first-order methods but with an improved behavior, in particular in ill-conditioned problems. Here n is the number of observations and df is the associated degrees of freedom. In particular, this is the first large-scale algorithm to solve logistic and softmax regressions in the non-parametric setting with large condition numbers and theoretical guarantees.

paragraphs: The paper studies Newton-based optimization for regularized convex losses in the generalized self-concordant family, including logistic and softmax regression. Its focus is on ill-conditioned problems, where optimization is sensitive to uneven curvature. The proposed scheme solves a sequence of problems whose regularization parameters gradually decrease, connecting successive optimization tasks.

The authors prove global convergence and a linear convergence rate whose constant factor grows only logarithmically with the condition number. In the parametric setting, the algorithm has the same scaling as standard first-order methods while offering improved behavior, especially for ill-conditioned problems. The result links a simple regularization schedule to a favorable dependence on conditioning.

For nonparametric learning, the scheme is combined with Nyström projections. The resulting algorithm achieves optimal generalization bounds with O(n df) time and O(df²) memory, without dependence on the condition number in these stated complexities. Here n counts observations and df denotes degrees of freedom. This extends guarantees previously available for least-squares regression to the broader loss setting studied.
summary.tldr: A decreasing-regularization Newton scheme provides convergence guarantees and efficient nonparametric learning for difficult convex regression problems.

title: Globally Convergent Newton Methods for Ill-conditioned Generalized Self-concordant Losses

abstract: Graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have recently received wide attentions, due to their successful applications in different graph tasks and different domains. Training GCNs for a large graph, however, is still a challenge. Original full-batch GCN training requires calculating the representation of all the nodes in the graph per GCN layer, which brings in high computation and memory costs. To alleviate this issue, several sampling-based methods are proposed to train GCNs on a subset of nodes. Among them, the node-wise neighbor-sampling method recursively samples a fixed number of neighbor nodes, and thus its computation cost suffers from exponential growing neighbor size across layers; while the layer-wise importance-sampling method discards the neighbor-dependent constraints, and thus the nodes sampled across layer suffer from sparse connection problem. To deal with the above two problems, we propose a new effective sampling algorithm called LAyer-Dependent ImportancE Sampling (LADIES). Based on the sampled nodes in the upper layer, LADIES selects nodes that are in the neighborhood of these nodes and uses the constructed bipartite graph to compute the importance probability. Then, it samples a fixed number of nodes according to the probability for the whole layer, and recursively conducts such procedure per layer to construct the whole computation graph. We prove theoretically and experimentally, that our proposed sampling algorithm outperforms the previous sampling methods regarding both time and memory. Furthermore, LADIES is shown to have better generalization accuracy than original full-batch GCN, due to its stochastic nature.
originalAbstract: Graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have recently received wide attentions, due to their successful applications in different graph tasks and different domains. Training GCNs for a large graph, however, is still a challenge. Original full-batch GCN training requires calculating the representation of all the nodes in the graph per GCN layer, which brings in high computation and memory costs. To alleviate this issue, several sampling-based methods are proposed to train GCNs on a subset of nodes. Among them, the node-wise neighbor-sampling method recursively samples a fixed number of neighbor nodes, and thus its computation cost suffers from exponential growing neighbor size across layers; while the layer-wise importance-sampling method discards the neighbor-dependent constraints, and thus the nodes sampled across layer suffer from sparse connection problem. To deal with the above two problems, we propose a new effective sampling algorithm called LAyer-Dependent ImportancE Sampling (LADIES). Based on the sampled nodes in the upper layer, LADIES selects nodes that are in the neighborhood of these nodes and uses the constructed bipartite graph to compute the importance probability. Then, it samples a fixed number of nodes according to the probability for the whole layer, and recursively conducts such procedure per layer to construct the whole computation graph. We prove theoretically and experimentally, that our proposed sampling algorithm outperforms the previous sampling methods regarding both time and memory. Furthermore, LADIES is shown to have better generalization accuracy than original full-batch GCN, due to its stochastic nature.

paragraphs: Training a graph convolutional network on every node at every layer can require substantial memory and computation. Sampling reduces that workload, but existing strategies introduce different problems. Sampling neighbors separately for each node can cause the required neighborhood to expand exponentially with depth. Sampling layers independently can leave too few useful connections between them.

LADIES makes sampling at one layer depend on the nodes already selected in the layer above. It restricts candidates to their neighbors and constructs a bipartite graph to calculate importance probabilities. It then samples a fixed number of nodes for the whole layer and repeats this process to build the computation graph.

This design combines a controlled layer size with explicit attention to connectivity across layers. The paper reports theoretical and experimental advantages over previous sampling approaches in both runtime and memory use. It also reports better generalization accuracy than full-batch GCN training, attributing that result to the method's stochastic nature. Sampling thus contributes to both training efficiency and predictive performance in the reported evaluation.
summary.tldr: LADIES samples graph-network layers conditionally on one another to control computation while preserving useful connections.

title: Layer-Dependent Importance Sampling for Training Deep and Large Graph Convolutional Networks

abstract: This paper studies Learning from Observations (LfO) for imitation learning with access to state-only demonstrations. In contrast to Learning from Demonstration (LfD) that involves both action and state supervisions, LfO is more practical in leveraging previously inapplicable resources (e.g., videos), yet more challenging due to the incomplete expert guidance. In this paper, we investigate LfO and its difference with LfD in both theoretical and practical perspectives. We first prove that the gap between LfD and LfO actually lies in the disagreement of inverse dynamics models between the imitator and expert, if following the modeling approach of GAIL. More importantly, the upper bound of this gap is revealed by a negative causal entropy which can be minimized in a model-free way. We term our method as Inverse-Dynamics-Disagreement-Minimization (IDDM) which enhances the conventional LfO method through further bridging the gap to LfD. Considerable empirical results on challenging benchmarks indicate that our method attains consistent improvements over other LfO counterparts.

paragraphs: Learning from observations asks an agent to imitate an expert using demonstrated states without access to the expert's actions. This could make resources such as videos useful for imitation, but removes part of the guidance available in learning from state-action demonstrations. The paper investigates what that missing information means theoretically and how to reduce its practical impact.

Within the modeling approach of generative adversarial imitation learning, the authors show that the gap between the two settings lies in disagreement between the expert's and imitator's inverse dynamics models. These models concern the actions associated with state changes. The result gives a specific mathematical account of what state-only imitation fails to constrain.

The authors identify negative causal entropy as an upper bound on this gap that can be minimized without a dynamics model. Their resulting method, Inverse-Dynamics-Disagreement-Minimization, augments conventional learning from observations with this objective. Experiments on challenging benchmarks show consistent improvements over other observation-only methods, supporting the usefulness of narrowing the theoretically identified gap.
summary.tldr: IDDM improves state-only imitation by minimizing an entropy-based bound on inverse-dynamics disagreement within a GAIL-based formulation.

title: Imitation Learning from Observations by Minimizing Inverse Dynamics Disagreement

abstract: We study the problem of maximizing a non-monotone, non-negative submodular function subject to a matroid constraint. The prior best-known deterministic approximation ratio for this problem is $\frac{1}{4}-\epsilon$ under $\mathcal{O}(({n^4}/{\epsilon})\log n)$ time complexity. We show that this deterministic ratio can be improved to $\frac{1}{4}$ under $\mathcal{O}(nr)$ time complexity, and then present a more practical algorithm dubbed TwinGreedyFast which achieves $\frac{1}{4}-\epsilon$ deterministic ratio in nearly-linear running time of $\mathcal{O}(\frac{n}{\epsilon}\log\frac{r}{\epsilon})$. Our approach is based on a novel algorithmic framework of simultaneously constructing two candidate solution sets through greedy search, which enables us to get improved performance bounds by fully exploiting the properties of independence systems. As a byproduct of this framework, we also show that TwinGreedyFast achieves $\frac{1}{2p+2}-\epsilon$ deterministic ratio under a $p$-set system constraint with the same time complexity. To showcase the practicality of our approach, we empirically evaluated the performance of TwinGreedyFast on two network applications, and observed that it outperforms the state-of-the-art deterministic and randomized algorithms with efficient implementations for our problem.

paragraphs: This paper studies selecting a feasible set to maximize a nonnegative submodular objective under a matroid constraint. Submodularity expresses diminishing returns, while non-monotonicity allows adding an element to reduce the objective. The goal is a fast deterministic algorithm with a guaranteed fraction of the best feasible value, without relying on random choices.

The central idea is to build two candidate sets simultaneously through greedy search. This framework yields a one-quarter approximation in O(nr) time, improving both the guarantee and runtime of the previous deterministic result. Its faster variant, TwinGreedyFast, achieves a one-quarter-minus-epsilon guarantee in O((n/epsilon) log(r/epsilon)) time, trading a small amount of approximation quality for nearly linear scaling.

The framework also covers p-set system constraints, where TwinGreedyFast guarantees a fraction of 1/(2p+2) minus epsilon with the same runtime expression. Experiments on two network applications report better performance than the compared efficiently implemented deterministic and randomized algorithms. Those empirical findings complement the worst-case guarantees: the method offers both a provable floor on solution quality and favorable results in the tested applications.
summary.tldr: Building two greedy candidate sets yields faster deterministic approximation algorithms for constrained non-monotone submodular maximization.

title: Deterministic Approximation for Submodular Maximization over a Matroid in Nearly Linear Time

abstract: This paper describes a simple technique to analyze Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and create interpretable controls for image synthesis, such as change of viewpoint, aging, lighting, and time of day. We identify important latent directions based on Principal Component Analysis (PCA) applied either in latent space or feature space. Then, we show that a large number of interpretable controls can be defined by layer-wise perturbation along the principal directions. Moreover, we show that BigGAN can be controlled with layer-wise inputs in a StyleGAN-like manner. We show results on different GANs trained on various datasets, and demonstrate good qualitative matches to edit directions found through earlier supervised approaches.

paragraphs: GANSpace investigates how to turn a generative adversarial network's internal variation into understandable image-editing controls. The desired changes include viewpoint, age, lighting, and time of day. Instead of treating image synthesis as an opaque mapping, the method analyzes directions in the generator's latent or feature space that can support meaningful edits.

The central tool is principal component analysis, which identifies prominent directions of variation. The authors then perturb the generator along those directions at particular layers. Choosing where to apply a direction provides many interpretable controls, making the layer of intervention part of the editing mechanism as well as the direction itself.

The paper demonstrates results across different GANs and training datasets, with qualitative matches to edit directions previously obtained through supervised approaches. It also shows that BigGAN can accept layer-wise control in a manner resembling StyleGAN. These findings make a relatively simple statistical analysis useful for exploring generator behavior and constructing controls whose visible effects people can understand.
summary.tldr: GANSpace uses principal components and layer-wise perturbations to discover understandable controls for generated images.

title: GANSpace: Discovering Interpretable GAN Controls

abstract: While Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) hold the promise of being flexible, well-calibrated statistical models, inference often requires approximations whose consequences are poorly understood. We study the quality of common variational methods in approximating the Bayesian predictive distribution. For single-hidden layer ReLU BNNs, we prove a fundamental limitation in function-space of two of the most commonly used distributions defined in weight-space: mean-field Gaussian and Monte Carlo dropout. We find there are simple cases where neither method can have substantially increased uncertainty in between well-separated regions of low uncertainty. We provide strong empirical evidence that exact inference does not have this pathology, hence it is due to the approximation and not the model. In contrast, for deep networks, we prove a universality result showing that there exist approximate posteriors in the above classes which provide flexible uncertainty estimates. However, we find empirically that pathologies of a similar form as in the single-hidden layer case can persist when performing variational inference in deeper networks. Our results motivate careful consideration of the implications of approximate inference methods in BNNs.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks aim to express uncertainty through a predictive distribution, but computing that distribution usually requires approximation. This paper investigates how two common approximations, mean-field Gaussian distributions and Monte Carlo dropout, constrain the uncertainty that a network can represent. The distinction between limitations of the model and of inference is central.

For ReLU networks with one hidden layer, the authors prove that simple cases exist where neither approximation can substantially raise uncertainty between separated regions of low uncertainty. Strong empirical evidence indicates that exact inference avoids this pathology. That comparison points to the approximation as the source of the problem, rather than to an inherent inability of the Bayesian network.

For deeper networks, the paper proves that approximate posteriors in these same families exist that can express flexible uncertainty. Yet experiments show that variational inference can still produce similar pathological behavior. The results distinguish representational possibility from the outcome of fitting: a sufficiently expressive approximation family does not by itself ensure that training finds a satisfactory uncertainty estimate.
summary.tldr: Common Bayesian neural-network approximations restrict shallow-network uncertainty, while deeper networks can express flexible uncertainty that variational training may still fail to recover.

title: On the Expressiveness of Approximate Inference in Bayesian Neural Networks

abstract: A decision tree is commonly restricted to use a single hyperplane to split the covariate space at each of its internal nodes. It often requires a large number of nodes to achieve high accuracy. In this paper, we propose convex polytope trees (CPT) to expand the family of decision trees by an interpretable generalization of their decision boundary. The splitting function at each node of CPT is based on the logical disjunction of a community of differently weighted probabilistic linear decision-makers, which also geometrically corresponds to a convex polytope in the covariate space. We use a nonparametric Bayesian prior at each node to infer the community's size, encouraging simpler decision boundaries by shrinking the number of polytope facets. We develop a greedy method to efficiently construct CPT and scalable end-to-end training algorithms for the tree parameters when the tree structure is given. We empirically demonstrate the efficiency of CPT over existing state-of-the-art decision trees in several real-world classification and regression tasks from diverse domains.

paragraphs: A conventional decision tree often divides the input space using one hyperplane at each internal node. Complex boundaries can consequently require many nodes. Convex polytope trees expand the kinds of splits available at a node while aiming to preserve an interpretable description of the decision boundary.

Each split combines a group of differently weighted probabilistic linear decision-makers through a logical disjunction. Geometrically, the construction corresponds to a convex polytope in the input space. A nonparametric Bayesian prior determines the size of this group and encourages simpler boundaries by shrinking the number of polytope facets. This lets the model adjust the complexity of individual splits.

The authors provide a greedy procedure for building the tree and scalable algorithms for jointly training its parameters once the structure is fixed. Experiments across real-world classification and regression tasks demonstrate efficiency relative to existing state-of-the-art decision trees. The approach therefore changes both the expressive capacity of a tree node and the way that capacity is controlled, rather than relying only on adding more nodes.
summary.tldr: Convex polytope trees learn more expressive, interpretable node boundaries while using Bayesian shrinkage to encourage simpler splits.

title: Convex Polytope Trees

abstract: Researchers and practitioners in the field of reinforcement learning (RL) frequently leverage parallel computation, which has led to a plethora of new algorithms and systems in the last few years. In this paper, we re-examine the challenges posed by distributed RL and try to view it through the lens of an old idea: distributed dataflow. We show that viewing RL as a dataflow problem leads to highly composable and performant implementations. We propose RLlib Flow, a hybrid actor-dataflow programming model for distributed RL, and validate its practicality by porting the full suite of algorithms in RLlib, a widely adopted distributed RL library. Concretely, RLlib Flow provides 2-9$\times$ code savings in real production code and enables the composition of multi-agent algorithms not possible by end users before. The open-source code is available as part of RLlib at https://github.com/ray-project/ray/tree/master/rllib.

paragraphs: Distributed reinforcement learning uses parallel computation, but expressing and combining its algorithms creates programming challenges. This paper revisits those challenges through distributed dataflow: organizing computation around the movement of data between processing stages. The authors argue that this perspective supports implementations that are both performant and easier to compose.

They introduce RLlib Flow, a programming model combining actors with dataflow. Its purpose is to provide a common structure for implementing distributed reinforcement learning algorithms and combining their components. To test whether the model works beyond isolated examples, the authors port the full algorithm suite of RLlib, a widely adopted distributed reinforcement learning library.

The reported results include two- to ninefold code savings in production implementations. RLlib Flow also lets end users compose multi-agent algorithms in ways that were previously unavailable to them. These outcomes concern the software structure used to build reinforcement learning systems: the contribution is an implementation and composition model, with practicality demonstrated across an existing library's algorithms.
summary.tldr: RLlib Flow combines actors and distributed dataflow to make reinforcement learning implementations more compact and composable.

title: RLlib Flow: Distributed Reinforcement Learning is a Dataflow Problem

abstract: The cooperative bandit problem is increasingly becoming relevant due to its applications in large-scale decision-making. However, most research for this problem focuses exclusively on the setting with perfect communication, whereas in most real-world distributed settings, communication is often over stochastic networks, with arbitrary corruptions and delays. In this paper, we study cooperative bandit learning under three typical real-world communication scenarios, namely, (a) message-passing over stochastic time-varying networks, (b) instantaneous reward-sharing over a network with random delays, and (c) message-passing with adversarially corrupted rewards, including byzantine communication. For each of these environments, we propose decentralized algorithms that achieve competitive performance, along with near-optimal guarantees on the incurred group regret as well. Furthermore, in the setting with perfect communication, we present an improved delayed-update algorithm that outperforms the existing state-of-the-art on various network topologies. Finally, we present tight network-dependent minimax lower bounds on the group regret. Our proposed algorithms are straightforward to implement and obtain competitive empirical performance.

paragraphs: Cooperative bandit learning lets multiple decision makers share information while learning which choices yield good rewards. Much of the research assumes communication works perfectly. This paper examines what happens when the communication network changes randomly, messages are delayed, or shared reward information is deliberately corrupted, bringing the learning problem closer to distributed operating conditions.

The authors study three communication scenarios separately: message passing over stochastic time-varying networks, reward sharing with random delays, and message passing with adversarial reward corruption, including Byzantine communication. They propose decentralized algorithms for each scenario and provide near-optimal guarantees on group regret, the collective performance loss measured against the relevant benchmark.

The paper also improves the perfect-communication setting through a delayed-update algorithm that outperforms existing approaches across various network topologies. Tight network-dependent minimax lower bounds characterize unavoidable group regret, helping assess how close the algorithms are to the best achievable performance. The authors report competitive empirical results and straightforward implementations. Together, the results connect communication conditions and network structure to both achievable learning performance and fundamental limits.
summary.tldr: Decentralized cooperative bandit algorithms achieve near-optimal group regret guarantees under changing networks, communication delays, and corrupted rewards.

title: One More Step Towards Reality: Cooperative Bandits with Imperfect Communication

abstract: We propose a fast algorithm for the probabilistic solution of boundary value problems (BVPs), which are ordinary differential equations subject to boundary conditions. In contrast to previous work, we introduce a Gauss-Markov prior and tailor it specifically to BVPs, which allows computing a posterior distribution over the solution in linear time, at a quality and cost comparable to that of well-established, non-probabilistic methods. Our model further delivers uncertainty quantification, mesh refinement, and hyperparameter adaptation. We demonstrate how these practical considerations positively impact the efficiency of the scheme. Altogether, this results in a practically usable probabilistic BVP solver that is (in contrast to non-probabilistic algorithms) natively compatible with other parts of the statistical modelling tool-chain.

paragraphs: Boundary value problems are ordinary differential equations whose solutions must satisfy specified boundary conditions. This paper develops a probabilistic solver that returns a distribution over possible solutions, making uncertainty part of the numerical result. Its goal is to make this approach practical at a quality and computational cost comparable to established non-probabilistic solvers.

The key modeling choice is a Gauss-Markov prior tailored specifically to boundary value problems. This structure allows the posterior distribution over the solution to be computed in linear time. The method also incorporates uncertainty quantification, mesh refinement, and hyperparameter adaptation, bringing several practical numerical decisions into the same probabilistic framework.

The authors demonstrate that these practical components improve the scheme's efficiency. The resulting solver combines competitive numerical quality and cost with uncertainty information and native compatibility with other statistical modeling components. This matters when a differential-equation solution is one part of a larger statistical workflow: the solver represents its output probabilistically, rather than providing only a single numerical approximation for subsequent analysis.
summary.tldr: A tailored Gauss-Markov model enables linear-time probabilistic boundary value solving with uncertainty estimates and practical adaptive features.

title: Linear-Time Probabilistic Solution of Boundary Value Problems

abstract: Actor-critic methods are widely used in offline reinforcement learningpractice, but are not so well-understood theoretically. We propose a newoffline actor-critic algorithm that naturally incorporates the pessimism principle, leading to several key advantages compared to the state of the art. The algorithm can operate when the Bellman evaluation operator is closed with respect to the action value function of the actor's policies; this is a more general setting than the low-rank MDP model. Despite the added generality, the procedure is computationally tractable as it involves the solution of a sequence of second-order programs.We prove an upper bound on the suboptimality gap of the policy returned by the procedure that depends on the data coverage of any arbitrary, possibly data dependent comparator policy.The achievable guarantee is complemented with a minimax lower bound that is matching up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns a policy from existing data. Actor-critic methods are widely used for this purpose, but their theoretical foundations are less developed than their practical adoption. This paper proposes an offline actor-critic algorithm that incorporates pessimism and establishes guarantees for the policy it returns.

The algorithm operates under a closure condition on the Bellman evaluation operator for the action-value functions associated with the actor's policies. This setting is more general than the low-rank Markov decision process model. Despite that broader scope, the procedure remains computationally tractable through a sequence of second-order programs, linking the theoretical construction to an explicit optimization procedure.

The performance bound depends on how well the available data cover a comparator policy. That comparator can be arbitrary and may itself depend on the data, making the guarantee flexible about the policy used for comparison. A minimax lower bound matches the achievable guarantee up to logarithmic factors, indicating that the analysis captures the fundamental difficulty of the studied setting closely.
summary.tldr: A pessimistic offline actor-critic algorithm provides tractable optimization and nearly matching performance bounds tied to comparator-policy data coverage.

title: Provable Benefits of Actor-Critic Methods for Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Variational autoencoder (VAE) is a deep generative model for unsupervised learning, allowing to encode observations into the meaningful latent space. VAE is prone to catastrophic forgetting when tasks arrive sequentially, and only the data for the current one is available. We address this problem of continual learning for VAEs. It is known that the choice of the prior distribution over the latent space is crucial for VAE in the non-continual setting. We argue that it can also be helpful to avoid catastrophic forgetting. We learn the approximation of the aggregated posterior as a prior for each task. This approximation is parametrised as an additive mixture of distributions induced by an encoder evaluated at trainable pseudo-inputs. We use a greedy boosting-like approach with entropy regularisation to learn the components. This method encourages components diversity, which is essential as we aim at memorising the current task with the fewest components possible. Based on the learnable prior, we introduce an end-to-end approach for continual learning of VAEs and provide empirical studies on commonly used benchmarks (MNIST, Fashion MNIST, NotMNIST) and CelebA datasets. For each dataset, the proposed method avoids catastrophic forgetting in a fully automatic way.

paragraphs: A variational autoencoder learns a latent representation from which it can generate observations. When tasks arrive sequentially and only the current task's data remain available, learning new material can erase earlier capabilities. BooVAE addresses this continual learning problem by making the prior distribution over the latent space a central part of remembering tasks.

For each task, the method learns a prior that approximates the aggregated posterior, the collection of latent distributions produced when the encoder processes that task's observations. It represents this approximation as an additive mixture. Each component comes from evaluating the encoder on a trainable pseudo-input, giving the method adjustable building blocks for representing the task.

A greedy procedure resembling boosting adds components, while entropy regularization encourages their diversity. The goal is to remember each task with as few components as possible. The authors integrate this learned prior into an end-to-end continual learning system and evaluate it on MNIST, Fashion MNIST, NotMNIST, and CelebA. They report automatic avoidance of catastrophic forgetting on each tested dataset, supporting the prior's role as a practical memory mechanism.
summary.tldr: BooVAE learns compact mixture priors to preserve earlier tasks when a variational autoencoder learns from sequential datasets.

title: BooVAE: Boosting Approach for Continual Learning of VAE

abstract: Recent work in iterative voting has defined the additive dynamic price of anarchy (ADPoA) as the difference in social welfare between the truthful and worst-case equilibrium profiles resulting from repeated strategic manipulations. While iterative plurality has been shown to only return alternatives with at most one less initial votes than the truthful winner, it is less understood how agents' welfare changes in equilibrium. To this end, we differentiate agents' utility from their manipulation mechanism and determine iterative plurality's ADPoA in the worst- and average-cases. We first prove that the worst-case ADPoA is linear in the number of agents. To overcome this negative result, we study the average-case ADPoA and prove that equilibrium winners have a constant order welfare advantage over the truthful winner in expectation. Our positive results illustrate the prospect for social welfare to increase due to strategic manipulation.

Our positive results illustrate the prospect for social welfare to increase due to strategic manipulation.

paragraphs: Iterative voting lets voters repeatedly change their ballots strategically until an equilibrium is reached. A winner’s initial vote count does not by itself describe how much voters value that outcome. This paper studies social welfare in iterative plurality while distinguishing voters’ utilities from the mechanism governing their strategic changes.

The authors analyze the additive dynamic price of anarchy, which compares welfare under truthful voting with welfare at the worst equilibrium reached through repeated manipulation. In the worst case, this welfare gap grows linearly with the number of voters. Strategic behavior can therefore have substantial negative consequences in unfavorable cases.

The average-case analysis gives a different result: equilibrium winners have a constant-order welfare advantage over the truthful winner in expectation. This establishes a positive possibility for strategic manipulation despite the worst-case bound. The distinction between the two analyses is essential. The paper shows that strategic behavior can improve expected welfare in the analyzed average-case setting, while retaining the possibility of large losses in particular cases.
summary.tldr: Iterative plurality can improve welfare in expectation under the paper’s average-case analysis, despite welfare losses that scale linearly in the worst case.

title: Strategic Behavior is Bliss: Iterative Voting Improves Social Welfare

abstract: In this study, we consider the infinite-horizon, discounted cost, optimal control of stochastic nonlinear systems with separable cost and constraints in the state and input variables. Using the linear-time Legendre transform, we propose a novel numerical scheme for implementation of the corresponding value iteration (VI) algorithm in the conjugate domain. Detailed analyses of the convergence, time complexity, and error of the proposed algorithm are provided. In particular, with a discretization of size $X$ and $U$ for the state and input spaces, respectively, the proposed approach reduces the time complexity of each iteration in the VI algorithm from $O(XU)$ to $O(X+U)$, by replacing the minimization operation in the primal domain with a simple addition in the conjugate domain.

paragraphs: The paper studies optimal control of stochastic nonlinear systems over an unlimited time horizon, with future costs discounted. It focuses on problems whose costs and constraints are separable between state and input variables. This structure is central to the proposed way of accelerating value iteration, an algorithm that repeatedly updates estimates of optimal future cost.

With discretized state and input spaces, a conventional value iteration update has time complexity O(XU), where X and U are their respective sizes. The proposed method moves the computation into a conjugate domain using a linear-time Legendre transform. In that representation, a minimization operation becomes a simple addition, reducing each iteration's complexity to O(X+U).

The authors analyze convergence, computational complexity, and approximation error. The speed improvement concerns the cost of each iteration for the stated problem structure, making the relationship between state-space and input-space sizes especially important. By replacing their multiplicative contribution with an additive one, the method offers a more efficient numerical route to approximate dynamic programming under the paper's separability assumptions.
summary.tldr: For the studied separable control problems, a conjugate-domain formulation reduces value iteration's per-iteration complexity from O(XU) to O(X+U).

title: Fast Approximate Dynamic Programming for Infinite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes

abstract: The reliable identification of the “best” arm while keeping the sample complexity as low as possible is a common task in the field of multi-armed bandits. In the multi-dueling variant of multi-armed bandits, where feedback is provided in the form of a winning arm among as set of k chosen ones, a reasonable notion of best arm is the generalized Condorcet winner (GCW). The latter is an the arm that has the greatest probability of being the winner in each subset containing it. In this paper, we derive lower bounds on the sample complexity for the task of identifying the GCW under various assumptions. As a by-product, our lower bound results provide new insights for the special case of dueling bandits (k = 2). We propose the Dvoretzky–Kiefer–Wolfowitz tournament (DKWT) algorithm, which we prove to be nearly optimal. In a numerical study, we show that DKWT empirically outperforms current state-of-the-art algorithms, even in the special case of dueling bandits or under a Plackett-Luce assumption on the feedback mechanism.

paragraphs: In multi-dueling bandits, a learner selects a group of options and observes which option wins. The goal is to identify the best option reliably while making as few comparisons as possible. This paper uses the generalized Condorcet winner as its definition of best: an option with the greatest winning probability in every comparison subset containing it.

The authors derive lower bounds on how many samples identifying this winner requires under various assumptions. These bounds describe fundamental information requirements, providing a reference for assessing an algorithm’s efficiency. The analysis also yields new insights into ordinary dueling bandits, where each comparison contains only two options.

The proposed Dvoretzky–Kiefer–Wolfowitz tournament algorithm, or DKWT, is proved nearly optimal. A numerical study finds that it outperforms the state-of-the-art algorithms considered, including in pairwise comparisons and under a Plackett-Luce feedback assumption. The paper thus combines limits on what any method can accomplish with an algorithm approaching those limits and empirical evidence of its effectiveness.
summary.tldr: DKWT nearly optimally identifies a generalized Condorcet winner from group-comparison feedback, supported by lower bounds and numerical results.

title: Identification of the Generalized Condorcet Winner in Multi-dueling Bandits

abstract: Recently, hypergraphs have attracted a lot of attention due to their ability to capture complex relations among entities. The insurgence of hypergraphs has resulted in data of increasing size and complexity that exhibit interesting small-scale and local structure, e.g., small-scale communities and localized node-ranking around a given set of seed nodes. Popular and principled ways to capture the local structure are the local hypergraph clustering problem and the related seed set expansion problem. In this work, we propose the first local diffusion method that achieves edge-size-independent Cheeger-type guarantee for the problem of local hypergraph clustering while applying to a rich class of higher-order relations that covers a number of previously studied special cases. Our method is based on a primal-dual optimization formulation where the primal problem has a natural network flow interpretation, and the dual problem has a cut-based interpretation using the $\ell_2$-norm penalty on associated cut-costs. We demonstrate the new technique is significantly better than state-of-the-art methods on both synthetic and real-world data.

paragraphs: Hypergraphs represent relations that can involve several entities at once. This paper studies how to find local structure within them, such as a small community near a chosen set of seed nodes. Local clustering and seed-set expansion provide ways to focus on these nearby structures as hypergraph data become larger and more complex.

The proposed local diffusion method comes with a Cheeger-type guarantee, connecting the diffusion approach to the quality of a resulting cluster boundary. Its guarantee is independent of hyperedge size and applies to a broad class of higher-order relations covering several previously studied cases. The authors identify this combination as a first for local hypergraph diffusion.

The method is built from paired optimization problems. The primal formulation has a network-flow interpretation, while the dual uses cuts and an L2 penalty on associated cut costs. These complementary views give the diffusion procedure its mathematical structure. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world data report significantly better performance than state-of-the-art methods, supporting the approach beyond its theoretical guarantee.
summary.tldr: A flow-based local hypergraph diffusion method combines an edge-size-independent clustering guarantee with strong reported empirical performance.

title: Local Hyper-Flow Diffusion

abstract: Stylized dialogue generation, which aims to generate a given-style response for an input context, plays a vital role in intelligent dialogue systems. Considering there is no parallel data between the contexts and the responses of target style S_1, existing works mainly use back translation to generate stylized synthetic data for training, where the data about context, target style S_1 and an intermediate style S_0 is used. However, the interaction among these texts is not fully exploited, and the pseudo contexts are not adequately modeled. To overcome the above difficulties, we propose multi-pass dual learning (MPDL), which leverages the duality among the context, response of style S_1 and response of style S_0. MPDL builds mappings among the above three domains, where the context should be reconstructed by the MPDL framework, and the reconstruction error is used as the training signal. To evaluate the quality of synthetic data, we also introduce discriminators that effectively measure how a pseudo sequence matches the specific domain, and the evaluation result is used as the weight for that data. Evaluation results indicate that our method obtains significant improvement over previous baselines.

paragraphs: Stylized dialogue generation aims to produce a response in a requested style while remaining connected to its conversational context. The paper considers the absence of paired contexts and target-style responses. Existing approaches create synthetic training pairs through back translation, but the authors argue that they insufficiently model generated contexts and interactions among the available text domains.

Multi-pass dual learning builds mappings among three domains: contexts, target-style responses, and responses in an intermediate style. The framework must reconstruct the context, and reconstruction error supplies a training signal. This uses relationships among all three domains to guide learning when direct target-style training pairs are unavailable.

The method also introduces discriminators to assess whether a synthetic sequence fits its intended domain. Their assessments determine how much weight the corresponding synthetic data receives during training. Evaluations report significant improvements over previous baselines. The contribution combines reconstruction-based learning with explicit assessment of generated training data, addressing both how synthetic examples are produced and how strongly they influence the dialogue model.
summary.tldr: Multi-pass dual learning improves stylized dialogue by reconstructing contexts across text domains and weighting synthetic examples by domain fit.

title: Stylized Dialogue Generation with Multi-Pass Dual Learning

abstract: Benchmark datasets play a central role in the organization of machine learning research. They coordinate researchers around shared research problems and serve as a measure of progress towards shared goals. Despite the foundational role of benchmarking practices in this field, relatively little attention has been paid to the dynamics of benchmark dataset use and reuse, within or across machine learning subcommunities. In this paper, we dig into these dynamics. We study how dataset usage patterns differ across machine learning subcommunities and across time from 2015-2020. We find increasing concentration on fewer and fewer datasets within task communities, significant adoption of datasets from other tasks, and concentration across the field on datasets that have been introduced by researchers situated within a small number of elite institutions. Our results have implications for scientific evaluation, AI ethics, and equity/access within the field.

paragraphs: Benchmark datasets help organize machine learning research by giving communities shared problems and measures of progress. This paper studies how those resources are actually used and reused. It examines differences among research communities and changes over the period from 2015 to 2020, treating dataset adoption itself as an object of investigation.

The authors find that individual task communities increasingly concentrate on fewer datasets. They also observe substantial use of datasets originally associated with other tasks. Together, these patterns show both concentration around common resources and movement of resources across research boundaries, revealing how benchmark use changes beyond the setting in which a dataset first appeared.

Across the field, usage is also concentrated on datasets introduced by researchers at a small number of elite institutions. The authors identify implications for scientific evaluation, AI ethics, and equity and access. The study makes clear that benchmark choices are part of the organization of research: they influence which shared resources become central to evaluating progress.
summary.tldr: An analysis of dataset use finds growing concentration, substantial reuse across tasks, and field-wide reliance on datasets from a few elite institutions.

title: Reduced, Reused and Recycled: The Life of a Dataset in Machine Learning Research

abstract: Knowledge distillation is an effective approach to learn compact models (students) with the supervision of large and strong models (teachers). As empirically there exists a strong correlation between the performance of teacher and student models, it is commonly believed that a high performing teacher is preferred. Consequently, practitioners tend to use a well trained network or an ensemble of them as the teacher. In this paper, we observe that an intermediate model, i.e., a checkpoint in the middle of the training procedure, often serves as a better teacher compared to the fully converged model, although the former has much lower accuracy. More surprisingly, a weak snapshot ensemble of several intermediate models from a same training trajectory can outperform a strong ensemble of independently trained and fully converged models, when they are used as teachers. We show that this phenomenon can be partially explained by the information bottleneck principle: the feature representations of intermediate models can have higher mutual information regarding the input, and thus contain more ``dark knowledge'' for effective distillation. We further propose an optimal intermediate teacher selection algorithm based on maximizing the total task-related mutual information. Experiments verify its effectiveness and applicability. Our code is available at https://github.com/LeapLabTHU/CheckpointKD.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a compact student using guidance from a larger teacher. A natural selection rule is to choose the most accurate teacher available. This paper challenges that rule by observing that an intermediate training checkpoint often teaches better than the fully converged model, even when the checkpoint has much lower accuracy.

The same effect can appear with ensembles. Several intermediate snapshots from one training trajectory can outperform an ensemble of independently trained, fully converged models when used as teachers. The authors partially explain this through the information bottleneck principle: intermediate representations can retain more mutual information about the input, leaving more useful knowledge available for transfer.

Building on that explanation, the paper proposes an intermediate-teacher selection algorithm based on maximizing total task-related mutual information. Experiments support its effectiveness and applicability. The findings distinguish a model's ability to predict correctly from its ability to teach another model. They suggest that saved checkpoints can be valuable distillation resources, without claiming that intermediate teachers always outperform fully trained ones.
summary.tldr: Intermediate training checkpoints can teach students better than more accurate final models, motivating information-based teacher selection.

title: Efficient Knowledge Distillation from Model Checkpoints

abstract: Polynomial Networks (PNs) have demonstrated promising performance on face and image recognition recently. However, robustness of PNs is unclear and thus obtaining certificates becomes imperative for enabling their adoption in real-world applications. Existing verification algorithms on ReLU neural networks (NNs) based on classical branch and bound (BaB) techniques cannot be trivially applied to PN verification. In this work, we devise a new bounding method, equipped with BaB for global convergence guarantees, called Verification of Polynomial Networks or VPN for short. One key insight is that we obtain much tighter bounds than the interval bound propagation (IBP) and DeepT-Fast [Bonaert et al., 2021] baselines. This enables sound and complete PN verification with empirical validation on MNIST, CIFAR10 and STL10 datasets. We believe our method has its own interest to NN verification. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/megaelius/PNVerification.

paragraphs: Polynomial networks have shown promising recognition performance, but that does not establish their robustness. This paper addresses the need for formal certificates by developing a verification method specifically for these networks. Existing branch-and-bound verifiers for ReLU networks cannot simply be transferred to the polynomial setting.

The proposed method, Verification of Polynomial Networks, combines a new bounding procedure with branch and bound. Bounds constrain the possible behavior of a network over regions considered during verification, while branch and bound organizes the global search. The paper reports much tighter bounds than interval bound propagation and DeepT-Fast, making the bounding component a central part of the contribution.

With branch and bound, the method obtains global convergence guarantees and enables sound and complete verification of polynomial networks. These are properties of the verification procedure, rather than a claim that every polynomial network is robust. Empirical validation uses MNIST, CIFAR10, and STL10. Together, the theoretical and experimental results provide a way to assess robustness formally for a network family that existing verification tools do not straightforwardly handle.
summary.tldr: VPN combines tighter bounds with branch and bound to provide sound and complete verification for polynomial networks.

title: Sound and Complete Verification of Polynomial Networks

abstract: The quintessential model-based reinforcement-learning agent iteratively refines its estimates or prior beliefs about the true underlying model of the environment. Recent empirical successes in model-based reinforcement learning with function approximation, however, eschew the true model in favor of a surrogate that, while ignoring various facets of the environment, still facilitates effective planning over behaviors. Recently formalized as the value equivalence principle, this algorithmic technique is perhaps unavoidable as real-world reinforcement learning demands consideration of a simple, computationally-bounded agent interacting with an overwhelmingly complex environment, whose underlying dynamics likely exceed the agent's capacity for representation. In this work, we consider the scenario where agent limitations may entirely preclude identifying an exactly value-equivalent model, immediately giving rise to a trade-off between identifying a model that is simple enough to learn while only incurring bounded sub-optimality. To address this problem, we introduce an algorithm that, using rate-distortion theory, iteratively computes an approximately-value-equivalent, lossy compression of the environment which an agent may feasibly target in lieu of the true model. We prove an information-theoretic, Bayesian regret bound for our algorithm that holds for any finite-horizon, episodic sequential decision-making problem. Crucially, our regret bound can be expressed in one of two possible forms, providing a performance guarantee for finding either the simplest model that achieves a desired sub-optimality gap or, alternatively, the best model given a limit on agent capacity.

Value equivalence offers a way to focus on details relevant to evaluating behavior. This paper considers the harder situation in which the agent cannot even represent an exactly value-equivalent model and must accept some loss in decision quality.

The proposed algorithm uses rate-distortion theory to construct an approximately value-equivalent compression of the environment. It repeatedly selects a simplified model that balances how much information must be learned against the resulting sub-optimality. The guarantee can be expressed in two ways: finding the simplest model compatible with a desired sub-optimality gap, or finding the best model under a capacity limit. These formulations give complementary accounts of the same tradeoff between limited representation and effective decisions.
summary.tldr: A rate-distortion algorithm trades environment-model complexity against decision quality, with Bayesian regret guarantees for finite-horizon episodic problems.

title: Deciding What to Model: Value-Equivalent Sampling for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Finding accurate solutions to the Schrödinger equation is the key unsolved challenge of computational chemistry. Given its importance for the development of new chemical compounds, decades of research have been dedicated to this problem, but due to the large dimensionality even the best available methods do not yet reach the desired accuracy.Recently the combination of deep learning with Monte Carlo methods has emerged as a promising way to obtain highly accurate energies and moderate scaling of computational cost. In this paper we significantly contribute towards this goal by introducing a novel deep-learning architecture that achieves 40-70% lower energy error at 6x lower computational cost compared to previous approaches. Using our method we establish a new benchmark by calculating the most accurate variational ground state energies ever published for a number of different atoms and molecules.We systematically break down and measure our improvements, focusing in particular on the effect of increasing physical prior knowledge.We surprisingly find that increasing the prior knowledge given to the architecture can actually decrease accuracy.

paragraphs: Accurately solving the Schrödinger equation is a central challenge in computational chemistry because the problem has very high dimensionality. Deep learning combined with Monte Carlo methods offers a promising route to accurate energy estimates at a manageable computational cost. This paper introduces an architecture intended to improve both sides of that tradeoff.

The authors report energy errors 40–70% lower than previous approaches while using six times less computation. They also calculate what they describe as the most accurate published variational ground-state energies for several atoms and molecules. These findings concern the tested chemical systems and the reported comparisons, establishing new reference results for those cases.

Beyond proposing an architecture, the paper systematically separates and measures the sources of improvement. A particular focus is the amount of physical prior knowledge built into the model. The authors find that adding more such knowledge can reduce accuracy. This makes architectural assumptions an empirical design question: physically motivated structure can be useful, but increasing it does not necessarily improve the computed energies.
summary.tldr: A new neural architecture improves quantum energy accuracy and computational cost while showing that additional physical prior knowledge can reduce accuracy.

title: Gold-standard solutions to the Schrödinger equation using deep learning: How much physics do we need?

abstract: Training convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with a strict 1-Lipschitz constraint under the l_{2} norm is useful for adversarial robustness, interpretable gradients and stable training. 1-Lipschitz CNNs are usually designed by enforcing each layer to have an orthogonal Jacobian matrix (for all inputs) to prevent the gradients from vanishing during backpropagation. However, their performance often significantly lags behind that of heuristic methods to enforce Lipschitz constraints where the resulting CNN is not provably 1-Lipschitz. In this work, we reduce this gap by introducing (a) a procedure to certify robustness of 1-Lipschitz CNNs by replacing the last linear layer with a 1-hidden layer MLP that significantly improves their performance for both standard and provably robust accuracy, (b) a method to significantly reduce the training time per epoch for Skew Orthogonal Convolution (SOC) layers (>30\% reduction for deeper networks) and (c) a class of pooling layers using the mathematical property that the l_{2} distance of an input to a manifold is 1-Lipschitz. Using these methods, we significantly advance the state-of-the-art for standard and provable robust accuracies on CIFAR-10 (gains of +1.79\% and +3.82\%) and similarly on CIFAR-100 (+3.78\% and +4.75\% across all networks.

paragraphs: A strictly 1-Lipschitz convolutional network limits how much its output can change relative to an input change measured in the l2 norm. Such constraints support adversarial robustness, interpretable gradients, and stable training. However, networks with provable constraints have often performed worse than approaches that enforce them only heuristically. This paper introduces three techniques to reduce that gap.

First, the authors replace the final linear layer with a multilayer perceptron containing one hidden layer and provide a robustness-certification procedure for this design. Second, they accelerate training of Skew Orthogonal Convolution layers. Third, they introduce pooling layers based on the fact that distance to a manifold is a 1-Lipschitz function.

The methods improve both ordinary accuracy and provably robust accuracy. Reported gains are 1.79 and 3.82 percentage points on CIFAR-10, and 3.78 and 4.75 on CIFAR-100, respectively. Training time per epoch for deeper networks using the SOC improvement falls by more than 30%. Together, these results address prediction quality, certification, and computational cost within the constrained-network setting.
summary.tldr: New output layers, pooling constructions, and faster orthogonal convolutions improve accuracy and certified l2 robustness.

title: Improved techniques for deterministic l2 robustness

abstract: Regularization can mitigate the generalization gap between training and inference by introducing inductive bias. Existing works have already proposed various inductive biases from diverse perspectives. However, none of them explores inductive bias from the perspective of class-dependent response distribution of individual neurons. In this paper, we conduct a substantial analysis of the characteristics of such distribution. Based on the analysis results, we articulate the Neuron Steadiness Hypothesis: the neuron with similar responses to instances of the same class leads to better generalization. Accordingly, we propose a new regularization method called Neuron Steadiness Regularization (NSR) to reduce neuron intra-class response variance. Based on the Complexity Measure, we theoretically guarantee the effectiveness of NSR for improving generalization. We conduct extensive experiments on Multilayer Perceptron, Convolutional Neural Networks, and Graph Neural Networks with popular benchmark datasets of diverse domains, which show that our Neuron Steadiness Regularization consistently outperforms the vanilla version of models with significant gain and low additional computational overhead.

Based on the analysis results, we articulate the Neuron Steadiness Hypothesis: the neuron with similar responses to instances of the same class leads to better generalization. Accordingly, we propose a new regularization method called Neuron Steadiness Regularization (NSR) to reduce neuron intra-class response variance. Based on the Complexity Measure, we theoretically guarantee the effectiveness of NSR for improving generalization. We conduct extensive experiments on Multilayer Perceptron, Convolutional Neural Networks, and Graph Neural Networks with popular benchmark datasets of diverse domains, which show that our Neuron Steadiness Regularization consistently outperforms the vanilla version of models with significant gain and low additional computational overhead.

paragraphs: Regularization introduces preferences about how a model should behave to help it generalize beyond training examples. This paper investigates a preference at the level of individual neurons: how consistently a neuron responds to examples belonging to the same class. The authors analyze these class-dependent response distributions as a source of inductive bias.

Their Neuron Steadiness Hypothesis proposes that similar responses within a class lead to better generalization. Neuron Steadiness Regularization implements this idea by reducing the variance of each neuron’s responses among same-class examples. The paper also provides a theoretical guarantee for the method’s generalization benefit based on a complexity measure.

Experiments cover multilayer perceptrons, convolutional networks, and graph neural networks across benchmark datasets from different domains. The regularized versions consistently outperform their unregularized counterparts in those experiments, with significant gains and little additional computation. The findings support neuron-level response consistency as a useful regularization target across the evaluated model families.
summary.tldr: Neuron Steadiness Regularization reduces within-class response variance and improves generalization across the tested neural network families.

title: Neuron with Steady Response Leads to Better Generalization

abstract: The Past Extragradient (PEG) [Popov, 1980] method, also known as the Optimistic Gradient method, has known a recent gain in interest in the optimization community with the emergence of variational inequality formulations for machine learning. Recently, in the unconstrained case, Golowich et al. [2020] proved that a $O(1/N)$ last-iterate convergence rate in terms of the squared norm of the operator can be achieved for Lipschitz and monotone operators with a Lipchitz Jacobian. In this work, by introducing a novel analysis through potential functions, we show that (i) this $O(1/N)$ last-iterate convergence can be achieved without any assumption on the Jacobian of the operator, and (ii) it can be extended to the constrained case, which was not derived before even under Lipschitzness of the Jacobian. The proof is significantly different from the one known from Golowich et al. [2020], and its discovery was computer-aided. Those results close the open question of the last iterate convergence of PEG for monotone variational inequalities.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes Past Extragradient, also known as the Optimistic Gradient method, for monotone variational inequalities. Its focus is last-iterate convergence: whether the algorithm's current output approaches a solution at a controlled rate. This matters because a guarantee for the final iterate directly describes the output available when the algorithm stops.

Their proof uses new potential functions and was discovered with computer assistance. The contribution is a broader convergence analysis of an existing method, resolving the stated open question for monotone variational inequalities and showing that the earlier derivative regularity requirement was unnecessary.
summary.tldr: A new analysis establishes Optimistic Gradient last-iterate convergence without Jacobian assumptions and extends the result to constrained problems.

title: Last-Iterate Convergence of Optimistic Gradient Method for Monotone Variational Inequalities

abstract: Detecting which nodes in graphs are outliers is a relatively new machine learning task with numerous applications. Despite the proliferation of algorithms developed in recent years for this task, there has been no standard comprehensive setting for performance evaluation. Consequently, it has been difficult to understand which methods work well and when under a broad range of settings. To bridge this gap, we present—to the best of our knowledge—the first comprehensive benchmark for unsupervised outlier node detection on static attributed graphs called BOND, with the following highlights. (1) We benchmark the outlier detection performance of 14 methods ranging from classical matrix factorization to the latest graph neural networks. (2) Using nine real datasets, our benchmark assesses how the different detection methods respond to two major types of synthetic outliers and separately to “organic” (real non-synthetic) outliers. (3) Using an existing random graph generation technique, we produce a family of synthetically generated datasets of different graph sizes that enable us to compare the running time and memory usage of the different outlier detection algorithms. Based on our experimental results, we discuss the pros and cons of existing graph outlier detection algorithms, and we highlight opportunities for future research. Importantly, our code is freely available and meant to be easily extendable: https://github.com/pygod-team/pygod/tree/main/benchmark

BOND supplies a comprehensive benchmark for unsupervised detection on static graphs with node attributes, helping organize evidence about which approaches work well under different conditions.

The benchmark compares 14 methods, spanning classical matrix factorization and graph neural networks. It uses nine real datasets and evaluates two major kinds of artificially introduced outliers separately from naturally occurring outliers. This distinction matters because performance on constructed anomalies and performance on real anomalies answer different questions about a detector's usefulness.
