paragraphs: GIC estimates physical properties from visual observations by connecting a reconstructed object’s geometry to a simulation representation. The central idea is to use 3D Gaussians for more than visual reconstruction: their shape and attributes also inform a continuum model that can participate in physical simulation. This gives the estimation process explicit geometric guidance.

A dynamic Gaussian framework uses motion factorization to reconstruct the object as Gaussian point sets at different times. A coarse-to-fine filling procedure then turns that reconstruction into density fields. From these fields, the method extracts the object’s continuum and surface while incorporating attributes from the Gaussian representation. This builds the bridge between visual reconstruction and simulation.

The resulting continuum can render object masks during simulation, providing two-dimensional shape evidence alongside the extracted surfaces. These masks help guide the estimation of physical properties by connecting simulated shape to observed shape. The authors report leading performance across multiple benchmarks and metrics, and include real-world demonstrations. The contribution is an integrated pipeline in which visual geometry remains useful throughout physical identification.
summary.tldr: GIC connects dynamic Gaussian reconstruction with continuum simulation to use visual shape evidence when estimating physical properties.

title: GIC: Gaussian-Informed Continuum for Physical Property Identification and Simulation

abstract: Two competing paradigms exist for self-supervised learning of data representations. Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) is a class of architectures in which semantically similar inputs are encoded into representations that are predictive of each other. A recent successful approach that falls under the JEPA framework is self-distillation, where an online encoder is trained to predict the output of the target encoder, sometimes with a lightweight predictor network. This is contrasted with the Masked Auto Encoder (MAE) paradigm, where an encoder and decoder are trained to reconstruct missing parts of the input in ambient space rather than its latent representation. A common motivation for using the JEPA approach over MAE is that the JEPA objective prioritizes abstract features over fine-grained pixel information (which can be unpredictable and uninformative). In this work, we seek to understand the mechanism behind this empirical observation by analyzing deep linear models. We uncover a surprising mechanism: in a simplified linear setting where both approaches learn similar representations, JEPAs are biased to learn high influence features, or features characterized by having high regression coefficients. Our results point to a distinct implicit bias of predicting in latent space that may shed light on its success in practice.

paragraphs: Self-supervised representation learning can predict either internal representations or missing parts of the original input. Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures, or JEPAs, follow the first approach. Masked autoencoders follow the second. A common motivation for JEPAs is that predicting representations may emphasize abstract information over fine details that are difficult to predict or uninformative.

This paper investigates the mechanism behind that intuition using deep linear models. It focuses on self-distillation, where an online encoder learns to predict a target encoder’s output, sometimes through an additional predictor. The simplified setting lets the authors examine the learning bias associated with prediction in representation space.

Even in a linear setting where the two approaches learn similar representations, the analysis finds a distinctive JEPA bias toward high-influence features, characterized by large regression coefficients. The result identifies a difference in what learning favors despite the similarity of the resulting representations. Because the analysis concerns simplified linear models, it offers a possible explanation for practical success rather than a universal account of nonlinear systems.
summary.tldr: A deep linear analysis finds that JEPA-style prediction favors high-influence features, offering a possible explanation for its practical behavior.

title: How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks

abstract: Reconstructing past events requires reasoning across long time horizons. To figure out what happened, humans draw on prior knowledge about the world and human behavior and integrate insights from various sources of evidence including visual, language, and auditory cues. We introduce MARPLE, a benchmark for evaluating long-horizon inference capabilities using multi-modal evidence. Our benchmark features agents interacting with simulated households, supporting vision, language, and auditory stimuli, as well as procedurally generated environments and agent behaviors. Inspired by classic ``whodunit'' stories, we ask AI models and human participants to infer which agent caused a change in the environment based on a step-by-step replay of what actually happened. The goal is to correctly identify the culprit as early as possible. Our findings show that human participants outperform both traditional Monte Carlo simulation methods and an LLM baseline (GPT-4) on this task. Compared to humans, traditional inference models are less robust and performant, while GPT-4 has difficulty comprehending environmental changes. We analyze factors influencing inference performance and ablate different modes of evidence, finding that all modes are valuable for performance. Overall, our experiments demonstrate that the long-horizon, multimodal inference tasks in our benchmark present a challenge to current models. Project website: https://marple-benchmark.github.io/.

paragraphs: MARPLE tests whether an observer can reconstruct responsibility for an event using evidence spread over time. Its scenarios place agents in simulated households and ask which agent caused a change in the environment. Observers receive a step-by-step replay, with the goal of identifying the responsible agent as early as possible.

The benchmark includes visual, language, and auditory evidence, along with procedurally generated environments and agent behaviors. This creates a setting where successful inference involves combining different kinds of observations across a longer sequence. The mystery-style task makes the evaluation concrete: participants must use accumulating evidence to attribute an observed change to an agent.

Human participants outperform both traditional Monte Carlo simulation methods and a GPT-4 baseline. The traditional methods show weaker robustness and performance, while GPT-4 struggles to understand environmental changes. Removing different evidence modes shows that each contributes to performance. These findings establish the benchmark's tasks as a challenge for the evaluated models and highlight the importance of integrating multiple evidence sources.
summary.tldr: MARPLE tests long-horizon, multimodal event reconstruction in simulated households, where humans outperform the evaluated inference methods and GPT-4 baseline.

title: MARPLE: A Benchmark for Long-Horizon Inference

abstract: Computational epidemiology is crucial in understanding and controlling infectious diseases, as highlighted by large-scale outbreaks such as COVID-19. Given the inherent uncertainty and variability of disease spread, Monte Carlo (MC) simulations are widely used to predict infection peaks, estimate reproduction numbers, and evaluate the impact of non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs). While effective, MC-based methods require numerous runs to achieve statistically reliable estimates and variance, which suffer from high computational costs. In this work, we present a unified theoretical framework for analyzing disease spread dynamics on both directed and undirected contact networks, and propose an algorithm, **RAPID**, that significantly improves computational efficiency. Our contributions are threefold. First, we derive an asymptotic variance lower bound for MC estimates and identify the key factors influencing estimation variance. Second, we provide a theoretical analysis of the probabilistic disease spread process using linear approximations and derive the convergence conditions under non-reinfection epidemic models. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on six real-world datasets, demonstrating our method's effectiveness and robustness in estimating the nodes' final state distribution. Specifically, our proposed method consistently produces accurate estimates aligned with results from a large number of MC simulations, while maintaining a runtime comparable to a single MC simulation. Our code and datasets are available at https://github.com/GuanghuiMin/RAPID.

paragraphs: Disease spread is uncertain, so estimating outcomes by simulation often requires many independent runs. That repetition can make reliable inference expensive on contact networks. This paper develops a theoretical framework for both directed and undirected networks and introduces RAPID to estimate disease outcomes more efficiently.

The analysis first establishes an asymptotic lower bound on the variance of Monte Carlo estimates and identifies factors affecting that variance. It then uses linear approximations to study the probabilistic spread process. The convergence conditions derived in this part apply to epidemic models without reinfection, making that modeling restriction part of the theoretical scope.

Experiments on six real-world datasets evaluate the distribution of final states for network nodes. RAPID's estimates consistently agree closely with results obtained from many Monte Carlo runs, while its runtime is comparable to one simulation. This finding matters because it suggests substantial savings for the evaluated inference task: useful outcome distributions can be estimated without paying the computational cost of repeated simulation at the same scale.
summary.tldr: RAPID estimates epidemic final-state distributions with accuracy matching many simulations and runtime comparable to a single simulation in reported experiments.

title: Scaling Epidemic Inference on Contact Networks: Theory and Algorithms

abstract: Deductive formal problem-solving (D-FPS) enables process-verified, human-aligned problem-solving by implementing deductive solving processes within formal theorem proving (FTP) environments. However, current methods fail to address the misalignment between informal and formal reasoning granularity and suffer from inefficiency due to backtracking and error propagation. Moreover, the extreme scarcity of formal problem-solution pairs further hinders progress. For the first gap, we propose **HAR** (_**H**ierarchical **A**utoregressive Formal **R**easoner_), a novel reasoning pipeline. HAR decouples informal-aligned drafting and detailed proving, and formulates solution construction as autoregressive generation with per-step feedback. Second, we propose **CoPA** (_**C**hain-**o**f-**P**roxy-**A**utoformalization_), a data generation pipeline that cascades statement autoformalization, proof drafting, and proof search as a proxy autoformalization path. Experiments demonstrate significant improvements: trained on data bootstrapped by CoPA, HAR achieves superior performance on FormalMath500 ($15.50\\%\mapsto 44.09\\%$) and MiniF2F-Solving ($21.87\\%\mapsto 56.58\\%$) with lower computational budget. Explorations reveal promising directions in formal solution pruning and informal dataset denoising.

paragraphs: Formal problem-solving places a deductive solution inside a theorem-proving environment so its steps can be checked. The paper addresses two obstacles: informal reasoning and formal proofs operate at different levels of detail, and formal problem-solution training pairs are extremely scarce. Additional explorations identify promising directions in pruning formal solutions and cleaning informal datasets.
summary.tldr: HAR combines hierarchical formal reasoning with CoPA-generated training data, substantially improving reported benchmark performance with a lower computational budget.

title: Bootstrapping Hierarchical Autoregressive Formal Reasoner with Chain-of-Proxy-Autoformalization

abstract: Multi-source transfer learning provides an effective solution to data scarcity in real-world supervised learning scenarios by leveraging multiple source tasks. In this field, existing works typically use all available samples from sources in training, which constrains their training efficiency and may lead to suboptimal results. To address this, we propose a theoretical framework that answers the question: what is the optimal quantity of source samples needed from each source task to jointly train the target model? Specifically, we introduce a generalization error measure based on K-L divergence, and minimize it based on high-dimensional statistical analysis to determine the optimal transfer quantity for each source task. Additionally, we develop an architecture-agnostic and data-efficient algorithm OTQMS to implement our theoretical results for target model training in multi-source transfer learning. Experimental studies on diverse architectures and two real-world benchmark datasets show that our proposed algorithm significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in both accuracy and data efficiency. The code is available at https://github.com/zqy0126/OTQMS.

paragraphs: When a target task has little training data, examples from several related tasks can help. A common practice is to include every available source example, but the paper argues that this can waste training effort and produce worse results. It studies a more selective question: how many examples should each source contribute when training the target model?

The authors develop a theoretical framework that measures generalization error using Kullback–Leibler divergence, a measure of difference between distributions. They use high-dimensional statistical analysis to minimize this error measure and determine transfer quantities for individual sources. This makes the amount of transferred data an explicit optimization decision, rather than treating larger source datasets as automatically better.

The proposed OTQMS algorithm turns that analysis into a training procedure designed to work across model architectures. Experiments with diverse architectures on two real-world benchmarks report significant improvements over state-of-the-art approaches in both accuracy and data efficiency. The findings support choosing source-specific quantities as a useful way to make multi-source transfer learning more effective.
summary.tldr: OTQMS uses statistical analysis to choose how much data to transfer from each source, improving accuracy and data efficiency in the reported experiments.

title: A High-Dimensional Statistical Method for Optimizing Transfer Quantities in Multi-Source Transfer Learning

abstract: We study contextual dynamic pricing when a target market can leverage $K$ auxiliary markets—offline logs or concurrent streams—whose *mean utilities differ by a structured preference shift*. We propose *Cross-Market Transfer Dynamic Pricing (CM-TDP)*, the first algorithm that *provably* handles such model-shift transfer and delivers minimax-optimal regret for *both* linear and non-parametric utility models. For linear utilities of dimension $d$, where the *difference* between source- and target-task coefficients is $s_{0}$-sparse, CM-TDP attains regret $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\bigl((dK^{-1}+s_{0})\log T\bigr)$. For nonlinear demand residing in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space with effective dimension $\alpha$, complexity $\beta$ and task-similarity parameter $H$, the regret becomes $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\bigl(K^{-2\alpha\beta/(2\alpha\beta+1)}T^{1/(2\alpha\beta+1)} + H^{2/(2\alpha+1)}T^{1/(2\alpha+1)}\bigr)$, matching information-theoretic lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. The RKHS bound is the first of its kind for transfer pricing and is of independent interest. Extensive simulations show up to 38\% higher cumulative revenue and $6\times$ faster convergence relative to single-market pricing baselines. By bridging transfer learning, robust aggregation, and revenue optimization, CM-TDP moves toward pricing systems that *transfer faster, price smarter*.

paragraphs: A pricing system can learn from other markets, but customer preferences may differ between those markets and its target market. This paper studies transfer under structured differences in mean utility. Its CM-TDP algorithm uses auxiliary markets supplied through offline records or concurrent data streams while accounting for those preference shifts.

The authors establish minimax-optimal regret guarantees for linear and nonparametric utility models. Regret measures the revenue shortfall relative to the pricing benchmark used in the analysis. In the linear setting, the source-to-target coefficient difference is assumed sparse. The nonlinear analysis uses a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, with bounds depending on effective dimension, complexity, and task similarity.

The bounds match information-theoretic lower bounds up to logarithmic factors, establishing optimality at that level under the studied conditions. Simulations report up to 38% higher cumulative revenue and sixfold faster convergence than single-market pricing baselines. Together, the theory and simulations support transferring market information while explicitly modeling the differences that could otherwise make it misleading.
summary.tldr: CM-TDP transfers pricing information across markets with structured preference shifts and achieves minimax-optimal regret under the studied utility assumptions.

title: Transfer Faster, Price Smarter: Minimax Dynamic Pricing under Cross-Market Preference Shift

abstract: Despite the impressive performance of general-purpose large language models (LLMs), they often require fine-tuning or post-training to excel at specific tasks. For instance, large reasoning models (LRMs), such as the DeepSeek-R1 series, demonstrate strong reasoning capabilities after post-training different general large language models on diverse chain-of-thought (CoT) datasets. However, this additional training frequently comes at the cost of reduced safety, as the fine-tuned or post-trained models tend to exhibit more harmful behaviors compared with the regular LLMs before post-training or fine-tuning, potentially leading to harmful outcomes due to their enhanced capabilities. Taking LRMs as an example, we first investigate the underlying cause of this safety degradation in this paper. Our analysis reveals that post-training can mask the original safety mechanisms of the base LLM, while over-amplifying representations related to their post-training ability. But luckily, we also find that LRMs' safety mechanisms still exist instead of being removed during their post-training. Based on these findings, we propose a lightweight and cost-effective solution called SafeReAct that restores the suppressed safety behaviors by aligning with LoRA adapters on a few layers. Experiments on four state-of-the-art LRMs show that our method significantly improves safety on harmful prompts without compromising reasoning performance. Besides LRMs, additional results on other domain-specific LLMs, like medical models, further confirm the generality and effectiveness of our approach.
originalAbstract: Despite the impressive performance of general-purpose large language models (LLMs), they often require fine-tuning or post-training to excel at specific tasks. For instance, large reasoning models (LRMs), such as the DeepSeek-R1 series, demonstrate strong reasoning capabilities after post-training different general large language models on diverse chain-of-thought (CoT) datasets. However, this additional training frequently comes at the cost of reduced safety, as the fine-tuned or post-trained models tend to exhibit more harmful behaviors compared with the regular LLMs before post-training or fine-tuning, potentially leading to harmful outcomes due to their enhanced capabilities. Taking LRMs as an example, we first investigate the underlying cause of this safety degradation in this paper. Our analysis reveals that post-training can mask the original safety mechanisms of the base LLM, while over-amplifying representations related to their post-training ability. But luckily, we also find that LRMs' safety mechanisms still exist instead of being removed during their post-training. Based on these findings, we propose a lightweight and cost-effective solution called SafeReAct that restores the suppressed safety behaviors by aligning with LoRA adapters on a few layers. Experiments on four state-of-the-art LRMs show that our method significantly improves safety on harmful prompts without compromising reasoning performance. Besides LRMs, additional results on other domain-specific LLMs, like medical models, further confirm the generality and effectiveness of our approach.

paragraphs: Post-training can improve a language model's specialized abilities while weakening its safety behavior. This paper investigates that trade-off using large reasoning models as its main example. The authors examine whether additional training removes the base model's safety mechanisms or changes how those mechanisms participate in the model's behavior.

Their analysis finds that post-training can suppress existing safety mechanisms while over-amplifying representations associated with the newly trained capability. In the reasoning models studied, the safety mechanisms remain present even though their behavioral influence is reduced. This finding motivates SafeReAct, a lightweight method that uses LoRA adapters on a few layers to restore the suppressed safety behavior through alignment.

Experiments on four state-of-the-art reasoning models show significant improvements in safety on harmful prompts without compromising reasoning performance. Additional results on specialized models, including medical language models, support broader applicability. The contribution is both an explanation of the observed degradation and a targeted intervention: retained internal safety mechanisms can provide a starting point for restoring safer behavior after specialization.
summary.tldr: SafeReAct uses adapters on a few layers to restore safety mechanisms suppressed by post-training, improving tested models' safety without reducing reasoning performance.

title: Finding and Reactivating Post-Trained LLMs' Hidden Safety Mechanisms

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often produce reasoning steps that are superficially coherent yet internally inconsistent, leading to unreliable outputs. Since such failures typically arise from implicit or poorly-grounded knowledge, we introduce \emph{Grounded Reasoning in Dependency (GRiD)}, a novel dependency-aware reasoning framework that explicitly grounds reasoning steps in structured knowledge. GRiD represents reasoning as a graph consisting of interconnected knowledge extraction nodes and reasoning nodes, enforcing logical consistency through explicit dependencies. Each reasoning step is validated via a lightweight, step-wise verifier that ensures logical correctness relative to its premises. Extensive experiments across diverse reasoning benchmarks—including StrategyQA, CommonsenseQA, GPQA, and TruthfulQA—demonstrate that GRiD substantially improves reasoning accuracy, consistency, and faithfulness compared to recent state-of-the-art structured reasoning methods. Notably, GRiD enhances performance even when applied purely as a lightweight verification module at inference time, underscoring its generalizability and practical utility. Code is available at: https://github.com/cure-lab/GRiD.

paragraphs: A sequence of reasoning steps can sound convincing while containing conclusions that do not follow from earlier claims. GRiD addresses this problem by making the knowledge supporting each step explicit. The paper attributes many such failures to knowledge that remains implicit or insufficiently grounded, leaving dependencies between claims poorly specified.

The framework represents reasoning as a graph with two kinds of nodes: nodes that extract knowledge and nodes that carry out reasoning. Connections record the dependencies between them. A lightweight verifier checks each reasoning step relative to its premises. This structure gives the checking process an explicit account of what a conclusion depends on, rather than relying only on the fluency of the explanation.

Across StrategyQA, CommonsenseQA, GPQA, and TruthfulQA, the authors report substantial improvements in accuracy, consistency, and faithfulness over recent structured reasoning methods. They also find benefits when GRiD is used solely as an inference-time verification module. That result matters practically because the dependency-aware checking component can improve reasoning even without using the entire framework to construct every step.
summary.tldr: GRiD makes reasoning dependencies explicit and verifies steps against their premises, improving measured accuracy, consistency, and faithfulness.

title: Dependency Matters: Enhancing LLM Reasoning with Explicit Knowledge Grounding

abstract: We introduce GS2E (Gaussian Splatting to Event Generation), a large-scale synthetic event dataset designed for high-fidelity event vision tasks, captured from real-world sparse multi-view RGB images. Existing event datasets are often synthesized from dense RGB videos, which typically suffer from limited viewpoint diversity and geometric inconsistency, or rely on expensive, hard-to-scale hardware setups. GS2E addresses these limitations by first reconstructing photorealistic static scenes using 3D Gaussian Splatting, followed by a novel, physically-informed event simulation pipeline. This pipeline integrates adaptive trajectory interpolation with physically-consistent event contrast threshold modeling. As a result, it generates temporally dense and geometrically consistent event streams under diverse motion and lighting conditions, while maintaining strong alignment with the underlying scene structure. Experimental results on event-based 3D reconstruction highlight GS2E’s superior generalization capabilities and its practical value as a benchmark for advancing event vision research.

Existing synthesis methods commonly depend on dense RGB videos, which can restrict viewpoint diversity and introduce geometric inconsistency. Dedicated hardware capture offers another route, but can be expensive and difficult to scale.

The method first reconstructs photorealistic static scenes using 3D Gaussian Splatting. It then runs a physically informed event simulation pipeline that combines adaptive trajectory interpolation with modeling of event contrast thresholds. These components generate temporally dense streams under varied motion and lighting while keeping the events aligned with the reconstructed scene geometry.

The resulting large-scale dataset is evaluated through event-based 3D reconstruction experiments. The authors report superior generalization and argue for its value as an event-vision benchmark. The contribution is a connection between sparse real-world RGB capture and controllable event simulation, with reconstructed static scenes providing a consistent geometric basis for generating diverse observations.
summary.tldr: GS2E turns sparse multi-view photographs into geometrically consistent synthetic event streams using Gaussian Splatting and physically informed simulation.

title: GS2E: Gaussian Splatting is an Effective Data Generator for Event Stream Generation

abstract: Adversarial attacks are widely used to evaluate model robustness, and in black-box scenarios, the transferability of these attacks becomes crucial. Existing generator-based attacks have excellent generalization and transferability due to their instance-agnostic nature. However, when training generators for multi-target tasks, the success rate of transfer attacks is relatively low due to the limitations of the model's capacity. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Dual-Flow framework for multi-target instance-agnostic adversarial attacks, utilizing Cascading Distribution Shift Training to develop an adversarial velocity function. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Dual-Flow significantly improves transferability over previous multi-target generative attacks. For example, it increases the success rate from Inception-v3 to ResNet-152 by 34.58%. Furthermore, our attack method shows substantially stronger robustness against defense mechanisms, such as adversarially trained models.

paragraphs: Adversarial attacks help evaluate whether a model remains reliable under deliberately challenging inputs. In black-box settings, an attack's usefulness depends on whether it transfers between models. Generator-based attacks can generalize across inputs because they learn a reusable attack mechanism, but handling multiple target outcomes places additional demands on the generator's capacity.

Dual-Flow addresses the low transfer success reported for existing multi-target generators. Its framework uses Cascading Distribution Shift Training to learn an adversarial velocity function. The approach targets the shared mechanism used across instances and multiple targets, making the training of that reusable attack function the central contribution.

Experiments report substantially better transferability than previous multi-target generative attacks. One example is a reported 34.58% increase in attack success when transferring from Inception-v3 to ResNet-152. The attacks also remain more effective against defense mechanisms, including adversarially trained models. These results indicate that the evaluated defenses and model changes provide less protection against this attack framework than against the compared methods, strengthening the robustness tests available in the studied settings.
summary.tldr: Dual-Flow improves the transferability of reusable multi-target adversarial attacks and reports stronger effectiveness against evaluated defenses.

title: Dual-Flow: Transferable Multi-Target, Instance-Agnostic Attacks via $\textit{In-the-wild}$ Cascading Flow Optimization

abstract: Clustering tabular data remains a significant open challenge in data analysis and machine learning. Unlike for image data, similarity between tabular records often varies across datasets, making the definition of clusters highly dataset-dependent. Furthermore, the absence of supervised signals complicates hyperparameter tuning in deep learning clustering methods, frequently resulting in unstable performance. To address these issues and minimize the need for per-dataset tuning, we adopt an emerging approach in deep learning: zero-shot learning. We propose ZEUS, a self-contained model capable of clustering new datasets without any additional training or fine-tuning. It operates by decomposing complex datasets into meaningful components that can then be clustered effectively. Thanks to pre-training on synthetic datasets generated from a latent-variable prior, it generalizes across various datasets without requiring user intervention. To the best of our knowledge, ZEUS is the first zero-shot method capable of generating embeddings for tabular data in a fully unsupervised manner. Experimental results demonstrate that it performs on par with or better than traditional clustering algorithms and recent deep learning-based methods, while being significantly faster and more user-friendly.

paragraphs: Clustering tables is difficult because the meaning of similarity changes between datasets. Without labels, choosing hyperparameters for deep clustering methods is also challenging and can lead to unstable results. ZEUS aims to reduce this dependence on dataset-specific choices by applying a pretrained model directly to previously unseen tabular data.

The model learns from synthetic datasets generated using a latent-variable prior. At application time, it decomposes a complex dataset into meaningful components and produces representations that can be clustered effectively. It requires no additional training or fine-tuning on the new dataset. This places the learning effort in pretraining and makes the resulting clustering capability available without per-dataset intervention.

Experiments show performance matching or exceeding traditional clustering algorithms and recent deep-learning methods, alongside substantially greater speed and ease of use. The authors describe ZEUS as, to their knowledge, the first fully unsupervised zero-shot embedding method for tabular data. Its main contribution is demonstrating that synthetic pretraining can support useful clustering representations across varied datasets without repeatedly fitting a new representation model.
summary.tldr: ZEUS learns from synthetic tables to produce clustering representations for new datasets without additional training or fine-tuning.

title: ZEUS: Zero-shot Embeddings for Unsupervised Separation of Tabular Data

abstract: System identification involving the geometry, appearance, and physical properties from video observations is a challenging task with applications in robotics and graphics. Recent approaches have relied on fully differentiable Material Point Method (MPM) and rendering for simultaneous optimization of these properties. However, they are limited to simplified object-environment interactions with planar colliders and fail in more challenging scenarios where objects collide with non-planar surfaces. We propose AS-DiffMPM, a differentiable MPM framework that enables physical property estimation with arbitrarily shaped colliders. Our approach extends existing methods by incorporating a differentiable collision handling mechanism, allowing the target object to interact with complex rigid bodies while maintaining end-to-end optimization. We show AS-DiffMPM can be easily interfaced with various novel view synthesis methods as a framework for system identification from visual observations.

paragraphs: Estimating an object's physical properties from video requires connecting its observed appearance and motion to a simulation. Recent approaches jointly optimize geometry, appearance, and physics using differentiable rendering and the Material Point Method. Their collision handling, however, is limited to simplified interactions with flat surfaces, making more complex environments difficult to model.

AS-DiffMPM extends this approach to arbitrarily shaped colliders. Its central addition is a differentiable collision-handling mechanism that allows the target object to interact with complex rigid bodies while retaining end-to-end optimization. Because collision handling remains inside the differentiable process, physical-property estimation can account for these richer interactions as part of the same optimization framework.

The authors also show that AS-DiffMPM can connect readily to different novel-view synthesis methods for system identification from visual observations. The contribution expands the range of object-environment interactions available to this form of video-based estimation. It connects a more capable physical simulator with visual reconstruction methods, addressing a specific obstacle to identifying systems whose motion involves non-planar contact.
summary.tldr: AS-DiffMPM adds differentiable collisions with arbitrarily shaped rigid bodies to support physical-property estimation from video.

title: Gaussian-Augmented Physics Simulation and System Identification with Complex Colliders

abstract: Automating the expert-dependent and labor-intensive task of 3D scene synthesis would significantly benefit fields such as architectural design, robotics simulation, and virtual reality. Recent approaches to 3D scene synthesis often rely on the commonsense reasoning of large language models (LLMs) or strong visual priors from image generation models. However, current LLMs exhibit limited 3D spatial reasoning, undermining the realism and global coherence of synthesized scenes, while image-generation-based methods often constrain viewpoint control and introduce multi-view inconsistencies. In this work, we present Video Perception models for 3D Scene synthesis (VIPScene), a novel framework that exploits the encoded commonsense knowledge of the 3D physical world in video generation models to ensure coherent scene layouts and consistent object placements across views. VIPScene accepts both text and image prompts and seamlessly integrates video generation, feedforward 3D reconstruction, and open-vocabulary perception models to semantically and geometrically analyze each object in a scene. This enables flexible scene synthesis with high realism and structural consistency. For a more sufficient evaluation on coherence and plausibility, we further introduce First-Person View Score (FPVScore), utilizing a continuous first-person perspective to capitalize on the reasoning ability of multimodal large language models. Extensive experiments show that VIPScene significantly outperforms existing methods and generalizes well across diverse scenarios.

paragraphs: Generating a coherent three-dimensional scene requires objects to make sense individually and remain consistently arranged across viewpoints. Existing approaches face difficulties with spatial reasoning, viewpoint control, or consistency between views. VIPScene explores using knowledge of the physical world encoded in video generation models to improve scene synthesis.

The framework accepts text or image prompts and combines video generation, feedforward three-dimensional reconstruction, and open-vocabulary perception. The approach uses video as a source of information for constructing layouts and placements that remain coherent when viewed from different positions.

The authors also introduce First-Person View Score, an evaluation measure that uses a continuous first-person perspective and the reasoning ability of multimodal language models to assess coherence and plausibility. Experiments report significant improvements over existing methods and good generalization across diverse scenarios. The paper thus contributes both a scene-generation framework and an evaluation approach oriented toward how a scene holds together as the viewpoint moves.
summary.tldr: VIPScene combines video generation, 3D reconstruction, and perception to synthesize coherent scenes from text or images.

title: Video Perception Models for 3D Scene Synthesis

abstract: Recent works of Mei et al. (2023, 2024) have deepened the theoretical understanding of the *Stochastic Gradient Bandit* (SGB) policy, showing that using a constant learning rate guarantees asymptotic convergence to the optimal policy, and that sufficiently *small* learning rates can yield logarithmic regret. However, whether logarithmic regret holds beyond small learning rates remains unclear. In this work, we take a step towards characterizing the regret *regimes* of SGB as a function of its learning rate. For two--armed bandits, we identify a sharp threshold, scaling with the sub-optimality gap $\Delta$, below which SGB achieves *logarithmic* regret on all instances, and above which it can incur *polynomial* regret on some instances. This result highlights the necessity of knowing (or estimating) $\Delta$ to ensure logarithmic regret with a constant learning rate. For general $K$-armed bandits, we further show the learning rate must scale inversely with $K$ to avoid polynomial regret. We introduce novel techniques to derive regret upper bounds for SGB, laying the groundwork for future advances in the theory of gradient-based bandit algorithms.

paragraphs: A bandit algorithm repeatedly chooses among actions while learning which rewards are best. Earlier theory showed that the Stochastic Gradient Bandit policy eventually converges to an optimal policy with a constant learning rate, and that sufficiently small rates can achieve logarithmic regret. This paper asks how the learning rate changes regret along the way, beyond eventual convergence.

For two actions, the authors identify a sharp threshold that scales with the suboptimality gap, the reward difference separating the inferior action from the best one. Below the threshold, the algorithm achieves logarithmic regret on all instances. Above it, some instances can produce polynomial regret. The latter is a possibility established by the result, rather than a claim about every instance.

For a general number of actions K, the learning rate must also scale inversely with K to avoid polynomial regret. The results show why choosing a constant rate requires knowing or estimating the reward gap to ensure logarithmic regret. New techniques for regret upper bounds further develop the theoretical analysis of gradient-based bandit policies.
summary.tldr: Stochastic Gradient Bandit's regret depends sharply on its learning rate, with rates above a gap-dependent threshold permitting polynomial regret.

title: Does Stochastic Gradient really succeed for bandits?

abstract: Optimization modeling is one of the most crucial but technical parts of operations research (OR). To automate the modeling process, existing works have leveraged large language models (LLMs), prompting them to break down tasks into steps for generating variables, constraints, and objectives. However, due to the highly complex mathematical structures inherent in OR problems, standard fixed-step decomposition often fails to achieve high performance. To address this challenge, we introduce OptiTree, a novel tree search approach designed to enhance modeling capabilities for complex problems through adaptive problem decomposition into simpler subproblems. Specifically, we develop a modeling tree that organizes a wide range of OR problems based on their hierarchical problem taxonomy and complexity, with each node representing a problem category and containing relevant high-level modeling thoughts. Given a problem to model, we recurrently search the tree to identify a series of simpler subproblems and synthesize the global modeling thoughts by adaptively integrating the hierarchical thoughts. Experiments show that OptiTree significantly improves the modeling accuracy compared to the state-of-the-art, achieving over 10% improvements on the challenging benchmarks.

paragraphs: Optimization modeling translates a problem into mathematical variables, constraints, and objectives. OptiTree addresses this by adapting the breakdown of a problem to its mathematical structure.

The method constructs a modeling tree organized by problem categories and complexity. Each node contains high-level modeling thoughts relevant to its category. For a new problem, the system repeatedly searches this hierarchy to find simpler subproblems, then combines the relevant thoughts into guidance for the overall model.

This organization gives the language model access to modeling ideas at several levels of abstraction, with the decomposition determined by the problem being solved. The findings support hierarchical, adaptive decomposition as a useful way to guide language models through mathematically complex modeling tasks.
summary.tldr: OptiTree searches a hierarchy of modeling knowledge to adaptively decompose optimization problems and improve mathematical modeling accuracy.

title: OptiTree: Hierarchical Thoughts Generation with Tree Search for LLM Optimization Modeling

abstract: Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) is an essential component of text-to-image diffusion models, and understanding and advancing its operational mechanisms remains a central focus of research. Existing approaches stem from divergent theoretical interpretations, thereby limiting the design space and obscuring key design choices. To address this, we propose a unified perspective that reframes conditional guidance as fixed point iterations, seeking to identify a golden path where latents produce consistent outputs under both conditional and unconditional generation. We demonstrate that CFG and its variants constitute a special case of single-step short-interval iteration, which is theoretically proven to exhibit inefficiency. To this end, we introduce Foresight Guidance (FSG), which prioritizes solving longer-interval subproblems in early diffusion stages with increased iterations. Extensive experiments across diverse datasets and model architectures validate the superiority of FSG over state-of-the-art methods in both image quality and computational efficiency. Our work offers novel perspectives for conditional guidance and unlocks the potential of adaptive design.

summary.tldr: Foresight Guidance uses a fixed-point view of diffusion guidance to improve reported image quality and computational efficiency.

abstract: We introduce EvaLearn, a pioneering benchmark designed to evaluate large language models (LLMs) on their learning capability and efficiency in challenging tasks, a critical, yet underexplored aspect of model potential. EvaLearn contains 648 challenging problems across six task types, grouped into 182 sequences, each sequence dedicated to one task type. Diverging from most existing benchmarks that evaluate models in parallel, EvaLearn requires models to solve problems sequentially, allowing them to leverage the experience gained from previous solutions. EvaLearn provides five comprehensive automated metrics to evaluate models and quantify their learning capability and efficiency. We extensively benchmark nine frontier models and observe varied performance profiles: some models, such as Claude-3.7-sonnet, start with moderate initial performance but exhibit strong learning ability, while some models struggle to benefit from experience and may even show negative transfer. Moreover, we investigate model performance under two learning settings and find that instance-level rubrics and teacher-model feedback further facilitate model learning. Importantly, we observe that current LLMs with stronger static abilities do not show a clear advantage in learning capability across all tasks, highlighting that EvaLearn evaluates a new dimension of model performance. We hope EvaLearn provides a novel evaluation perspective for assessing LLM potential and understanding the gap between models and human capabilities, promoting the development of deeper and more dynamic evaluation approaches. All datasets, the automatic evaluation framework, and the results studied in this paper are available in the supplementary materials.

EvaLearn evaluates this second capability by presenting problems sequentially, allowing earlier solutions to inform later ones. Its 648 challenging problems cover six task types and are organized into 182 sequences, each focused on one type.

Tests of nine frontier models reveal different patterns: some begin with moderate performance and improve strongly, while others gain little from previous experience or exhibit negative transfer. Claude-3.7-sonnet is highlighted as an example of the former pattern.

The authors also examine two learning settings and find that instance-level rubrics and feedback from a teacher model can help learning. Across tasks, stronger static performance does not consistently translate into stronger learning capability. The benchmark therefore adds a distinct evaluation perspective: assessing how a model’s performance develops through a sequence, alongside what it can already do when problems are assessed independently.
summary.tldr: EvaLearn measures how LLMs improve through sequential problem solving and finds that strong initial performance does not consistently predict stronger learning.

title: EvaLearn: Quantifying the Learning Capability and Efficiency of LLMs via Sequential Problem Solving

abstract: Multi-frame video enhancement tasks aim to improve the spatial and temporal resolution and quality of video sequences by leveraging temporal information from multiple frames, which are widely used in streaming video processing, surveillance, and generation. Although numerous Transformer-based enhancement methods have achieved impressive performance, their computational and memory demands hinder deployment on edge devices. Quantization offers a practical solution by reducing the bit-width of weights and activations to improve efficiency. However, directly applying existing quantization methods to video enhancement tasks often leads to significant performance degradation and loss of fine details. This stems from two limitations: (a) inability to allocate varying representational capacity across frames, which results in suboptimal dynamic range adaptation; (b) over-reliance on full-precision teachers, which limits the learning of low-bit student models. To tackle these challenges, we propose a novel quantization method for video enhancement: Progressive Multi-Frame Quantization for Video Enhancement (PMQ-VE). This framework features a coarse-to-fine two-stage process: Backtracking-based Multi-Frame Quantization (BMFQ) and Progressive Multi-Teacher Distillation (PMTD). BMFQ utilizes a percentile-based initialization and iterative search with pruning and backtracking for robust clipping bounds. PMTD employs a progressive distillation strategy with both full-precision and multiple high-bit (INT) teachers to enhance low-bit models' capacity and quality. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple tasks and benchmarks. The code will be made publicly available.

Its two stages aim to retain the temporal information and fine details that can be damaged when quantization is applied directly.
summary.tldr: PMQ-VE combines frame-aware quantization search with progressive multi-teacher training to improve low-bit video enhancement quality.

title: PMQ-VE: Progressive Multi-Frame Quantization for Video Enhancement

abstract: Math reasoning has been one crucial ability of large language models (LLMs), where significant advancements have been achieved in recent years. However, most efforts focus on LLMs by curating high-quality annotation data and intricate training (or inference) paradigms, while the math reasoning performance of multi-modal LLMs (MLLMs) remains lagging behind. Since the MLLM typically consists of an LLM and vision block, we wonder: \textit{Can MLLMs directly absorb math reasoning abilities from off-the-shelf math LLMs without tuning?} Recent model-merging approaches may offer insights into this question. However, they overlook the alignment between the MLLM and LLM, where we find that there is a large gap between their parameter spaces, resulting in lower performance. Our empirical evidence reveals two key factors behind this issue: the identification of crucial reasoning-associated layers in the model and the mitigation of the gaps in parameter space. Based on the empirical insights, we propose \textbf{IP-Merging} that first \textbf{I}dentifies the reasoning-associated parameters in both MLLM and Math LLM, then \textbf{P}rojects them into the subspace of MLLM aiming to maintain the alignment, finally merges parameters in this subspace. IP-Merging is a tuning-free approach since parameters are directly adjusted. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our IP-Merging method can enhance the math reasoning ability of MLLMs directly from Math LLMs without compromising their other capabilities.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models combine language and vision components, but their mathematical reasoning can lag behind specialized text-only models. This paper asks whether an existing math language model can improve a multimodal model through direct parameter changes, avoiding an additional tuning stage. Model merging offers a possible route, but the authors find that straightforward merging can reduce performance.

Their empirical analysis identifies two issues: reasoning depends especially on particular layers, and the models occupy substantially different parameter spaces. IP-Merging addresses both. It identifies reasoning-related parameters in each model, projects them into a subspace of the multimodal model to help preserve alignment, and then merges parameters within that space.

The method is tuning-free because it directly adjusts parameters rather than running a new tuning procedure. Across the reported experiments, it improves mathematical reasoning without compromising other evaluated capabilities. The findings suggest that transferring reasoning through merging benefits from selecting relevant parameters and respecting the multimodal model's existing alignment.
summary.tldr: IP-Merging transfers mathematical reasoning into multimodal models by aligning and merging selected parameters without additional tuning.

title: Can MLLMs Absorb Math Reasoning Abilities from LLMs as Free Lunch?

abstract: Video understanding is fundamental to tasks such as action recognition, video reasoning, and robotic control. Early video understanding methods based on large vision-language models (LVLMs) typically adopt a single-pass reasoning paradigm without dynamic feedback, limiting the model’s capacity to self-correct and adapt in complex scenarios. Recent efforts have attempted to address this limitation by incorporating reward models and reinforcement learning to enhance reasoning, or by employing tool-agent frameworks. However, these approaches face several challenges, including high annotation costs, reward signals that fail to capture real-time reasoning states, and low inference efficiency. To overcome these issues, we propose ReAgent-V, a novel agentic video understanding framework that integrates efficient frame selection with real-time reward generation during inference. These reward signals not only guide iterative answer refinement through a multi-perspective reflection mechanism—adjusting predictions from conservative, neutral, and aggressive viewpoints—but also enable automatic filtering of high-quality data for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), and group relative policy optimization (GRPO). ReAgent-V is lightweight, modular, and extensible, supporting flexible tool integration tailored to diverse tasks. Extensive experiments on 12 datasets across three core applications—video understanding, video reasoning enhancement, and vision-language-action model alignment—demonstrate significant gains in generalization and reasoning, with improvements of up to 6.9%, 2.1%, and 9.8%, respectively, highlighting the effectiveness and versatility of the proposed framework.

title: ReAgent-V: A Reward-Driven Multi-Agent Framework for Video Understanding

abstract: Using a long-standing conjecture from combinatorial group theory, we explore, from multiple perspectives, the challenges of finding rare instances carrying disproportionately high rewards. Based on lessons learned in the context defined by the Andrews--Curtis conjecture, we analyze how reinforcement learning agents handle problems of varying hardness. We also address many mathematical questions as a part of our study. Notably, we demonstrate the length reducibility of all but two presentations in the Akbulut--Kirby series (1981), and resolve various potential counterexamples in the Miller--Schupp series (1991), including three infinite subfamilies.

paragraphs: This paper uses the Andrews-Curtis conjecture from combinatorial group theory as a case study of difficult reinforcement learning problems. Its focus is the search for rare instances that carry unusually high rewards. Such a setting puts the relationship between mathematical problem difficulty and an agent's ability to find valuable outcomes at the center of the investigation.

The authors examine the challenge from multiple perspectives and analyze how reinforcement learning agents handle problems of varying hardness within this mathematical context. The study also addresses mathematical questions directly. This gives the work two connected purposes: investigating learning behavior and advancing understanding of the concrete instances used in that investigation.

The stated mathematical results include length reducibility for all but two presentations in the Akbulut-Kirby series and resolution of several potential counterexamples in the Miller-Schupp series, including three infinite subfamilies. These are specific advances within the case study, rather than a claimed resolution of the overall conjecture. They provide substantive mathematical outcomes alongside the examination of rare-reward search.
summary.tldr: A group-theory case study examines reinforcement learning on rare-reward problems while resolving specific mathematical instances and infinite subfamilies.

title: WHAT MAKES MATH PROBLEMS HARD FOR REINFORCEMENT LEARNING: A CASE STUDY

abstract: The increasing use of 360$^\circ$ images across various domains has emphasized the need for robust depth estimation techniques tailored for omnidirectional images. However, obtaining large-scale labeled datasets for 360$^\circ$ depth estimation remains a significant challenge. In this paper, we propose RPG360, a training-free robust 360$^\circ$ monocular depth estimation method that leverages perspective foundation models and graph optimization. Our approach converts 360$^\circ$ images into six- face cubemap representations, where a perspective foundation model is employed to estimate depth and surface normals. To address depth scale inconsistencies across different faces of the cubemap, we introduce a novel depth scale alignment technique using graph-based optimization, which parameterizes the predicted depth and normal maps while incorporating an additional per-face scale parameter. This optimization ensures depth scale consistency across the six-face cubemap while preserving 3D structural integrity. Furthermore, as foundation models exhibit inherent robustness in zero-shot settings, our method achieves superior performance across diverse datasets, including Matterport3D, Stanford2D3D, and 360Loc. We also demonstrate the versatility of our depth estimation approach by validating its benefits in downstream tasks such as feature matching 3.2 ∼ 5.4% and Structure from Motion 0.2 ∼ 9.7% in AUC@5$^\circ$.

paragraphs: RPG360 estimates depth from a single 360-degree image without additional training. It addresses the shortage of large labeled datasets for panoramic depth estimation by reusing foundation models designed for ordinary perspective images. The central challenge is making their separate predictions agree across an entire surrounding scene.

The method first converts the panorama into six faces of a cube. A perspective foundation model estimates depth and surface normals for each face. These predictions can use inconsistent depth scales, so simply combining them would not provide a coherent reconstruction. RPG360 applies graph-based optimization with parameterized depth and normal maps, including an extra scale parameter for each face, to align them while preserving 3D structure.

The authors report superior depth-estimation performance across Matterport3D, Stanford2D3D, and 360Loc, drawing on the foundation models’ zero-shot robustness. They also demonstrate benefits for feature matching and Structure from Motion. Those downstream results show that aligning the face predictions can help subsequent geometric tasks as well as panoramic depth estimation itself.
summary.tldr: RPG360 combines perspective-model predictions with graph-based scale alignment to estimate coherent panoramic depth without additional training.

title: RPG360: Robust 360 Depth Estimation with Perspective Foundation Models and Graph Optimization

abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting has recently emerged as an efficient solution for high-quality and real-time novel view synthesis. However, its capability for accurate surface reconstruction remains underexplored. Due to the discrete and unstructured nature of Gaussians, supervision based solely on image rendering loss often leads to inaccurate geometry and inconsistent multi-view alignment. In this work, we propose a novel method that enhances the geometric representation of 3D Gaussians through view alignment (VA). Specifically, we incorporate edge-aware image cues into the rendering loss to improve surface boundary delineation. To enforce geometric consistency across views, we introduce a visibility-aware photometric alignment loss that models occlusions and encourages accurate spatial relationships among Gaussians. To further mitigate ambiguities caused by lighting variations, we incorporate normal-based constraints to refine the spatial orientation of Gaussians and improve local surface estimation. Additionally, we leverage deep image feature embeddings to enforce cross-view consistency, enhancing the robustness of the learned geometry under varying viewpoints and illumination. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in both surface reconstruction and novel view synthesis. The source code is available at https://github.com/LeoQLi/VA-GS.

paragraphs: Gaussian splatting can render convincing new views, but good rendered images do not necessarily imply accurate surfaces. The discrete, unstructured Gaussian representation can produce inconsistent geometry when trained only through image-rendering loss. VA-GS adds view-alignment signals to strengthen the spatial structure learned by the Gaussians.

The method incorporates edge-aware image cues to improve surface boundaries. A visibility-aware photometric alignment loss accounts for occlusions while encouraging consistent spatial relationships across views. Normal-based constraints refine Gaussian orientations and local surface estimates, helping reduce ambiguities associated with changes in lighting.

Deep image feature embeddings provide an additional cross-view consistency signal, improving robustness across viewpoints and illumination conditions. These components collectively supervise boundaries, visibility, orientation, and agreement between images. On standard benchmarks, the authors report state-of-the-art performance in both surface reconstruction and novel-view synthesis. The result supports view alignment as a way to improve the geometry underlying Gaussian splatting while also improving its rendered output. The contribution makes geometric consistency an explicit part of learning the representation.
summary.tldr: VA-GS combines boundary, visibility, orientation, and feature-alignment signals to improve Gaussian-splatting geometry and novel-view rendering.

title: VA-GS: Enhancing the Geometric Representation of Gaussian Splatting via View Alignment

abstract: Transfer learning algorithms are used when one has sufficient training data for one supervised learning task (the source task) but only very limited training data for a second task (the target task) that is similar but not identical to the first. These algorithms use varying assumptions about the similarity between the tasks to carry information from the source to the target task. Common assumptions are that only certain specific marginal or conditional distributions have changed while all else remains the same. Alternatively, if one has only the target task, but also has the ability to choose a limited amount of additional training data to collect, then active learning algorithms are used to make choices which will most improve performance on the target task. These algorithms may be combined into active transfer learning, but previous efforts have had to apply the two methods in sequence or use restrictive transfer assumptions. We propose two transfer learning algorithms that allow changes in all marginal and conditional distributions but assume the changes are smooth in order to achieve transfer between the tasks. We then propose an active learning algorithm for the second method that yields a combined active transfer learning algorithm. We demonstrate the algorithms on synthetic functions and a real-world task on estimating the yield of vineyards from images of the grapes.

paragraphs: Transfer learning uses information from a well-supported source task to help a related target task with little training data. Active learning addresses a complementary problem: deciding which additional target examples would be most useful to collect. This paper develops methods that bring these two decisions together while allowing substantial differences between the tasks.

The authors propose two transfer algorithms that permit changes in all marginal and conditional distributions. Instead of requiring particular distributions to remain fixed, they assume the changes are smooth. That assumption provides the connection needed to transfer information even when the source and target differ in several ways. It is a broader shift model, not an absence of assumptions.

For the second transfer method, the authors also develop an active learning algorithm, producing an integrated active transfer approach. They demonstrate the methods on synthetic functions and on estimating vineyard yields from grape images. These applications illustrate how transferred information and selective data collection can be combined when the target task is related to, but differs from, the source.
summary.tldr: The paper combines transfer and active learning under a smooth-change assumption that allows all marginal and conditional distributions to differ between tasks.

title: Active Transfer Learning under Model Shift

abstract: We consider the problem of undiscounted reinforcement learning in continuous state space. Regret bounds in this setting usually hold under various assumptions on the structure of the reward and transition function. Under the assumption that the rewards and transition probabilities are Lipschitz, for 1-dimensional state space a regret bound of O(T^3/4) after any T steps has been given by Ortner and Ryabko (2012). Here we improve upon this result by using non-parametric kernel density estimation for estimating the transition probability distributions, and obtain regret bounds that depend on the smoothness of the transition probability distributions. In particular, under the assumption that the transition probability functions are smoothly differentiable, the regret bound is shown to be O(T^2/3) asymptotically for reinforcement learning in 1-dimensional state space. Finally, we also derive improved regret bounds for higher dimensional state space.

Regret bounds in this setting usually hold under various assumptions on the structure of the reward and transition function. Under the assumption that the rewards and transition probabilities are Lipschitz, for 1-dimensional state space a regret bound of O(T^3/4) after any T steps has been given by Ortner and Ryabko (2012). Here we improve upon this result by using non-parametric kernel density estimation for estimating the transition probability distributions, and obtain regret bounds that depend on the smoothness of the transition probability distributions. In particular, under the assumption that the transition probability functions are smoothly differentiable, the regret bound is shown to be O(T^2/3) asymptotically for reinforcement learning in 1-dimensional state space. paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning with continuous states and undiscounted rewards. Its performance measure is regret, which tracks accumulated shortfall during learning. Guarantees in this setting depend on structural assumptions about rewards and state transitions, because a continuous state space requires learning behavior across more than a finite collection of states.

The proposed approach uses nonparametric kernel density estimation to estimate transition probability distributions. Its regret bounds depend on how smooth those distributions are. For one-dimensional states, earlier work under Lipschitz assumptions gave a bound of O(T^(3/4)) after T steps. Under smoothly differentiable transition probability functions, the paper obtains an asymptotic bound of O(T^(2/3)).

The smaller exponent means the stated regret guarantee grows more slowly with experience in that smoother setting. The improvement is therefore tied to assumptions that the transition estimator can exploit. The authors also derive improved bounds for higher-dimensional state spaces. Overall, the contribution links the regularity of transition distributions to stronger guarantees for learning in continuous environments.
summary.tldr: Kernel estimates of transition distributions yield improved continuous-state reinforcement-learning regret bounds under smoothness assumptions.

title: Improved Regret Bounds for Undiscounted Continuous Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We study the convergence properties of the VR-PCA algorithm introduced by (Shamir, 2015) for fast computation of leading singular vectors. We prove several new results, including a formal analysis of a block version of the algorithm, and convergence from random initialization. We also make a few observations of independent interest, such as how pre-initializing with just a single exact power iteration can significantly improve the analysis, and what are the convexity and non-convexity properties of the underlying optimization problem.
originalAbstract: We study the convergence properties of the VR-PCA algorithm introduced by (Shamir, 2015) for fast computation of leading singular vectors. We prove several new results, including a formal analysis of a block version of the algorithm, and convergence from random initialization. We also make a few observations of independent interest, such as how pre-initializing with just a single exact power iteration can significantly improve the analysis, and what are the convexity and non-convexity properties of the underlying optimization problem.

paragraphs: The paper strengthens the theoretical understanding of VR-PCA, an existing stochastic algorithm for quickly computing leading singular vectors. Its focus is on convergence: establishing how the algorithm reaches the desired solution and clarifying which features of its formulation matter to that analysis. This is relevant to both singular value decomposition and principal component analysis.

The authors formally analyze a block version of the algorithm, extending the theoretical treatment to a version that works with multiple directions together. They also prove convergence from random initialization. This addresses an important part of the algorithm’s use, since its starting point is itself part of the convergence question.

Another finding concerns preparation before the stochastic iterations: performing just one exact power iteration can substantially improve the analysis. The stated improvement concerns the theoretical account, rather than a reported experimental speedup. The paper also examines where the underlying optimization problem is convex or nonconvex. Together, these results explain more of the relationship between initialization, algorithm structure, and convergence.
summary.tldr: New convergence results for VR-PCA cover a block variant, random initialization, and the analytical benefit of one exact power iteration.

title: Fast Stochastic Algorithms for SVD and PCA: Convergence Properties and Convexity

abstract: The use of convex regularizers allow for easy optimization, though they often produce biased estimation and inferior prediction performance. Recently, nonconvex regularizers have attracted a lot of attention and outperformed convex ones. However, the resultant optimization problem is much harder. In this paper, for a large class of nonconvex regularizers, we propose to move the nonconvexity from the regularizer to the loss. The nonconvex regularizer is then transformed to a familiar convex regularizer, while the resultant loss function can still be guaranteed to be smooth. Learning with the convexified regularizer can be performed by existing efficient algorithms originally designed for convex regularizers (such as the standard proximal algorithm and Frank-Wolfe algorithm). Moreover, it can be shown that critical points of the transformed problem are also critical points of the original problem. Extensive experiments on a number of nonconvex regularization problems show that the proposed procedure is much faster than the state-of-the-art nonconvex solvers.

paragraphs: Nonconvex regularizers can improve estimation and prediction, but they make optimization harder. This paper addresses that computational difficulty for a large class of such regularizers. Its central move is to change where nonconvexity appears in the learning objective, making familiar optimization tools usable in the transformed formulation.

The authors transfer the nonconvex part of the regularizer into the loss. The remaining regularizer becomes convex, while the modified loss is guaranteed to remain smooth. This structure permits efficient algorithms originally designed for convex regularizers, including proximal methods and Frank–Wolfe methods. The overall objective still contains nonconvexity, now located in a part handled differently by those algorithms.

The paper proves that critical points of the transformed problem are also critical points of the original problem. That establishes a connection between the solutions reached under the two formulations without claiming global optimality. Extensive experiments across several nonconvex regularization problems report much faster performance than state-of-the-art nonconvex solvers, supporting the computational value of redistributing the difficult part of the objective.
summary.tldr: Moving nonconvexity from the regularizer into a smooth loss enables efficient existing algorithms while preserving the stated critical-point relationship.

title: Efficient Learning with a Family of Nonconvex Regularizers by Redistributing Nonconvexity

abstract: We introduce a model that learns active learning algorithms via metalearning. For a distribution of related tasks, our model jointly learns: a data representation, an item selection heuristic, and a prediction function. Our model uses the item selection heuristic to construct a labeled support set for training the prediction function. Using the Omniglot and MovieLens datasets, we test our model in synthetic and practical settings.
originalAbstract: We introduce a model that learns active learning algorithms via metalearning. For a distribution of related tasks, our model jointly learns: a data representation, an item selection heuristic, and a prediction function. Our model uses the item selection heuristic to construct a labeled support set for training the prediction function. Using the Omniglot and MovieLens datasets, we test our model in synthetic and practical settings.

paragraphs: Active learning involves choosing which items to obtain labels for, making the selection procedure part of the learning problem. This paper proposes learning that procedure through metalearning across a distribution of related tasks. Its focus is on developing an active learning algorithm whose components are learned together.

The model jointly learns a representation of the data, a heuristic for selecting items, and a function for making predictions. The selection heuristic constructs a labeled support set, which is then used to train the prediction function. These components form a connected process: the representation describes the items, selection determines the labeled evidence available, and prediction uses that evidence. Joint learning brings all three decisions into the same framework.

The authors test the model using Omniglot and MovieLens in both synthetic and practical settings. The stated contribution is the integrated metalearning approach and its evaluation across these settings. It treats deciding what to label as a capability that can itself be learned from related tasks, alongside how to represent data and make predictions.
summary.tldr: A metalearning model jointly learns data representations, label-selection heuristics, and predictors across related tasks.

title: Learning Algorithms for Active Learning

abstract: Co-training is a well-known semi-supervised learning approach which trains classifiers on two different views and exchanges labels of unlabeled instances in an iterative way. During co-training process, labels of unlabeled instances in the training pool are very likely to be false especially in the initial training rounds, while the standard co-training algorithm utilizes a “draw without replacement” manner and does not remove these false labeled instances from training. This issue not only tends to degenerate its performance but also hampers its fundamental theory. Besides, there is no optimization model to explain what objective a cotraining process optimizes. To these issues, in this study we design a new co-training algorithm named self-paced cotraining (SPaCo) with a “draw with replacement” learning mode. The rationality of SPaCo can be proved under theoretical assumptions utilized in traditional co-training research, and furthermore, the algorithm exactly complies with the alternative optimization process for an optimization model of self-paced curriculum learning, which can be finely explained in robust learning manner. Experimental results substantiate the superiority of the proposed method as compared with current state-of-the-art co-training methods.

SPaCo changes the selection process to a draw-with-replacement mode, allowing training selections to be revisited. The authors also give the procedure an explicit optimization interpretation: its steps correspond exactly to alternating optimization of a self-paced curriculum-learning objective. This provides a robust-learning explanation for a process that previously lacked a clear optimization model.

Its scope therefore depends on those assumptions, rather than applying unconditionally to any pair of classifiers or data views. Experiments show superiority over the compared state-of-the-art co-training methods. The contribution combines reconsideration of training examples with a formal objective, addressing both persistent labeling errors and the interpretation of the learning process.
summary.tldr: SPaCo revisits co-training selections and connects the procedure to a self-paced optimization objective to address persistent labeling errors.

title: Self-Paced Co-training

abstract: We study the problem of attributing the prediction of a deep network to its input features, a problem previously studied by several other works. We identify two fundamental axioms—Sensitivity and Implementation Invariance that attribution methods ought to satisfy. We show that they are not satisfied by most known attribution methods, which we consider to be a fundamental weakness of those methods. We use the axioms to guide the design of a new attribution method called Integrated Gradients. Our method requires no modification to the original network and is extremely simple to implement; it just needs a few calls to the standard gradient operator. We apply this method to a couple of image models, a couple of text models and a chemistry model, demonstrating its ability to debug networks, to extract rules from a network, and to enable users to engage with models better.
