paragraphs: This paper asks how to assign a deep network's prediction to its input features. Such assignments are intended to help people understand which parts of an input contribute to an output. The authors approach the problem by first identifying properties that an attribution method ought to satisfy, rather than judging explanations only by how plausible they appear.

They propose two fundamental axioms, Sensitivity and Implementation Invariance, and show that most known attribution methods do not satisfy them. These requirements guide the development of Integrated Gradients. The method works with the original network without modifying it and needs only a few calls to the standard gradient operator, making the proposed approach straightforward to implement.

The authors apply Integrated Gradients to image models, text models, and a chemistry model. These applications demonstrate uses in debugging networks, extracting rules, and helping users engage with model behavior. The contribution combines a principled way to assess attribution methods with a practical procedure, connecting desired explanation properties to a method that can be applied across different kinds of networks.
summary.tldr: Integrated Gradients uses two attribution axioms to guide a simple method for explaining network predictions through input-feature contributions.

title: Axiomatic Attribution for Deep Networks

abstract: The past few years have witnessed growth in the computational requirements for training deep convolutional neural networks. Current approaches parallelize training onto multiple devices by applying a single parallelization strategy (e.g., data or model parallelism) to all layers in a network. Although easy to reason about, these approaches result in suboptimal runtime performance in large-scale distributed training, since different layers in a network may prefer different parallelization strategies. In this paper, we propose layer-wise parallelism that allows each layer in a network to use an individual parallelization strategy. We jointly optimize how each layer is parallelized by solving a graph search problem. Our evaluation shows that layer-wise parallelism outperforms state-of-the-art approaches by increasing training throughput, reducing communication costs, achieving better scalability to multiple GPUs, while maintaining original network accuracy.

paragraphs: Training a convolutional network across multiple devices requires deciding how to divide its work. A common approach applies one strategy, such as data parallelism or model parallelism, throughout the network. This paper argues that such uniform choices can waste performance because different layers may benefit from different ways of distributing computation.

The proposed approach allows each layer to use its own parallelization strategy. These choices are optimized jointly by solving a graph-search problem. Joint optimization matters because the desired outcome is an efficient complete training process: the strategy chosen for one layer is part of a larger arrangement across the network.

The evaluation reports higher training throughput, lower communication costs, and better scaling across multiple GPUs than leading existing approaches, while preserving the original network accuracy. These findings support treating parallelization as a collection of coordinated layer-level decisions. The contribution concerns how training is organized across hardware, with the reported gains coming from greater flexibility in assigning work throughout the network.
summary.tldr: Jointly choosing a parallelization strategy for each network layer improves reported distributed-training efficiency while maintaining accuracy.

title: Exploring Hidden Dimensions in Accelerating Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: We seek to automate the design of molecules based on specific chemical properties. In computational terms, this task involves continuous embedding and generation of molecular graphs. Our primary contribution is the direct realization of molecular graphs, a task previously approached by generating linear SMILES strings instead of graphs. Our junction tree variational autoencoder generates molecular graphs in two phases, by first generating a tree-structured scaffold over chemical substructures, and then combining them into a molecule with a graph message passing network. This approach allows us to incrementally expand molecules while maintaining chemical validity at every step. We evaluate our model on multiple tasks ranging from molecular generation to optimization. Across these tasks, our model outperforms previous state-of-the-art baselines by a significant margin.

paragraphs: The paper aims to automate molecular design around desired chemical properties. Its main contribution is to generate the graphs directly, where earlier approaches had produced linear SMILES strings as the route to representing molecules.

A graph message-passing network then combines those components into a complete molecular graph. Separating scaffold generation from assembly gives the model a structured way to build a molecule from smaller chemical pieces.

The authors state that this process permits incremental expansion while maintaining chemical validity at every step. They evaluate it on several tasks spanning molecular generation and optimization, reporting significant improvements over previous leading baselines. The findings support the usefulness of organizing generation around chemical substructures: the representation serves both valid graph construction and the broader goal of searching for molecules with desirable properties.
summary.tldr: A two-stage variational autoencoder assembles chemically valid molecular graphs from substructure scaffolds and improves reported generation and optimization results.

title: Junction Tree Variational Autoencoder for Molecular Graph Generation

abstract: Many large-scale machine learning (ML) applications need to perform decentralized learning over datasets generated at different devices and locations. Such datasets pose a significant challenge to decentralized learning because their different contexts result in significant data distribution skew across devices/locations. In this paper, we take a step toward better understanding this challenge by presenting a detailed experimental study of decentralized DNN training on a common type of data skew: skewed distribution of data labels across devices/locations. Our study shows that: (i) skewed data labels are a fundamental and pervasive problem for decentralized learning, causing significant accuracy loss across many ML applications, DNN models, training datasets, and decentralized learning algorithms; (ii) the problem is particularly challenging for DNN models with batch normalization; and (iii) the degree of data skew is a key determinant of the difficulty of the problem. Based on these findings, we present SkewScout, a system-level approach that adapts the communication frequency of decentralized learning algorithms to the (skew-induced) accuracy loss between data partitions. We also show that group normalization can recover much of the accuracy loss of batch normalization.

paragraphs: Decentralized learning combines training across devices or locations whose datasets may have different distributions. This paper studies one common form of that mismatch: unequal distributions of labels across participants. Its experimental investigation examines how this label skew affects deep-network training across applications, architectures, datasets, and decentralized learning algorithms.

The study finds significant accuracy losses across the examined settings and identifies skew severity as an important determinant of difficulty. Networks using batch normalization are particularly affected. These findings connect the decentralized data distribution to both training-system behavior and a specific architectural choice, showing that the same degree of coordination may not suit every partitioning of data.

The authors introduce SkewScout, which adapts communication frequency according to accuracy loss induced by differences between data partitions. They also show that replacing batch normalization with group normalization can recover much of the lost accuracy. The proposed responses therefore operate at two levels: communication adapts to observed consequences of skew, while the normalization choice addresses a particularly vulnerable part of the model.
summary.tldr: Label skew harms decentralized learning, motivating adaptive communication through SkewScout and accuracy recovery through group normalization.

title: The Non-IID Data Quagmire of Decentralized Machine Learning

abstract: Variational Autoencoders (VAE) and their variants have been widely used in a variety of applications, such as dialog generation, image generation and disentangled representation learning. However, the existing VAE models may suffer from KL vanishing in language modeling and low reconstruction quality for disentangling. To address these issues, we propose a novel controllable variational autoencoder framework, ControlVAE, that combines a controller, inspired by automatic control theory, with the basic VAE to improve the performance of resulting generative models. Specifically, we design a new non-linear PI controller, a variant of the proportional-integral-derivative (PID) control, to automatically tune the hyperparameter (weight) added in the VAE objective using the output KL-divergence as feedback during model training. The framework is evaluated using three applications; namely, language modeling, disentangled representation learning, and image generation. The results show that ControlVAE can achieve much better reconstruction quality than the competitive methods for the comparable disentanglement performance. For language modeling, it not only averts the KL-vanishing, but also improves the diversity of generated text. Finally, we also demonstrate that ControlVAE improves the reconstruction quality for image generation compared to the original VAE.

paragraphs: Variational autoencoders can encounter different training problems across applications. In language modeling, their KL-divergence term may vanish; in disentangled representation learning, reconstruction quality can be poor. ControlVAE addresses these issues by making an objective weight responsive to what happens during training. It combines a basic variational autoencoder with a controller inspired by automatic control theory.

The controller uses the model’s output KL divergence as feedback and automatically adjusts the weight in the training objective. Specifically, the authors design a nonlinear proportional-integral controller, a variant of PID control. This turns the weighting choice into an ongoing feedback process, allowing the training objective to respond to the model’s observed behavior.

The framework is evaluated in language modeling, disentangled representation learning, and image generation. It achieves substantially better reconstruction than competing methods at comparable disentanglement performance. In language modeling, it avoids KL vanishing and increases generated-text diversity. For image generation, it improves reconstruction relative to the original VAE, supporting the usefulness of feedback-controlled weighting across the three applications.
summary.tldr: ControlVAE uses KL-divergence feedback to adjust an objective weight during training, improving reconstruction and addressing KL vanishing in the reported applications.

title: ControlVAE: Controllable Variational Autoencoder

abstract: We propose a new framework for designing estimators for off-policy evaluation in contextual bandits. Our approach is based on the asymptotically optimal doubly robust estimator, but we shrink the importance weights to minimize a bound on the mean squared error, which results in a better bias-variance tradeoff in finite samples. We use this optimization-based framework to obtain three estimators: (a) a weight-clipping estimator, (b) a new weight-shrinkage estimator, and (c) the first shrinkage-based estimator for combinatorial action sets. Extensive experiments in both standard and combinatorial bandit benchmark problems show that our estimators are highly adaptive and typically outperform state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: This paper studies off-policy evaluation in contextual bandits: estimating a policy's performance from data collected under another policy. Its starting point is the doubly robust estimator, which has an asymptotic optimality property. The authors focus on finite datasets, where an estimator's behavior depends on the balance between systematic error, or bias, and variability across samples.

Their method shrinks importance weights by optimizing an upper bound on mean squared error. This makes weight adjustment part of a stated optimization problem. The resulting tradeoff permits some bias in exchange for reduced variance, improving finite-sample behavior. The framework produces a weight-clipping estimator, a new weight-shrinkage estimator, and a shrinkage-based estimator for combinatorial action sets.

The combinatorial extension broadens the framework beyond the standard bandit setting to problems with structured collections of possible actions. Extensive experiments examine both standard and combinatorial benchmarks. The authors find that their estimators adapt well and typically outperform state-of-the-art methods. The claim is an empirical tendency across the evaluated problems, supported by a framework designed around finite-sample error rather than asymptotic optimality alone.
summary.tldr: Optimizing shrinkage of importance weights improves the finite-sample bias–variance tradeoff in doubly robust policy evaluation.

title: Doubly robust off-policy evaluation with shrinkage

abstract: The goal of universal machine translation is to learn to translate between any pair of languages. Despite impressive empirical results and an increasing interest in massively multilingual models, theoretical analysis on translation errors made by such universal machine translation models is only nascent. In this paper, we formally prove certain impossibilities of this endeavour in general, as well as prove positive results in the presence of additional (but natural) structure of data. For the former, we derive a lower bound on the translation error in the many-to-many translation setting, which shows that any algorithm aiming to learn shared sentence representations among multiple language pairs has to make a large translation error on at least one of the translation tasks, if no assumption on the structure of the languages is made. For the latter, we show that if the paired documents in the corpus follow a natural \emph{encoder-decoder} generative process, we can expect a natural notion of “generalization”: a linear number of language pairs, rather than quadratic, suffices to learn a good representation. Our theory also explains what kinds of connection graphs between pairs of languages are better suited: ones with longer paths result in worse sample complexity. We believe our theoretical insights and implications contribute to the future algorithmic design of universal machine translation.

paragraphs: Universal machine translation aims to translate between any pair of languages using shared representations. This paper studies when that ambition is theoretically possible. It establishes a lower bound showing that, without assumptions about language structure, algorithms learning shared sentence representations must incur large error on at least one translation task.

The positive result depends on additional structure: paired documents must arise from a natural encoder-decoder generative process. Under that assumption, a number of language pairs growing linearly with the number of languages can suffice to learn a good representation. This offers a theoretical basis for generalizing without observing the full quadratic collection of language pairs.

The arrangement of available pairs also matters. The paper analyzes connection graphs between languages and shows that longer paths lead to worse sample complexity. Its findings therefore identify both a barrier to unrestricted sharing and conditions that make sharing useful, while explaining why the pattern of multilingual training connections affects the amount of data needed.
summary.tldr: Shared translation representations face general impossibility results, but structured language generation allows learning from linearly many language pairs.

title: On Learning Language-Invariant Representations for Universal Machine Translation

abstract: Perception of time from sequentially acquired sensory inputs is rooted in everyday behaviors of individual organisms. Yet, most algorithms for time-series modeling fail to learn dynamics of random event timings directly from visual or audio inputs, requiring timing annotations during training that are usually unavailable for real-world applications. For instance, neuroscience perspectives on postdiction imply that there exist variable temporal ranges within which the incoming sensory inputs can affect the earlier perception, but such temporal ranges are mostly unannotated for real applications such as automatic speech recognition (ASR). In this paper, we present a probabilistic ordinary differential equation (ODE), called STochastic boundaRy ODE (STRODE), that learns both the timings and the dynamics of time series data without requiring any timing annotations during training. STRODE allows the usage of differential equations to sample from the posterior point processes, efficiently and analytically. We further provide theoretical guarantees on the learning of STRODE. Our empirical results show that our approach successfully infers event timings of time series data. Our method achieves competitive or superior performances compared to existing state-of-the-art methods for both synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Time-series models often need annotations identifying when events happen, even though those annotations may be unavailable for sensory data. The paper studies learning event timing directly alongside temporal dynamics. Its motivation includes perception processes in which later sensory input can influence earlier perception over variable, unannotated time ranges.

STRODE is a probabilistic ordinary differential equation model that learns both event timings and the dynamics of a time series without timing annotations during training. It also uses differential equations to sample efficiently and analytically from posterior point processes. This brings uncertainty about when events occur into the modeling approach rather than requiring their timing to be supplied.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees for learning STRODE and empirical evidence that it successfully infers event timings. Across synthetic and real datasets, its performance is competitive with or superior to existing state-of-the-art methods. The findings support jointly learning temporal structure and dynamics when the event boundaries needed by other approaches have not been annotated.
summary.tldr: STRODE learns event timings and time-series dynamics together through a probabilistic ODE without requiring timing annotations.

title: STRODE: Stochastic Boundary Ordinary Differential Equation

abstract: Active learning is widely used to reduce labeling effort and training time by repeatedly querying only the most beneficial samples from unlabeled data. In real-world problems where data cannot be stored indefinitely due to limited storage or privacy issues, the query selection and the model update should be performed as soon as a new data sample is observed. Various online active learning methods have been studied to deal with these challenges; however, there are difficulties in selecting representative query samples and updating the model efficiently without forgetting. In this study, we propose Message Passing Adaptive Resonance Theory (MPART) that learns the distribution and topology of input data online. Through message passing on the topological graph, MPART actively queries informative and representative samples, and continuously improves the classification performance using both labeled and unlabeled data. We evaluate our model in stream-based selective sampling scenarios with comparable query selection strategies, showing that MPART significantly outperforms competitive models.

paragraphs: Active learning reduces labeling work by asking for labels on selected examples. In streaming settings, however, storage or privacy constraints can prevent retaining data indefinitely. A model must decide what to query and how to update as examples arrive. This makes it difficult to choose representative examples while learning efficiently without forgetting earlier information.

Message Passing Adaptive Resonance Theory, or MPART, learns the distribution and connectivity structure of incoming data online. It represents that structure with a topological graph and passes information through the graph to guide label requests. The selection process seeks examples that are both informative and representative, while classification learning uses labeled and unlabeled data.

The authors evaluate MPART in stream-based selective-sampling settings using comparable query-selection strategies. They report that it significantly outperforms competitive models in those evaluations. The approach matters because it links immediate labeling decisions to an evolving picture of the data’s structure, allowing unlabeled observations to support continued learning as the stream arrives.
summary.tldr: MPART uses an evolving data graph and message passing to select labels and learn from streams, outperforming competitive models in reported evaluations.

title: Message Passing Adaptive Resonance Theory for Online Active Semi-supervised Learning

abstract: In neural machine translation, Cross Entropy loss (CE) is the standard loss function in two training methods of auto-regressive models, i.e., teacher forcing and scheduled sampling. In this paper, we propose mixed Cross Entropy loss (mixed CE) as a substitute for CE in both training approaches. In teacher forcing, the model trained with CE regards the translation problem as a one-to-one mapping process, while in mixed CE this process can be relaxed to one-to-many. In scheduled sampling, we show that mixed CE has the potential to encourage the training and testing behaviours to be similar to each other, more effectively mitigating the exposure bias problem. We demonstrate the superiority of mixed CE over CE on several machine translation datasets, WMT’16 Ro-En, WMT’16 Ru-En, and WMT’14 En-De in both teacher forcing and scheduled sampling setups. Furthermore, in WMT’14 En-De, we also find mixed CE consistently outperforms CE on a multi-reference set as well as a challenging paraphrased reference set. We also found the model trained with mixed CE is able to provide a better probability distribution defined over the translation output space. Our code is available at https://github.com/haorannlp/mix.

paragraphs: Machine translation can admit multiple valid outputs for the same input. This paper proposes mixed cross entropy as a replacement for standard cross entropy in two ways of training autoregressive translation models: teacher forcing and scheduled sampling. The motivation is to change how training represents acceptable outputs and relates to prediction at test time.

Under teacher forcing, the authors describe standard cross entropy as treating translation as a one-to-one mapping. Mixed cross entropy relaxes that treatment toward a one-to-many relationship. Under scheduled sampling, they argue that the replacement has the potential to make training and testing behavior more similar, thereby mitigating exposure bias more effectively.

Experiments on Romanian–English, Russian–English, and English–German translation datasets show improvements over standard cross entropy under both training approaches. On the English–German task, mixed cross entropy also consistently performs better with multiple references and challenging paraphrased references. The authors additionally report a better probability distribution over possible translation outputs. These findings support the loss as a way to accommodate output diversity while improving the evaluated translation models.
summary.tldr: Mixed cross entropy improves the evaluated translation models while allowing training to better accommodate multiple valid translations.

title: Mixed Cross Entropy Loss for Neural Machine Translation

abstract: In this work, we focus on the ability of graph neural networks (GNNs) to learn long-range patterns in graphs with edge features. Learning patterns that involve longer paths in the graph, requires using deeper GNNs. However, GNNs suffer from a drop in performance with increasing network depth. To improve the performance of deeper GNNs, previous works have investigated normalization techniques and various types of skip connections. While they are designed to improve depth-wise backpropagation between the representations of the same node in successive layers, they do not improve breadth-wise backpropagation between representations of neighbouring nodes. To analyse the consequences, we design synthetic datasets serving as a testbed for the ability of GNNs to learn long-range patterns. Our analysis shows that several commonly used GNN variants with only depth-wise skip connections indeed have problems learning long-range patterns. They are clearly outperformed by an attention-based GNN architecture that we propose for improving both depth- and breadth-wise backpropagation. We also verify that the presented architecture is competitive on real-world data.

paragraphs: Learning graph patterns that span longer paths requires deeper graph neural networks in the setting studied here. Yet increasing depth often reduces performance. The paper examines graphs with edge features and argues that common approaches to this problem address only part of how training signals travel through the network.

Normalization and skip connections often help signals pass between successive representations of the same node. The authors distinguish this depth-wise flow from breadth-wise flow between neighboring nodes. They construct synthetic datasets to examine long-range learning and propose an attention-based architecture designed to improve backpropagation along both kinds of connections.

On these testbeds, several common architectures with only depth-wise skip connections struggle to learn long-range patterns. The proposed architecture clearly outperforms them, and the authors also find it competitive on real-world data. These results make the distinction between the two directions consequential: improving connections through layers alone did not provide the same long-range learning performance in the reported tests.
summary.tldr: An attention-based graph network improves training signals across both layers and neighboring nodes, helping it learn long-range patterns.

title: Improving Breadth-Wise Backpropagation in Graph Neural Networks Helps Learning Long-Range Dependencies.

abstract: It is not trivial to optimally learn a 3D Convolutional Neural Networks (3D ConvNets) due to high complexity and various options of the training scheme. The most common hand-tuning process starts from learning 3D ConvNets using short video clips and then is followed by learning long-term temporal dependency using lengthy clips, while gradually decaying the learning rate from high to low as training progresses. The fact that such process comes along with several heuristic settings motivates the study to seek an optimal "path" to automate the entire training. In this paper, we decompose the path into a series of training "states" and specify the hyper-parameters, e.g., learning rate and the length of input clips, in each state. The estimation of the knee point on the performance-epoch curve triggers the transition from one state to another. We perform dynamic programming over all the candidate states to plan the optimal permutation of states, i.e., optimization path. Furthermore, we devise a new 3D ConvNets with a unique design of dual-head classifier to improve spatial and temporal discrimination. Extensive experiments on seven public video recognition benchmarks demonstrate the advantages of our proposal. With the optimization planning, our 3D ConvNets achieves superior results when comparing to the state-of-the-art recognition methods. More remarkably, we obtain the top-1 accuracy of 80.5% and 82.7% on Kinetics-400 and Kinetics-600 datasets, respectively.

This paper turns that sequence of training choices into an explicit planning problem.

The authors divide training into states, each specifying hyperparameters. An estimated knee point in the performance-versus-epoch curve triggers movement between states. The paper also introduces a 3D network with a dual-head classifier designed to improve spatial and temporal discrimination.

These findings support the combined training and architecture design, with the planning optimum defined over the candidate training states.
summary.tldr: Dynamic programming plans training-state sequences for 3D video networks, paired with a dual-head classifier that achieves strong recognition results.

title: Optimization Planning for 3D ConvNets

abstract: We address the problem of learning binary decision trees that partition data for some downstream task. We propose to learn discrete parameters (i.e., for tree traversals and node pruning) and continuous parameters (i.e., for tree split functions and prediction functions) simultaneously using argmin differentiation. We do so by sparsely relaxing a mixed-integer program for the discrete parameters, to allow gradients to pass through the program to continuous parameters. We derive customized algorithms to efficiently compute the forward and backward passes. This means that our tree learning procedure can be used as an (implicit) layer in arbitrary deep networks, and can be optimized with arbitrary loss functions. We demonstrate that our approach produces binary trees that are competitive with existing single tree and ensemble approaches, in both supervised and unsupervised settings. Further, apart from greedy approaches (which do not have competitive accuracies), our method is faster to train than all other tree-learning baselines we compare with.

paragraphs: Learning a binary decision tree involves both discrete choices and continuous parameters. Discrete choices determine traversal and pruning, while continuous parameters define splits and predictions. This paper proposes learning these parts together, so the tree's structure and its numerical parameters can be optimized for the same downstream task.

The authors formulate the discrete decisions through a mixed-integer program and introduce a sparse relaxation that permits gradients to pass through its solution. Argmin differentiation then connects that optimization problem to the continuous parameters. Customized forward and backward algorithms make the procedure efficient enough to serve as an implicit layer inside deep networks and to work with arbitrary loss functions.

Experiments show competitive binary trees against the single-tree and ensemble approaches tested, in both supervised and unsupervised settings. Training is faster than all compared tree-learning baselines except greedy methods, whose accuracies are not competitive in those comparisons. The result combines flexibility in how trees are trained with evidence of useful accuracy and training efficiency.
summary.tldr: Argmin differentiation lets binary trees learn discrete structure and continuous parameters together and function as trainable layers in deep networks.

title: Learning Binary Decision Trees by Argmin Differentiation

abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are considered a promising alternative to Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) for their event-driven computing paradigm when deployed on energy-efficient neuromorphic hardware. Recently, deep SNNs have shown breathtaking performance improvement through cutting-edge training strategy and flexible structure, which also scales up the number of parameters and computational burdens in a single network. Inspired by the state transition of dendritic spines in the filopodial model of spinogenesis, we model different states of SNN weights, facilitating weight optimization for pruning. Furthermore, the pruning speed can be regulated by using different functions describing the growing threshold of state transition. We organize these techniques as a dynamic pruning algorithm based on nonlinear reparameterization mapping from spine size to SNN weights. Our approach yields sparse deep networks on the large-scale dataset (SEW ResNet18 on ImageNet) while maintaining state-of-the-art low performance loss ( 3% at 88.8% sparsity) compared to existing pruning methods on directly trained SNNs. Moreover, we find out pruning speed regulation while learning is crucial to avoiding disastrous performance degradation at the final stages of training, which may shed light on future work on SNN pruning.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks offer an event-driven computing approach suited to energy-efficient neuromorphic hardware. As their performance improves through deeper and more flexible structures, parameter counts and computational burdens also grow. This paper develops a pruning method inspired by the changing states of dendritic spines.

The method assigns different states to network weights and uses a nonlinear mapping from spine size to weight value. State-transition thresholds grow during learning, and different growth functions control how quickly pruning proceeds. These elements form a dynamic pruning algorithm that couples weight optimization with the progression toward a sparse network.

For SEW ResNet18 on ImageNet, the authors report 88.8% sparsity with a 3% performance loss, described as state-of-the-art low loss compared with existing pruning methods for directly trained spiking networks. They also find that regulating pruning speed during learning is crucial to avoiding severe degradation late in training. The result emphasizes that the timing of pruning, alongside the weight-state model, matters for retaining performance.
summary.tldr: A dendritic-spine-inspired weight model enables dynamic pruning of spiking networks, with pruning speed crucial to preserving late-training performance.

title: State Transition of Dendritic Spines Improves Learning of Sparse Spiking Neural Networks

abstract: We study and compare different Graph Neural Network extensions that increase the expressive power of GNNs beyond the Weisfeiler-Leman test. We focus on (i) GNNs based on higher order WL methods, (ii) GNNs that preprocess small substructures in the graph, (iii) GNNs that preprocess the graph up to a small radius, and (iv) GNNs that slightly perturb the graph to compute an embedding. We begin by presenting a simple improvement for this last extension that strictly increases the expressive power of this GNN variant. Then, as our main result, we compare the expressiveness of these extensions to each other through a series of example constructions that can be distinguished by one of the extensions, but not by another one. We also show negative examples that are particularly challenging for each of the extensions, and we prove several claims about the ability of these extensions to count cliques and cycles in the graph.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can differ in which graph structures they can distinguish. This paper compares extensions designed to exceed the expressive power associated with the Weisfeiler–Leman test. Its focus is the structural information these architectures can represent, making expressiveness itself the object of study.

The comparison covers four approaches: higher-order Weisfeiler–Leman methods, preprocessing small substructures, preprocessing neighborhoods within a small radius, and slightly perturbing a graph before computing its representation. The authors first improve the perturbation-based approach and prove that the change strictly increases that variant’s expressive power.

The main comparisons use carefully constructed examples that one extension can distinguish while another cannot. Such examples make differences between approaches concrete without requiring a single ranking to capture every capability. The paper also provides difficult examples for each extension and proves results about counting cliques and cycles. Together, these findings clarify which structural distinctions different design choices can capture and where their expressive limits remain.
summary.tldr: The paper proves differences in the structural distinctions several powerful graph neural network extensions can express.

title: A Theoretical Comparison of Graph Neural Network Extensions

abstract: Transformers based on the attention mechanism have achieved impressive success in various areas. However, the attention mechanism has a quadratic complexity, significantly impeding Transformers from dealing with numerous tokens and scaling up to bigger models. Previous methods mainly utilize the similarity decomposition and the associativity of matrix multiplication to devise linear-time attention mechanisms. They avoid degeneration of attention to a trivial distribution by reintroducing inductive biases such as the locality, thereby at the expense of model generality and expressiveness. In this paper, we linearize Transformers free from specific inductive biases based on the flow network theory. We cast attention as the information flow aggregated from the sources (values) to the sinks (results) through the learned flow capacities (attentions). Within this framework, we apply the property of flow conservation into attention and propose the Flow-Attention mechanism of linear complexity. By respectively conserving the incoming flow of sinks for source competition and the outgoing flow of sources for sink allocation, Flow-Attention inherently generates informative attentions without using specific inductive biases. Empowered by the Flow-Attention, Flowformer yields strong performance in linear time for wide areas, including long sequence, time series, vision, natural language, and reinforcement learning. The code and settings are available at this repository: https://github.com/thuml/Flowformer.

paragraphs: Standard attention becomes expensive as the number of tokens increases because its computational cost grows quadratically. Previous linear-time approaches can need added assumptions, such as favoring nearby tokens, to keep attention from collapsing into an uninformative distribution. Flowformer seeks efficient attention without imposing those particular biases, preserving flexibility across different kinds of data.

The paper interprets attention as a flow network. Values supply information, output representations receive it, and learned attention determines the capacities connecting them. Flow-Attention imposes conservation constraints on this flow: conserving incoming flow at outputs creates competition among sources, while conserving outgoing flow from sources governs allocation to outputs. These constraints generate informative attention within a mechanism of linear complexity.

The resulting Flowformer is reported to perform strongly across long sequences, time series, vision, language, and reinforcement learning. The breadth of these evaluations matters because the mechanism is designed to avoid assumptions tied to a particular application. The central contribution is a conservation-based way to structure efficient attention, together with empirical evidence of usefulness across several domains.
summary.tldr: Flowformer uses conservation constraints on information flow to create linear-complexity attention without specific inductive biases such as locality.

title: Flowformer: Linearizing Transformers with Conservation Flows

abstract: Mixup is a data augmentation technique that relies on training using random convex combinations of data points and their labels. In recent years, Mixup has become a standard primitive used in the training of state-of-the-art image classification models due to its demonstrated benefits over empirical risk minimization with regards to generalization and robustness. In this work, we try to explain some of this success from a feature learning perspective. We focus our attention on classification problems in which each class may have multiple associated features (or $\textit{views}$) that can be used to predict the class correctly. Our main theoretical results demonstrate that, for a non-trivial class of data distributions with two features per class, training a 2-layer convolutional network using empirical risk minimization can lead to learning only one feature for almost all classes while training with a specific instantiation of Mixup succeeds in learning both features for every class. We also show empirically that these theoretical insights extend to the practical settings of image benchmarks modified to have multiple features.

paragraphs: Mixup trains models on combinations of examples and their labels. This paper investigates its benefits through the features a classifier learns. The focus is on classes that have multiple useful cues, where learning one predictive cue can leave another available cue unused.

The theoretical analysis considers a nontrivial class of data distributions with two features per class and a two-layer convolutional network. Ordinary empirical risk minimization can learn only one feature for almost all classes. Under the analyzed setting, a particular Mixup variant succeeds in learning both features for every class, establishing a concrete difference in feature coverage.

Experiments on image benchmarks modified to contain multiple features support the relevance of these insights beyond the theoretical construction. The results offer an explanation for some of Mixup's observed benefits: its training procedure can encourage a model to acquire more of the available predictive information. The formal claim remains tied to the specified distributions, architecture, and Mixup instantiation, while the experiments provide evidence of broader practical relevance.
summary.tldr: For an analyzed two-feature setting, midpoint Mixup learns both class cues where ordinary training can learn only one.

title: Provably Learning Diverse Features in Multi-View Data with Midpoint Mixup

abstract: The state-of-the-art memory model is the General Associative Memory Model, a generalization of the classical Hopfield network. Like its ancestor, the general associative memory has a well-defined state-dependant energy surface, and its memories correlate with its fixed points. This is unlike human memories, which are commonly sequential rather than separated fixed points. In this paper, we introduce a class of General Sequential Episodic Memory Models (GSEMM) that, in the adiabatic limit, exhibit a dynamic energy surface, leading to a series of meta-stable states capable of encoding memory sequences. A multiple-timescale architecture enables the dynamic nature of the energy surface with newly introduced asymmetric synapses and signal propagation delays. We demonstrate its dense capacity under polynomial activation functions. GSEMM combines separate memories, short and long sequential episodic memories, under a unified theoretical framework, demonstrating how energy-based memory modeling can provide richer, human-like episodes.

paragraphs: Classical Hopfield-style memory models associate memories with fixed points on an energy surface. This makes individual stored states central to the description of memory. The paper asks how an energy-based framework can also represent sequences, motivated by the sequential character of many human memories.

The authors introduce General Sequential Episodic Memory Models, which use multiple timescales, asymmetric synapses, and delays in signal propagation. In the adiabatic limit, these ingredients yield an energy surface that changes over time. The resulting succession of metastable states can encode a memory sequence: states can persist temporarily while still forming part of an evolving episode.

The paper demonstrates dense capacity when using polynomial activation functions and places separate memories alongside short and long episodic sequences in one theoretical framework. Its contribution is a model class that expands what energy-based memory dynamics can represent. The connection to human-like episodes concerns the richer sequential structure supported by the model, with the dynamic-energy description explicitly tied to the stated adiabatic limit.
summary.tldr: A memory model with multiple timescales and delayed asymmetric interactions represents sequences through a changing energy surface.

title: General Sequential Episodic Memory Model

abstract: We propose a simple and general framework for nonparametric estimation of heterogeneous treatment effects under fairness constraints. Under standard regularity conditions, we show that the resulting estimators possess the double robustness property. We use this framework to characterize the trade-off between fairness and the maximum welfare achievable by the optimal policy. We evaluate the methods in a simulation study and illustrate them in a real-world case study.
originalAbstract: We propose a simple and general framework for nonparametric estimation of heterogeneous treatment effects under fairness constraints. Under standard regularity conditions, we show that the resulting estimators possess the double robustness property. We use this framework to characterize the trade-off between fairness and the maximum welfare achievable by the optimal policy. We evaluate the methods in a simulation study and illustrate them in a real-world case study.

paragraphs: Treatment effects can differ across people, so a policy that assigns treatments needs information about those differences. This paper proposes a general framework for estimating such heterogeneous effects while imposing fairness constraints. Its nonparametric approach addresses the estimation problem without fixing a particular finite-dimensional formula for how treatment effects vary.

A central theoretical result is that the resulting estimators have the double robustness property under standard regularity conditions. This gives the framework a robustness guarantee alongside its fairness constraints. The qualification matters: the stated result depends on those regularity conditions. Fairness and statistical robustness are therefore considered together within the estimation framework, rather than being evaluated as entirely separate concerns.

The authors then use the framework to characterize a trade-off between fairness and the greatest welfare an optimal policy can achieve. This connects constraints on estimation to the quality of decisions made using those estimates. A simulation study evaluates the methods, and a real-world case study illustrates their use. The contribution combines a general estimation framework, a conditional robustness result, and an analysis of the welfare consequences of fairness requirements.
summary.tldr: A fairness-constrained treatment-effect framework provides conditional double robustness and characterizes the trade-off between fairness and achievable policy welfare.

title: Fair and Robust Estimation of Heterogeneous Treatment Effects for Policy Learning

abstract: Neural Controlled Differential equations (NCDE) are a powerful mechanism to model the dynamics in temporal sequences, e.g., applications involving physiological measures, where apart from the initial condition, the dynamics also depend on subsequent measures or even a different "control" sequence. But NCDEs do not scale well to longer sequences. Existing strategies adapt rough path theory, and instead model the dynamics over summaries known as log signatures. While rigorous and elegant, invertibility of these summaries is difficult, and limits the scope of problems where these ideas can offer strong benefits (reconstruction, generative modeling). For tasks where it is sensible to assume that the (long) sequences in the training data are a fixed length of temporal measurements – this assumption holds in most experiments tackled in the literature – we describe an efficient simplification. First, we recast the regression/classification task as an integral transform. We then show how restricting the class of operators (permissible in the integral transform), allows the use of a known algorithm that leverages non-standard Wavelets to decompose the operator. Thereby, our task (learning the operator) radically simplifies. A neural variant of this idea yields consistent improvements across a wide gamut of use cases tackled in existing works. We also describe a novel application on modeling tasks involving coupled differential equations.

paragraphs: Neural controlled differential equations describe evolving systems whose behavior depends on measurements arriving after the initial state. They are useful for temporal data but become difficult to scale to long sequences. Existing approaches summarize sequences using log signatures, yet difficulties in inverting these summaries restrict their usefulness for tasks such as reconstruction and generation.

This paper develops a simplification for settings where training sequences can reasonably be assumed to have a fixed length. The authors express regression or classification as an integral transform. By restricting which operators the transform can use, they make it possible to apply an established decomposition algorithm based on non-standard wavelets, substantially simplifying the operator-learning task.

A neural version of this construction produces consistent improvements across a broad collection of use cases considered in earlier work. The paper also presents an application involving coupled differential equations. The approach matters because it connects a structured mathematical representation to practical sequence modeling, with the fixed-length assumption and restricted operator class forming explicit parts of the construction.
summary.tldr: For fixed-length temporal sequences, a restricted integral-operator formulation enables wavelet decompositions that simplify learning and improve reported performance.

title: Controlled Differential Equations on Long Sequences via Non-standard Wavelets

abstract: Cardinality sketches are popular data structures that enhance the efficiency of working with large data sets. The sketches are randomized representations of sets that are only of logarithmic size but can support set merges and approximate cardinality (i.e., distinct count) queries. When queries are not adaptive, that is, they do not depend on preceding query responses, the design provides strong guarantees of correctly answering a number of queries exponential in the sketch size $k$. In this work, we investigate the performance of cardinality sketches in adaptive settings and unveil inherent vulnerabilities. We design an attack against the “standard” estimators that constructs an adversarial input by post-processing responses to a set of simple non-adaptive queries of size linear in the sketch size $k$. Empirically, our attack used only $4k$ queries with the widely used HyperLogLog (HLL++) Flajolet et al., 2007; Heule et al., 2013) sketch. The simple attack technique suggests it can be effective with post-processed natural workloads. Finally and importantly, we demonstrate that the vulnerability is inherent as any estimator applied to known sketch structures can be attacked using a number of queries that is quadratic in $k$, matching a generic upper bound.

paragraphs: Cardinality sketches compactly represent sets while supporting merges and approximate distinct counts. For queries chosen independently of earlier responses, these randomized structures offer strong guarantees over very large numbers of queries. This paper investigates what happens when responses can influence the construction of later inputs.

The authors give an attack on standard estimators that constructs an adversarial input by post-processing answers to a simple collection of nonadaptive queries. The required collection grows linearly with sketch size k. In experiments with HLL++, the attack used only 4k queries. Its simplicity also suggests possible effectiveness when applied to post-processed natural workloads, although that is presented as a possibility.

The paper further shows that changing the estimator alone cannot remove the vulnerability for known sketch structures: any estimator on those structures can be attacked with a number of queries quadratic in k. This matches a generic upper bound. The results distinguish strong guarantees for nonadaptive querying from the substantially different behavior possible when query responses shape future inputs.
summary.tldr: Cardinality sketches can fail under adaptively constructed inputs, with attacks requiring only linear or quadratic numbers of queries in sketch size.

title: Unmasking Vulnerabilities: Cardinality Sketches under Adaptive Inputs

abstract: This work focuses on the training dynamics of one associative memory module storing outer products of token embeddings. We reduce this problem to the study of a system of particles, which interact according to properties of the data distribution and correlations between embeddings. Through theory and experiments, we provide several insights. In overparameterized regimes, we obtain logarithmic growth of the “classification margins.” Yet, we show that imbalance in token frequencies and memory interferences due to correlated embeddings lead to oscillatory transitory regimes. The oscillations are more pronounced with large step sizes, which can create benign loss spikes, although these learning rates speed up the dynamics and accelerate the asymptotic convergence. We also find that underparameterized regimes lead to suboptimal memorization schemes. Finally, we assess the validity of our findings on small Transformer models.

The interactions depend on the data distribution and on correlations among embeddings, connecting the mathematical model to properties of the stored tokens.

summary.tldr: A particle-system analysis links associative-memory learning dynamics to token imbalance, embedding interference, and step-size-dependent loss spikes.

title: Learning Associative Memories with Gradient Descent

abstract: Robust and effective scaling of models from small to large width typically requires the precise adjustment of many algorithmic and architectural details, such as parameterization and optimizer choices. In this work, we propose a new perspective on parameterization by investigating a key assumption in prior work about the alignment between parameters and data and derive new theoretical results under weaker assumptions and a broader set of optimizers. Our extensive empirical investigation includes tens of thousands of models trained with all combinations of three optimizers, four parameterizations, several alignment assumptions, more than a dozen learning rates, and fourteen model sizes up to 27B parameters. We find that the best learning rate scaling prescription would often have been excluded by the assumptions in prior work. Our results show that all parameterizations, not just maximal update parameterization (muP), can achieve hyperparameter transfer; moreover, our novel per-layer learning rate prescription for standard parameterization outperforms muP. Finally, we demonstrate that an overlooked aspect of parameterization, the epsilon parameter in Adam, must be scaled correctly to avoid gradient underflow and propose Adam-atan2, a new numerically stable, scale-invariant version of Adam that eliminates the epsilon hyperparameter entirely.

paragraphs: Increasing a model’s width requires coordinated choices about parameterization, learning rates, and optimization. This paper revisits assumptions about alignment between parameters and data that underlie earlier scaling prescriptions. It derives theoretical results using weaker assumptions and covering a broader range of optimizers.

The empirical study trains tens of thousands of models across three optimizers, four parameterizations, multiple alignment assumptions, more than twelve learning rates, and fourteen sizes reaching 27 billion parameters. The best learning-rate scaling rules often fall outside what earlier assumptions would permit. All studied parameterizations can support hyperparameter transfer, and the proposed per-layer learning rates for standard parameterization outperform maximal update parameterization in the reported study.

The authors also identify Adam’s epsilon parameter as an important part of scaling: it must be adjusted correctly to avoid gradient underflow. They introduce Adam-atan2, a numerically stable, scale-invariant variant that removes epsilon entirely. Together, the findings broaden the available routes to successful scaling and show that optimizer details can materially affect whether a parameterization works well.
summary.tldr: Weaker scaling assumptions reveal effective learning-rate rules across parameterizations, while Adam-atan2 removes a numerically consequential epsilon setting.

title: Scaling Exponents Across Parameterizations and Optimizers

abstract: Existing research of video understanding still struggles to achieve in-depth comprehension and reasoning in complex videos, primarily due to the under-exploration of two key bottlenecks: fine-grained spatial-temporal perceptive understanding and cognitive-level video scene comprehension. This paper bridges the gap by presenting a novel solution. We first introduce a novel video Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM), MotionEpic, which achieves fine-grained pixel-level spatial-temporal video grounding by integrating video spatial-temporal scene graph (STSG) representation. Building upon MotionEpic, we then develop a Video-of-Thought (VoT) reasoning framework. VoT inherits the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) core, breaking down a complex task into simpler and manageable sub-problems, and addressing them step-by-step from a low-level pixel perception to high-level cognitive interpretation. Extensive experiments across various complex video QA benchmarks demonstrate that our overall framework strikingly boosts existing state-of-the-art. To our knowledge, this is the first attempt at successfully implementing the CoT technique for achieving human-level video reasoning, where we show great potential in extending it to a wider range of video understanding scenarios. Systems and codes will be open later.

paragraphs: Understanding a complex video requires both detailed perception across space and time and interpretation of what the scene means. This paper treats those as linked bottlenecks. It introduces MotionEpic, a multimodal language model that incorporates spatial-temporal scene graphs to support fine-grained, pixel-level grounding of video content.

On top of MotionEpic, the authors build Video-of-Thought, a reasoning framework inspired by chain-of-thought prompting. It divides a complex task into smaller subproblems and addresses them progressively, moving from low-level visual perception toward higher-level interpretation. The design connects the model's ability to locate relevant video content with its ability to reason about that content.

The authors describe the work as, to their knowledge, a first successful use of chain-of-thought toward human-level video reasoning and suggest potential applications to broader video-understanding settings. The stated benchmark findings support the combined perception-and-reasoning framework; the broader extension is presented as an opportunity.
summary.tldr: Video-of-Thought combines detailed video grounding with stepwise reasoning to improve performance on complex video question-answering benchmarks.

title: Video-of-Thought: Step-by-Step Video Reasoning from Perception to Cognition

abstract: Learning high-quality $Q$-value functions plays a key role in the success of many modern off-policy deep reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms. Previous works primarily focus on addressing the value overestimation issue, an outcome of adopting function approximators and off-policy learning. Deviating from the common viewpoint, we observe that $Q$-values are often underestimated in the latter stage of the RL training process, potentially hindering policy learning and reducing sample efficiency. We find that such a long-neglected phenomenon is often related to the use of inferior actions from the current policy in Bellman updates as compared to the more optimal action samples in the replay buffer. We propose the Blended Exploitation and Exploration (BEE) operator, a simple yet effective approach that updates $Q$-value using both historical best-performing actions and the current policy. Based on BEE, the resulting practical algorithm BAC outperforms state-of-the-art methods in over 50 continuous control tasks and achieves strong performance in failure-prone scenarios and real-world robot tasks. Benchmark results and videos are available at https://jity16.github.io/BEE/.

paragraphs: Off-policy reinforcement learning relies on Q-values to estimate how useful actions are. Much prior work addresses overestimation, but this paper observes that underestimation often appears later in training. Such pessimistic values may slow policy learning and reduce sample efficiency, making the opposite direction of estimation error worth addressing as well.

The authors connect this behavior to Bellman updates that use actions from the current policy even when the replay buffer contains better actions. Their Blended Exploitation and Exploration operator, or BEE, updates Q-values using both historically successful actions and the current policy. This allows past successes to contribute to value learning alongside the policy's present behavior.

The resulting practical algorithm, BAC, outperforms state-of-the-art methods across more than 50 continuous control tasks and performs strongly in failure-prone settings and real-world robot tasks. These results support using successful stored experience more directly in value updates. The diagnosis remains qualified: underestimation is observed often, and inferior current-policy actions are frequently related to it, rather than being asserted as the only cause of value-learning problems.
summary.tldr: BEE blends historically successful replay-buffer actions with current-policy actions to address value underestimation and improve off-policy learning.

title: Seizing Serendipity: Exploiting the Value of Past Success in Off-Policy Actor-Critic

abstract: We provide an efficient replicable algorithm for the problem of learning large-margin halfspaces. Our results improve upon the algorithms provided by Impagliazzo, Lei, Pitassi, and Sorrell (STOC, 2022). We design the first dimension-independent replicable algorithm for this task which runs in polynomial time, is proper, and has strictly improved sample complexity compared to the one achieved by Impagliazzo et al. (STOC, 2022) with respect to all the relevant parameters. Moreover, our algorithm has sample complexity that is optimal with respect to the accuracy parameter $\epsilon$. Departing from the requirement of polynomial time algorithms, using the DP-to-Replicability reduction of Bun et al. (STOC 2023), we show how to obtain a replicable algorithm for large-margin halfspaces with improved sample complexity with respect to the margin parameter $\tau$, but running time doubly exponential in $1/\tau^2$ and worse sample complexity dependence on $\epsilon$ than our previous algorithm. We then design an improved algorithm with better sample complexity than both of our previous algorithms and running time exponential in $1/\tau^{2}.$

paragraphs: The paper studies replicable learning of large-margin halfspaces, a setting involving linear decision boundaries with a margin. It develops algorithms that improve the amount of training data required while examining how those improvements interact with computational cost. The results distinguish efficient learning from alternatives that spend considerably more time to reduce sample requirements.

The first algorithm runs in polynomial time, is dimension-independent, and is proper, meaning it returns a hypothesis from the class being learned. Its sample complexity improves on the cited earlier replicable algorithms across all relevant parameters. Its dependence on the accuracy parameter is also optimal.

The authors then explore two more computationally expensive constructions. A reduction from differential privacy to replicability improves dependence on the margin but requires doubly exponential time in the inverse squared margin and worsens accuracy dependence relative to the first algorithm. Their final construction improves sample complexity over both earlier constructions and needs exponential time in the inverse squared margin. Together, these results sharpen the available tradeoffs between data requirements and computation for replicable learning.
summary.tldr: New replicable halfspace learners improve sample complexity, with distinct tradeoffs between polynomial-time efficiency and more data-efficient exponential-time algorithms.

title: Replicable Learning of Large-Margin Halfspaces

abstract: Independent evaluation and red teaming are critical for identifying the risks posed by generative AI systems. However, the terms of service and enforcement strategies used by prominent AI companies to deter model misuse have disincentives on good faith safety evaluations. This causes some researchers to fear that conducting such research or releasing their findings will result in account suspensions or legal reprisal. Although some companies offer researcher access programs, they are an inadequate substitute for independent research access, as they have limited community representation, receive inadequate funding, and lack independence from corporate incentives. We propose that major generative AI developers commit to providing a legal and technical safe harbor, protecting public interest safety research and removing the threat of account suspensions or legal reprisal. These proposals emerged from our collective experience conducting safety, privacy, and trustworthiness research on generative AI systems, where norms and incentives could be better aligned with public interests, without exacerbating model misuse. We believe these commitments are a necessary step towards more inclusive and unimpeded community efforts to tackle the risks of generative AI.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that independent safety evaluation faces obstacles from the same company rules intended to prevent model misuse. Researchers may fear losing access or facing legal action for conducting good-faith investigations or publishing findings. The authors view those incentives as a barrier to identifying risks in generative AI systems.

They propose that major developers establish both legal and technical safe harbors for public-interest safety research. These commitments would remove threats of account suspension or legal reprisal for protected work. The paper also argues that company-run researcher access programs are inadequate substitutes because of limited community representation, insufficient funding, and dependence on corporate incentives.

The proposal draws on the authors’ collective experience studying safety, privacy, and trustworthiness. Their stated goal is to align research norms and incentives with public interests without worsening misuse. They present safe-harbor commitments as a necessary step toward broader, less obstructed community participation. The contribution is an institutional argument about enabling independent scrutiny, grounded in researchers’ experiences of existing access and enforcement practices.
summary.tldr: The authors call for legal and technical safe harbors that protect independent, good-faith AI safety research.

title: Position: A Safe Harbor for AI Evaluation and Red Teaming

abstract: Learning representations of well-trained neural network models holds the promise to provide an understanding of the inner workings of those models. However, previous work has either faced limitations when processing larger networks or was task-specific to either discriminative or generative tasks. This paper introduces the SANE approach to weight-space learning. SANE overcomes previous limitations by learning task-agnostic representations of neural networks that are scalable to larger models of varying architectures and that show capabilities beyond a single task. Our method extends the idea of hyper-representations towards sequential processing of subsets of neural network weights, thus allowing one to embed larger neural networks as a set of tokens into the learned representation space. SANE reveals global model information from layer-wise embeddings, and it can sequentially generate unseen neural network models, which was unattainable with previous hyper-representation learning methods. Extensive empirical evaluation demonstrates that SANE matches or exceeds state-of-the-art performance on several weight representation learning benchmarks, particularly in initialization for new tasks and larger ResNet architectures.

paragraphs: SANE learns representations of trained neural networks by processing their weights. Earlier approaches struggled with larger models or focused on one type of task, such as discrimination or generation. This paper aims for representations that work across tasks and scale to larger networks with varying architectures, broadening what weight-space learning can support.

The authors show that embeddings formed at the layer level reveal global information about the model, and that SANE can sequentially generate previously unseen neural networks.

In extensive empirical evaluations, SANE matches or exceeds state-of-the-art performance on several weight-representation benchmarks. The reported strengths are particularly evident in initialization for new tasks and larger ResNet architectures. The contribution combines a way to handle larger weight collections with evidence that the resulting representations support multiple uses, including understanding model properties and producing new models.
summary.tldr: SANE sequentially represents neural-network weights as tokens, supporting scalable model analysis, initialization, and generation.

title: Towards Scalable and Versatile Weight Space Learning

abstract: The success of SGD in deep learning has been ascribed by prior works to the implicit bias induced by finite batch sizes (”SGD noise”). While prior works focused on offline learning (i.e., multiple-epoch training), we study the impact of SGD noise on online (i.e., single epoch) learning. Through an extensive empirical analysis of image and language data, we demonstrate that small batch sizes do not confer any implicit bias advantages in online learning. In contrast to offline learning, the benefits of SGD noise in online learning are strictly computational, facilitating more cost-effective gradient steps. This suggests that SGD in the online regime can be construed as taking noisy steps along the ”golden path” of the noiseless gradient descent algorithm. We study this hypothesis and provide supporting evidence in loss and function space. Our findings challenge the prevailing understanding of SGD and offer novel insights into its role in online learning.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent estimates training updates from batches of examples, introducing noise compared with a noiseless gradient. Earlier work has attributed some of its success to the way this noise favors particular solutions. This paper examines that explanation in online learning, defined here as training for a single epoch, rather than repeatedly revisiting the data.

Through extensive experiments on image and language data, the authors find no implicit-bias advantage from small batches in the online setting they study. They instead identify a computational benefit: smaller batches make individual gradient steps cheaper. This changes the interpretation of why noisy updates are useful in this regime.

The authors propose that online stochastic gradient descent follows noisy steps along the trajectory of noiseless gradient descent. They investigate this picture through both losses and the functions learned by the models, finding supporting evidence. The contribution is an empirical challenge to transferring explanations from multiple-epoch training directly to single-epoch training; the distinction between those regimes is central to the claim.
summary.tldr: Experiments suggest that small batches benefit single-epoch learning through cheaper updates, without an additional implicit-bias advantage.

title: Beyond Implicit Bias: The Insignificance of SGD Noise in Online Learning

abstract: Discovery of causal relationships is a fundamental goal of science and vital for sound decision making. As such, there has been considerable interest in causal discovery methods with provable guarantees. Existing works have thus far largely focused on discovery under hard intervention and infinite-samples, in which intervening on a node readily reveals the orientation of every edge incident to the node. This setup however overlooks the stochasticity inherent in real-world, finite-sample settings. Our work takes a step towards studying finite-sample causal discovery, wherein multiple interventions on a node are now needed for edge orientation. In this work, we study the canonical setup in theoretical causal discovery literature, where one assumes causal sufficiency and access to the graph skeleton. Our key observation is that discovery may be viewed as structured, multiple testing, and we develop a novel testing framework to this end. Crucially, our framework allows for anytime valid testing as multiple tests are needed to conclude an edge orientation. It also allows for flexible combination of structured test-statistics (enabling one to use Meek rules to propagate edge orientation) as well as robust testing. Through empirical simulations, we confirm the usefulness of our framework. In closing, using this testing framework, we show how one may efficiently verify graph structure by drawing a connection to multi-constraint bandits and designing a novel algorithm to this end.

This paper moves beyond an idealized setting where interventions reveal edge directions with unlimited samples. It studies a setting in which repeated interventions on a node may be needed before the direction of a connection can be established.

The framework assumes causal sufficiency and access to the graph skeleton: the connections are available, while their directions remain to be determined. The authors formulate discovery as a structured multiple-testing problem. Their tests remain valid as evidence accumulates, and the framework can combine structured test statistics while using Meek rules to propagate conclusions about edge directions.

The method also accommodates robust testing, and simulations support its usefulness. The contribution is a statistical framework that treats uncertainty from finite data as part of causal discovery while exploiting relationships among the decisions being tested.
summary.tldr: An anytime-valid testing framework uses finite intervention data to orient causal edges under causal sufficiency and a known graph skeleton.

title: Foundations of Testing for Finite-Sample Causal Discovery

abstract: We study the role of contextual information in the online learning problem of brokerage between traders. In this sequential problem, at each time step, two traders arrive with secret valuations about an asset they wish to trade. The learner (a broker) suggests a trading (or brokerage) price based on contextual data about the asset and the market conditions. Then, the traders reveal their willingness to buy or sell based on whether their valuations are higher or lower than the brokerage price. A trade occurs if one of the two traders decides to buy and the other to sell, i.e., if the broker’s proposed price falls between the smallest and the largest of their two valuations. We design algorithms for this problem and prove optimal theoretical regret guarantees under various standard assumptions.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a broker can learn to propose trading prices using information about an asset and current market conditions. Each round brings two traders whose valuations are hidden. The broker must select a price before learning whether each trader would buy or sell at that price, making the task a sequence of decisions with incomplete information.

A trade happens when the proposed price lies between the two valuations: one trader is willing to buy and the other to sell. The feedback therefore tells the broker how the valuations compare with the proposed price, without directly revealing their numerical values. Context provides information that the broker can use when choosing prices across rounds.

The authors develop algorithms and prove optimal regret guarantees under several standard assumptions. Regret measures the cost of learning relative to a comparison strategy. The results establish how well brokerage decisions can perform in the studied settings, with optimality tied to the assumptions used for each guarantee.
summary.tldr: The paper develops brokerage algorithms that use contextual information and achieve optimal regret guarantees under the studied assumptions.

title: A Parametric Contextual Online Learning Theory of Brokerage

abstract: We study how inherent randomness in the training process—where each sample (or client in federated learning) contributes only to a randomly selected portion of training—can be leveraged for privacy amplification. This includes (1) data partitioning, where a sample participates in only a subset of training iterations, and (2) model partitioning, where a sample updates only a subset of the model parameters. We apply our framework to model parallelism in federated learning, where each client updates a randomly selected subnetwork to reduce memory and computational overhead, and show that existing methods, e.g. model splitting or dropout, provide a significant privacy amplification gain not captured by previous privacy analysis techniques. Additionally, we introduce balanced iteration subsampling, a new data partitioning method where each sample (or client) participates in a fixed number of training iterations. We show that in certain regimes, this method yields stronger privacy amplification than Poisson (i.i.d.) sampling of data (or clients). Our results demonstrate that randomness in the training process, which is structured rather than i.i.d. and interacts with data in complex ways, can be systematically leveraged for nontrivial privacy amplification.
