paragraphs: Training procedures often let each example or federated client contribute to only part of the overall computation. This paper studies how randomness in that participation can strengthen privacy guarantees. It considers both data partitioning, where participation covers selected iterations, and model partitioning, where contributions update selected parameters.

For federated model parallelism, each client updates a randomly chosen subnetwork to save memory and computation. The authors show that techniques such as model splitting and dropout also provide significant privacy amplification that earlier analyses did not capture. The contribution is partly analytical: existing training randomness can offer privacy gains beyond those recognized by previous accounting methods.

The paper also introduces balanced iteration subsampling, which gives each example or client a fixed number of participating iterations. In certain regimes, this produces stronger privacy amplification than independently sampling participation with a Poisson scheme. The broader finding is that useful privacy randomness need not be independent across training steps. Structured participation patterns, including those that interact with model parameters, can be analyzed systematically.
summary.tldr: Structured randomness in training participation can amplify privacy, with balanced iteration subsampling outperforming Poisson sampling in certain regimes.

title: Leveraging Randomness in Model and Data Partitioning for Privacy Amplification

abstract: We propose Score-of-Mixture Training (SMT), a novel framework for training one-step generative models by minimizing a class of divergences called the $\alpha$-skew Jensen–Shannon divergence. At its core, SMT estimates the score of mixture distributions between real and fake samples across multiple noise levels. Similar to consistency models, our approach supports both training from scratch (SMT) and distillation using a pretrained diffusion model, which we call Score-of-Mixture Distillation (SMD). It is simple to implement, requires minimal hyperparameter tuning, and ensures stable training. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet 64$\times$64 show that SMT/SMD are competitive with and can even outperform existing methods.

paragraphs: One-step generative models aim to produce samples with a single generation step. Score-of-Mixture Training, or SMT, provides a framework for learning these models by reducing a particular discrepancy between real and generated data: the alpha-skew Jensen–Shannon divergence. Its central learning signal comes from mixtures of the two kinds of samples.

SMT estimates the score of those mixture distributions at multiple noise levels. A score describes how a distribution's log density changes with the input, providing information about its local structure. The framework supports training a generator from scratch. It also supports transferring knowledge from a pretrained diffusion model through a variant called Score-of-Mixture Distillation, or SMD.

The authors describe the approach as simple to implement, requiring little hyperparameter tuning and providing stable training. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and 64-by-64 ImageNet show competitive performance, including cases where SMT or SMD surpass existing methods. The contribution is a common mixture-score formulation that accommodates both direct training and diffusion-model distillation for one-step generation.
summary.tldr: Score-of-Mixture Training learns one-step generators from real–generated mixture scores, supporting both training from scratch and diffusion-model distillation.

title: Score-of-Mixture Training: One-Step Generative Model Training Made Simple via Score Estimation of Mixture Distributions

abstract: Warning: Contains harmful model outputs. Despite significant advancements, the propensity of Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate harmful and unethical content poses critical challenges. Measuring value alignment of LLMs becomes crucial for their regulation and responsible deployment. Although numerous benchmarks have been constructed to assess social bias, toxicity, and ethical issues in LLMs, those static benchmarks suffer from evaluation chronoeffect, in which, as models rapidly evolve, existing benchmarks may leak into training data or become saturated, overestimating ever-developing LLMs. To tackle this problem, we propose GETA, a novel generative evolving testing approach based on adaptive testing methods in measurement theory. Unlike traditional adaptive testing methods that rely on a static test item pool, GETA probes the underlying moral boundaries of LLMs by dynamically generating test items tailored to model capability. GETA co-evolves with LLMs by learning a joint distribution of item difficulty and model value conformity, thus effectively addressing evaluation chronoeffect. We evaluated various popular LLMs with GETA and demonstrated that 1) GETA can dynamically create difficulty-tailored test items and 2) GETA’s evaluation results are more consistent with models’ performance on unseen OOD and i.i.d. items, laying the groundwork for future evaluation paradigms.

paragraphs: Static tests of language-model values can become less informative as models evolve. Test questions may enter training data, or models may become good enough to saturate existing benchmarks, causing evaluations to overestimate alignment. This paper calls that problem evaluation chronoeffect and proposes GETA, a testing approach that generates new items tailored to the model being evaluated.

GETA draws on adaptive testing from measurement theory but replaces a fixed pool of questions with dynamically generated items. It learns a joint distribution connecting item difficulty with model value conformity. That relationship guides the creation of questions suited to the model’s capability, allowing the evaluation to change alongside models and probe their moral boundaries.

Evaluations across popular language models show that GETA can generate items at tailored difficulty levels. Its results also correspond more closely to performance on unseen items drawn both from the same distribution and from different distributions. These findings support adaptive generation as a way to maintain informative alignment evaluations as model capabilities and exposure to benchmarks change.
summary.tldr: GETA dynamically generates difficulty-matched value-alignment tests whose results better reflect evaluated models’ performance on unseen questions.

title: Raising the Bar: Investigating the Values of Large Language Models via Generative Evolving Testing

abstract: In continual learning scenarios, catastrophic forgetting of previously learned tasks is a critical issue, making it essential to effectively measure such forgetting. Recently, there has been growing interest in focusing on representation forgetting, the forgetting measured at the hidden layer. In this paper, we provide the first theoretical analysis of representation forgetting and use this analysis to better understand the behavior of continual learning. First, we introduce a new metric called representation discrepancy, which measures the difference between representation spaces constructed by two snapshots of a model trained through continual learning. We demonstrate that our proposed metric serves as an effective surrogate for the representation forgetting while remaining analytically tractable. Second, through mathematical analysis of our metric, we derive several key findings about the dynamics of representation forgetting: the forgetting occurs more rapidly to a higher degree as the layer index increases, while increasing the width of the network slows down the forgetting process. Third, we support our theoretical findings through experiments on real image datasets, including Split-CIFAR100 and ImageNet1K.

paragraphs: When a model learns tasks sequentially, its internal representations can change in ways that undermine earlier learning. This paper studies that hidden-layer form of forgetting. It introduces representation discrepancy, a metric comparing the representation spaces produced by two snapshots of a model during continual learning.

The metric is designed to serve as an effective surrogate for representation forgetting while remaining manageable for mathematical analysis. This matters because a measure that can be analyzed provides a route from observing representational change to understanding its dynamics. The paper uses this route to develop a theoretical account of how forgetting varies with network structure.

The analysis finds that forgetting becomes faster and more pronounced at higher layer indices, while increasing network width slows the process. Experiments on real image datasets, including Split-CIFAR100 and ImageNet1K, support these theoretical findings. The contribution therefore combines a measurement tool with structural insights: depth within the network and network width help explain differences in representational forgetting in the analyzed and evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Representation discrepancy makes hidden-layer forgetting analytically tractable and reveals how layer position and network width affect its dynamics.

title: Measuring Representational Shifts in Continual Learning: A Linear Transformation Perspective

abstract: A significant challenge in maintaining real-world machine learning models is responding to the continuous and unpredictable evolution of data. Most practitioners are faced with the difficult question: when should I retrain or update my machine learning model? This seemingly straightforward problem is particularly challenging for three reasons: 1) decisions must be made based on very limited information - we usually have access to only a few examples, 2) the nature, extent, and impact of the distribution shift are unknown, and 3) it involves specifying a cost ratio between retraining and poor performance, which can be hard to characterize. Existing works address certain aspects of this problem, but none offer a comprehensive solution. Distribution shift detection falls short as it cannot account for the cost trade-off; the scarcity of the data, paired with its unusual structure, makes it a poor fit for existing offline reinforcement learning methods, and the online learning formulation overlooks key practical considerations. To address this, we present a principled formulation of the retraining problem and propose an uncertainty-based method that makes decisions by continually forecasting the evolution of model performance evaluated with a bounded metric. Our experiments, addressing classification tasks, show that the method consistently outperforms existing baselines on 7 datasets. We thoroughly assess its robustness to varying cost trade-off values and mis-specified cost trade-offs.

paragraphs: Deciding when to retrain requires balancing the expense of updating a model against the cost of leaving a degrading model in service. The authors formulate retraining as a decision problem and propose an uncertainty-based method that continually forecasts how model performance will evolve. These findings support forecasting performance as a useful basis for retraining decisions under limited information, with the empirical evidence coming from the classification settings evaluated in the paper.
summary.tldr: An uncertainty-based method forecasts model performance to decide when retraining is worthwhile, outperforming baselines across seven classification datasets.

title: When to retrain a machine learning model

abstract: Reliable estimation of treatment effects from observational data is important in many disciplines such as medicine. However, estimation is challenging when unconfoundedness as a standard assumption in the causal inference literature is violated. In this work, we leverage arbitrary (potentially high-dimensional) instruments to estimate bounds on the conditional average treatment effect (CATE). Our contributions are three-fold: (1) We propose a novel approach for partial identification through a mapping of instruments to a discrete representation space so that we yield valid bounds on the CATE. This is crucial for reliable decision-making in real-world applications. (2) We derive a two-step procedure that learns tight bounds using a tailored neural partitioning of the latent instrument space. As a result, we avoid instability issues due to numerical approximations or adversarial training. Furthermore, our procedure aims to reduce the estimation variance in finite-sample settings to yield more reliable estimates. (3) We show theoretically that our procedure obtains valid bounds while reducing estimation variance. We further perform extensive experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness across various settings. Overall, our procedure offers a novel path for practitioners to make use of potentially high-dimensional instruments (e.g., as in Mendelian randomization).

paragraphs: Estimating treatment effects from observational data becomes difficult when the usual assumption of no unmeasured confounding fails. This paper uses instruments, including potentially high-dimensional ones, to estimate bounds on conditional average treatment effects. The aim is partial identification: determining a valid range for an effect rather than requiring a single fully identified value.

The proposed approach maps instruments into a discrete representation space while preserving valid effect bounds. The contribution provides a way to use complex instruments without discarding the goal of reliable causal inference. The authors identify Mendelian randomization as a possible application, illustrating the relevance of handling instruments with many dimensions.
summary.tldr: Learned discrete representations of instruments support valid treatment-effect bounds with reduced estimation variance.

title: Learning Representations of Instruments for Partial Identification of Treatment Effects

abstract: The emergence of multi-dimensional data presents significant challenges for traditional regression models based on matrices or vectors, particularly in capturing multi-directional correlations. In response, tensor regression has been proposed as a powerful framework for modeling linear relationships among multi-dimensional variables. In this paper, we introduce a high-dimensional tensor-response tensor regression model under low-dimensional structural assumptions, such as sparsity and low-rankness. Assuming the underlying tensor lies within an unknown low-dimensional subspace, we consider a least squares estimation framework with non-convex penalties. Theoretically, we derive general risk bounds for the resulting estimators and demonstrate that they achieve the oracle statistical rates under mild technical conditions. To compute the proposed estimators efficiently, we introduce an accelerated proximal gradient algorithm demonstrating rapid convergence in practice. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed regression model and showcase the practical utility of the theoretical findings.

paragraphs: This paper develops regression for multidimensional predictors and responses while preserving their tensor structure. Such data can contain correlations along several directions that vector- or matrix-based models struggle to capture. The proposed model handles high dimensionality by assuming that the relevant tensor structure occupies an unknown, lower-dimensional subspace.

The estimation approach combines least squares with nonconvex penalties that express structural properties such as sparsity and low rank. These assumptions narrow the effective complexity of the regression problem. The authors derive general bounds on estimation risk and show that, under mild technical conditions, the estimators attain oracle statistical rates, matching rates associated with knowing the relevant underlying structure.

To compute the estimators, the paper introduces an accelerated proximal-gradient algorithm and reports rapid convergence in practice. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support the model’s effectiveness. The contribution connects a structured model, statistical guarantees, and a practical optimization procedure, showing how low-dimensional organization can make high-dimensional tensor regression more tractable.
summary.tldr: Structured tensor regression with nonconvex penalties achieves oracle statistical rates under stated conditions and is paired with an efficient optimization algorithm.

title: High-Dimensional Tensor Regression With Oracle Properties

abstract: In multi-view multi-label classification (MVML), each object has multiple heterogeneous views and is annotated with multiple labels. The key to deal with such problem lies in how to capture cross-view consistent correlations while excavate multi-label semantic relationships. Existing MVML methods usually employ two independent components to address them separately, and ignores their potential interaction relationships. To address this issue, we propose a novel Tensorized MVML method named TMvML, which formulates an MVML tensor classifier to excavate comprehensive cross-view feature correlations while characterize complete multi-label semantic relationships. Specifically, we first reconstruct the MVML mapping matrices as an MVML tensor classifier. Then, we rotate the tensor classifier and introduce a low-rank tensor constraint to ensure view-level feature consistency and label-level semantic co-occurrence simultaneously. To better characterize the low-rank tensor structure, we design a new Laplace Tensor Rank (LTR), which serves as a tighter surrogate of tensor rank to capture high-order fiber correlations within the tensor space. By conducting the above operations, our method can easily address the two key challenges in MVML via a concise LTR tensor classifier and achieve the extraction of both cross-view consistent correlations and multi-label semantic relationships simultaneously. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TMvML significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: In multi-view multi-label classification, an object has several different feature views and may belong to multiple labels. A useful model must capture both agreement across views and relationships among labels. The paper argues that handling these with independent components overlooks their interactions, and proposes TMvML to represent them jointly.

TMvML reorganizes the mapping matrices used for classification into a tensor classifier. It rotates this tensor and imposes a low-rank constraint to encourage feature consistency across views alongside semantic co-occurrence among labels. The shared tensor representation lets these two kinds of structure influence the same classifier rather than being addressed in separate components.

This provides a concise constraint for extracting view and label relationships together. Extensive experiments show significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods, supporting the value of jointly modeling these interacting structures within the evaluated multi-view, multi-label classification problems.
summary.tldr: TMvML uses a low-rank tensor classifier to jointly capture consistency across feature views and relationships among multiple labels.

title: Tensorized Multi-View Multi-Label Classification via Laplace Tensor Rank

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in complex reasoning tasks, yet generating reliable reasoning processes remains a significant challenge. We present a unified probabilistic framework that formalizes LLM reasoning through a novel graphical model incorporating latent thinking processes and evaluation signals. Our framework addresses two critical questions: (1) how to generate high-quality reasoning processes during inference automatically, and (2) how to integrate these processes into post-training. We propose the Bootstrapping Reinforced Thinking Process (BRiTE) algorithm and demonstrate its theoretical convergence at a rate of $1/T$, where $T$ is the number of iterations. The algorithm operates in two steps. First, it generates high-quality rationales by approximating the desired posterior distribution using a reinforcement learning approach with a novel reward shaping mechanism. Second, it fine-tunes the base LLM by maximizing the joint probability of rationale generation with respect to LLM parameters. Empirical evaluation on GSM8K and MATH benchmarks demonstrates that our approach consistently improves performance across different model sizes without requiring human-annotated thinking processes, outperforming standard chain-of-thought prompting while enhancing existing post-training methods.

paragraphs: A language model can produce a correct-looking answer without reliably generating the reasoning needed to reach it. BRiTE addresses how to automatically obtain useful reasoning processes and then use them to improve the model. The paper introduces a probabilistic graphical model that connects hidden thinking processes with evaluation signals, providing a shared framework for inference and post-training.

The algorithm alternates between two steps. First, reinforcement learning with a new reward-shaping mechanism generates rationales by approximating a desired posterior distribution. In plain terms, it seeks reasoning processes favored by the probabilistic framework and its evaluation information. Second, it fine-tunes the base model by maximizing the joint probability associated with rationale generation.

The authors establish theoretical convergence at a rate of 1/T, where T counts iterations. On GSM8K and MATH, BRiTE consistently improves results across model sizes without human-annotated thinking processes. It outperforms standard chain-of-thought prompting and strengthens existing post-training methods, supporting the usefulness of repeatedly generating and learning from better rationales.
summary.tldr: BRiTE alternates reinforcement-based rationale generation with model fine-tuning to improve mathematical reasoning without human-annotated thinking processes.

title: BRiTE: Bootstrapping Reinforced Thinking Process to Enhance Language Model Reasoning

abstract: When gradient information is unavailable, black-box optimization (BBO) methods provide a practical alternative. While Evolution Strategies (ES), Consensus-Based Optimization (CBO), Optimization via Integration (OVI), and related methods have each been studied independently, their connections remain underexplored. We unify these approaches within a common theoretical framework, revealing that they differ primarily in two design choices: fitness aggregation (controlling sharpness preference) and consensus scope (controlling modality). Leveraging these insights, we introduce hybrid optimizers that interpolate between existing methods. Our ES-OVI hybrid allows explicit control over the preference for flat minima, enabling a trade-off between performance and robustness in continuous control tasks. Our CBO-OVI hybrids combine the higher-dimensional efficiency of parametric methods with the multimodal capabilities of particle-based approaches, achieving competitive results on language model merging under limited evaluation budgets. We validate our methods on standard BBO benchmarks and higher-dimensional locomotion tasks, demonstrating that the hybrid methods can outperform their constituent algorithms.

paragraphs: Black-box optimization searches for good solutions when gradients are unavailable. Several established approaches solve this problem using seemingly different mechanisms. This paper places Evolution Strategies, Consensus-Based Optimization, Optimization via Integration, and related methods in a common framework, making their relationships explicit rather than treating them as separate algorithm families.

The framework identifies two main design choices. Fitness aggregation governs preference for sharper or flatter solutions, while consensus scope governs how the search handles multiple promising regions. These choices become adjustable ingredients for constructing hybrids. An Evolution Strategies–Integration hybrid explicitly controls the preference for flat minima, exposing a trade-off between performance and robustness.

Other hybrids combine the efficiency of parametric methods in higher dimensions with particle methods’ ability to represent multiple search regions. Evaluations cover standard optimization benchmarks, locomotion, and language model merging with limited evaluations. The hybrids can outperform their constituent methods, suggesting that understanding shared structure can directly guide useful algorithm design.
summary.tldr: A shared framework for black-box optimizers reveals two design choices that enable effective hybrid algorithms.

title: Bridging Spherical Black-Box Optimizers

abstract: Understanding how neural networks arrive at their predictions is essential for debugging, auditing, and deployment. Mechanistic interpretability pursues this goal by identifying circuits—minimal subnetworks responsible for specific behaviors. However, existing circuit discovery methods are brittle: circuits depend strongly on the chosen concept dataset and often fail to transfer out-of-distribution, raising doubts whether they capture the concept or merely dataset-specific artifacts. We introduce Certified Circuits, which provide provable stability guarantees for circuit discovery. Our framework wraps any black-box discovery algorithm with randomized data subsampling to certify that inclusion decisions over circuit components—neurons or edges of the model graph, depending on the base algorithm—are invariant to bounded edit-distance perturbations of the concept dataset. Unstable components are abstained from, yielding circuits that are more compact and more accurate. We validate across three architectures (ResNet, ViT, GPT-2) on vision (ImageNet and four OOD datasets) and language (IOI, IOI-Hard, Greater-Than) tasks. Certified circuits achieve up to 56% higher accuracy and up to 80% fewer components, and remain reliable where baselines degrade. Certified Circuits puts circuit discovery on formal ground by producing mechanistic explanations that are provably stable and better aligned with the target concept. Code: https://github.com/AlaaAnani/certified-circuits.

paragraphs: Mechanistic interpretability identifies small subnetworks, or circuits, associated with particular behaviors. However, a discovered circuit can depend heavily on the examples used to define the behavior. This paper addresses that instability by certifying whether decisions to include individual components survive bounded changes to the concept dataset.

Certified Circuits wraps an existing discovery algorithm with randomized data subsampling. Depending on the underlying algorithm, the components are neurons or edges in the model graph. The framework certifies invariance of component inclusion decisions under bounded edit-distance perturbations to the dataset. When a component's inclusion is unstable, the method abstains from including it rather than treating the discovery as dependable.

The authors evaluate the framework on ResNet, ViT, and GPT-2 across vision and language tasks, including distribution shifts. They report up to 56% higher accuracy and up to 80% fewer components. These empirical improvements accompany a specific formal guarantee about dataset perturbations, giving circuit explanations a measurable notion of stability alongside their observed accuracy and compactness.
summary.tldr: Randomized subsampling certifies circuit-component stability under bounded dataset edits and yields smaller, more accurate circuits in the reported evaluations.

title: Certified Circuits: Stability Guarantees for Mechanistic Circuits

abstract: Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) leverage extensive pretraining to accurately predict unseen time series during inference, without the need for task-specific fine-tuning. Through large-scale evaluations of standard benchmarks, we find that leading transformer-based TSFMs exhibit redundant components in their intermediate layers. We introduce a set of tools for mechanistic interpretability of TSFMs, including ablations of specific components and direct logit attribution on the residual stream. Our findings are consistent across several leading TSFMs with diverse architectures, and across a diverse set of real-world and synthetic time-series datasets. We discover that all models in our study are robust to ablations of entire layers. Furthermore, we develop a theoretical framework framing transformers as kernel regressors, motivating a purely intrinsic strategy for ablating heads based on the stable rank of the per-head projection matrices. Using this approach, we uncover the specific heads responsible for degenerate phenomena widely observed in TSFMs, such as parroting of motifs from the context and seasonality bias. Our study sheds light on the universal properties of this emerging class of architectures for continuous-time sequence modeling.
originalAbstract: Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) leverage extensive pretraining to accurately predict unseen time series during inference, without the need for task-specific fine-tuning. Through large-scale evaluations of standard benchmarks, we find that leading transformer-based TSFMs exhibit redundant components in their intermediate layers. We introduce a set of tools for mechanistic interpretability of TSFMs, including ablations of specific components and direct logit attribution on the residual stream. Our findings are consistent across several leading TSFMs with diverse architectures, and across a diverse set of real-world and synthetic time-series datasets. We discover that all models in our study are robust to ablations of entire layers. Furthermore, we develop a theoretical framework framing transformers as kernel regressors, motivating a purely intrinsic strategy for ablating heads based on the stable rank of the per-head projection matrices. Using this approach, we uncover the specific heads responsible for degenerate phenomena widely observed in TSFMs, such as parroting of motifs from the context and seasonality bias. Our study sheds light on the universal properties of this emerging class of architectures for continuous-time sequence modeling.

Across evaluations of leading transformer-based models, it finds redundant intermediate components and reports that every model studied remains robust when entire layers are ablated.

The authors introduce interpretability tools that remove selected components and trace their direct contributions through the residual stream. They apply these tools across diverse architectures and real-world and synthetic datasets. A theoretical view of transformers as kernel regressors further motivates selecting attention heads for ablation using the stable rank of their projection matrices, an intrinsic property of the model.

This head-selection approach identifies particular heads responsible for undesirable patterns, including repetition of motifs from the context and a bias toward seasonality. The results connect internal structure with recognizable forecasting behavior. Their consistency across the studied models suggests shared properties within this emerging model class, while the component-level analysis offers a way to investigate both redundant computation and the mechanisms behind specific prediction tendencies.
summary.tldr: The studied time-series foundation models tolerate whole-layer ablations, while specific attention heads drive motif repetition and seasonality bias.

title: Universal Redundancies in Time Series Foundation Models

abstract: Precise property prediction of organic materials is pivotal for next-generation electronic and energy devices. In density functional theory (DFT), the electron density (ED) serves as the fundamental determinant of material properties. Yet, establishing it as an input modality for material property prediction has been impeded by two practical barriers: scarce large-scale ED data and the enormous computational complexity of ED representation. To bridge these gaps, we introduce VisionED, an efficient physics-informed model pre-trained on electron-density images. We curate a dataset of 2 million molecules and represent ED as multi-shot images that efficiently encode both geometric and electronic structure. VisionED is then pre-trained on 12 million multi-shot ED images via cross-scale, physics-informed pretext tasks. Empirical evaluations on photovoltaic and organic chromophore datasets show that VisionED outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by up to 27.0%, exhibiting superior robustness under distribution shifts and data scarcity. Notably, the model generalizes to unseen device-scale applications, successfully recovering experimental trends and mixing-ratio effects in ternary blends with an average accuracy of 92.77%. Moreover, relative to the previous ED point cloud, the ED image improves performance by 26.2% with 2.6$\times$ fewer memory and 4.6$\times$ lower time. The code and data are available at https://github.com/ZhixiangCheng/VisionED.

abstract: Effective skill grounding is essential for deploying reusable skills in embodied agents, as even minor embodiment or environmental differences can render an entire skill incompatible. This challenge is particularly pronounced in embodied settings, where agents must operate in dynamic, partially observable environments without access to large language models (LLMs). In this setting, reliance on LLMs is impractical, while small language models (sLMs) remain insufficient for the effective skill grounding required for reliable long-horizon control. We present RECENT, a refactoring-centric agent framework that enables efficient skill grounding with sLMs by decoupling skill semantics from embodiment- and environment-specific execution binding. By representing skills as executable code, RECENT preserves the semantic intent encoded in a skill’s control structure while grounding it by modifying only execution bindings through localized refactoring, rather than regenerating code from scratch. We evaluate RECENT across diverse skill grounding scenarios spanning multiple robot embodiments in dynamic environments, demonstrating robust long-horizon performance when deployed with an sLM. Across all scenarios, RECENT achieves the best performance among sLM-based Code-as-Policies (CaP) methods and matches the task performance of LLM-based CaP.

paragraphs: A reusable robotic skill can become unusable when the robot's body or environment changes, even if the intended task stays the same. It preserves the control structure expressing what the skill should accomplish, then performs localized refactoring of the bindings needed to execute it. This focuses adaptation on the incompatible parts rather than asking the model to regenerate the entire program.

The authors evaluate multiple robot embodiments and skill-grounding scenarios in dynamic environments. RECENT delivers robust long-horizon performance with a small language model, achieves the strongest results among the evaluated small-model Code-as-Policies methods across all scenarios, and matches the task performance of large-model Code-as-Policies. The findings support preserving existing skill structure as a useful aid to efficient adaptation.
summary.tldr: RECENT enables small language models to adapt robotic skills by refactoring execution bindings while preserving the skills' existing control structure.

title: Efficient Skill Grounding via Code Refactoring with Small Language Models

abstract: Recent efforts to improve the reasoning abilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) have focused on integrating formal logic solvers within neurosymbolic frameworks. A key challenge is that formal solvers lack commonsense world knowledge, preventing them from making reasoning steps that humans find obvious. Prior methods address this by using LLMs to supply missing commonsense assumptions, but these approaches implicitly assume universal agreement on such commonsense facts. In reality, commonsense beliefs vary across individuals. We propose a probabilistic framework for abductive commonsense reasoning that explicitly models this variation, aiming to determine whether most people would judge a statement as true or false. We introduce Probabilistic Abductive CommonSense (PACS), a novel algorithm that uses an LLM and a formal solver to sample proofs as observations of individuals’ distinct commonsense beliefs, and aggregates conclusions across these samples. Empirically, PACS outperforms chain-of-thought reasoning, prior neurosymbolic methods, and search-based approaches across multiple benchmarks.

paragraphs: Formal logic solvers can check reasoning, but they lack the everyday assumptions people use to fill gaps in an argument. Existing approaches ask language models to supply those assumptions. This paper questions the idea that the supplied commonsense beliefs should be treated as facts on which everyone agrees.

The authors instead frame commonsense reasoning probabilistically, explicitly allowing beliefs to differ across individuals. Their target is whether most people would judge a statement true or false. The resulting algorithm, Probabilistic Abductive CommonSense, or PACS, combines a language model with a formal solver to sample proofs that represent distinct sets of commonsense beliefs.

PACS aggregates conclusions across these sampled proofs, allowing variation in assumptions to influence the final judgment. The approach therefore connects formal reasoning with disagreement about the premises that reasoning needs. Across multiple benchmarks, the authors report better performance than chain-of-thought reasoning, earlier neurosymbolic methods, and search-based approaches. The stated empirical finding supports modeling commonsense variation rather than relying on a single shared set of assumptions.
summary.tldr: PACS combines language models and formal solvers to reason across differing commonsense beliefs and aggregate their conclusions.

title: Abductive Reasoning with Probabilistic Commonsense

abstract: Recently, large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable reasoning abilities by producing long reasoning traces. However, as the sequence length grows, the key-value (KV) cache expands linearly, incurring significant memory and computation costs. Existing KV cache eviction methods mitigate this issue by discarding less important KV pairs, but often fail to capture complex KV dependencies, resulting in performance degradation. To better balance efficiency and performance, we introduce ForesightKV, a training-based KV cache eviction framework that learns to predict which KV pairs to evict during long-text generations. We first design the Golden Eviction algorithm, which identifies the optimal eviction KV pairs at each step using future attention scores. These traces and the scores at each step are then distilled via supervised training with a Pairwise Ranking Loss. Furthermore, we formulate cache eviction as a Markov Decision Process and apply the GRPO algorithm to mitigate the significant language modeling loss increase on low-entropy tokens. Experiments on AIME2024 and AIME2025 benchmarks of three reasoning models demonstrate that ForesightKV consistently outperforms prior methods under only half the cache budget, while benefiting synergistically from both supervised and reinforcement learning approaches. Code is available at https://github.com/RUCAIBox/ForesightKV.

paragraphs: Long reasoning traces increase the memory and computation devoted to a language model’s key-value cache. ForesightKV learns which entries to remove by using their future contribution as a training signal, aiming to improve the trade-off between cache size and performance.

Its Golden Eviction algorithm uses future attention scores to identify optimal eviction choices at each step. The experiments also report complementary benefits from supervised training and reinforcement learning.
summary.tldr: ForesightKV learns cache eviction from future-aware supervision and reinforcement learning, improving reasoning performance under reduced cache budgets.

title: ForesightKV: Optimizing KV Cache Eviction for Reasoning Models by Learning Long-Term Contribution

abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) are a state-of-the-art generative method to approximately sample from an unknown distribution. Their training and evaluation primarily rely on an Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO), which relates the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence of model samples to the score matching loss along the path, which serves as a tractable surrogate. The difference between sample quality and the score matching loss produced by this bound leads to the score matching gap, which is known to be tight in the worst-case but not descriptive of sample quality in general. In this work, we provide a theoretical analysis of this gap, developing tighter bounds for three metrics: KL divergence, reverse KL divergence, and Wasserstein distance, effectively exploiting the regularity of the class of score estimators. Our results suggest that the quality of the score approximation has more impact on closing the score matching gap for low noise scales. To obtain these bounds, our key technical insight is to exploit the contraction properties of the backward processes. In particular, we rely on entropy flows, logarithmic Sobolev inequalities and reflection couplings, rigorously linking the ergodicity of the Langevin diffusion to the score matching gap problem.

title: Tightening the Score Matching Gap for Diffusion Models

abstract: Neural architecture design lacks first principles: innovations are discovered empirically and justified post-hoc, with no systematic way to diagnose why an architecture fails or derive what repair will succeed. We introduce the Axiomatic Atlas, encoding requirements as composable axioms over graph connectivity, operator contracts, numerical stability, and information preservation. Given an operator library and wiring conventions, the Atlas constructs certificates lower-bounding output variation via min-cut analysis and diagnoses failures by locating axiom violations. Crucially, the framework is prescriptive: each violation implies a targeted repair, reducing architecture design to constraint satisfaction. We prove variation bounds under exact and finite-precision arithmetic, enabling modular verification across transformers, MoEs, SSMs, and GNNs. Four Atlas-derived interventions validate the approach: +46 percentage points on GNN bottlenecks, $3\times$ robustness to MoE quantization, 83% gap closure with adaptive expert budgets, and 0%$\to$100% retrieval via orthogonal keys—each against matched negative controls.

title: Axiomatic Atlas: A Prescriptive Framework for Neural Architecture Design

abstract: Data markets promise to unlock data value by matching data suppliers with ML consumers. However, market design involves addressing intricate challenges, including data pricing, fairness, and robustness. We propose a pragmatic data-augmented AutoML market that seamlessly integrates with existing cloud-based AutoML platforms, such as Google’s Vertex AI. Unlike standard AutoML solutions, our design automatically augments buyer-submitted training data with valuable external datasets, pricing the resulting models based on their measurable performance improvements rather than computational costs as the status quo. Our key innovation is a pricing mechanism grounded in the instrumental value—the marginal model quality improvement—of externally sourced data. This approach bypasses direct dataset pricing complexities and accommodates diverse buyer valuations through menu-based options, thus providing an economically sustainable framework for monetizing external data.

paragraphs: External datasets can improve a buyer's machine-learning model, but deciding how to price those datasets creates a difficult market-design problem. This paper proposes an AutoML marketplace in which buyers submit their own training data and the platform automatically supplements it with useful external data. The design is intended to integrate with existing cloud AutoML services.

The central pricing idea is instrumental value: how much the external data improves the resulting model's quality. Rather than directly assigning a standalone price to a dataset, the marketplace prices models according to measurable performance improvements. This shifts the object of pricing toward the benefit delivered by data augmentation, instead of the computational resources consumed during training.

The proposed market also offers menu-based choices to accommodate buyers who value improvements differently. The authors present this combination as an economically sustainable way to monetize externally supplied data while avoiding some complexities of direct dataset pricing. Its main contribution is the market structure and pricing mechanism: it connects data suppliers to ML consumers through the quality of the trained model that the consumer receives.
summary.tldr: The proposed AutoML marketplace prices data-augmented models by their performance improvements and offers options for differing buyer valuations.

title: Optimal Pricing for Data-Augmented AutoML Marketplaces

abstract: Recent advancements in tabular deep learning have demonstrated exceptional practical performance, yet the field often lacks a clear understanding of why these techniques actually succeed. To address this gap, our paper highlights the importance of the concept of data (aleatoric) uncertainty for explaining the effectiveness of recent tabular DL methods. While data uncertainty leads to irreducible prediction errors on test samples, it also introduces stochasticity into the training signal that can impede effective learning. We demonstrate that tabular methods differ significantly in their ability to cope with this optimization challenge. Specifically, we reveal that the success of many beneficial design choices in tabular DL, such as numerical feature embeddings, advanced ensembling strategies, retrieval-augmented models, and tabular Prior-Fitted Networks, can be partially attributed to their respective implicit mechanisms for performing well under high data uncertainty. By dissecting these varied mechanisms, we provide a unifying understanding of recent performance improvements. Furthermore, leveraging insights from this perspective, we design a novel, more effective numerical feature embedding method as an immediate practical outcome of our analysis. Overall, our work paves the way toward a principled understanding of the benefits introduced by modern tabular methods that results in the concrete advancements of existing techniques and outlines future research directions for tabular DL.

This paper argues that such aleatoric uncertainty also matters during training: it makes the learning signal stochastic and can obstruct optimization. This provides a shared explanation for improvements that otherwise arise from quite different model designs.

The contribution therefore connects an explanation of existing methods to an improvement in one of their components. Its central claim is partial attribution: coping with uncertain training signals helps explain modern tabular methods’ success alongside their other benefits.
summary.tldr: Handling data uncertainty partly explains successful tabular deep-learning designs and motivates a better numerical feature embedding.

title: Unveiling the Role of Data Uncertainty in Tabular Deep Learning

abstract: Existing backdoor attacks on Reinforcement Learning (RL) typically rely on unrealistic white-box access to victim parameters, rewards, or observations. Inspired by real world behaviors, we introduce the Supply-Chain Backdoor (SCAB) attack to demonstrate that such assumptions are unnecessary. SCAB targets the common practice of training with third-party policies, poisoning the dataset solely through a black-box of legitimate agent-environment interactions. With only 3% data corruption, SCAB demonstrates a peak attack success rate exceeding 90% and reduces victim returns by 80%. These findings expose a critical vulnerability in the modern RL supply chain, highlighting that reliance on untrusted external agents constitutes a severe and practical security risk.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning systems may train using policies supplied by third parties. This paper examines how that dependency creates an opening for backdoor attacks. Earlier attacks commonly assumed access to a victim’s parameters, rewards, or observations; the proposed Supply-Chain Backdoor attack, or SCAB, demonstrates an attack route without those white-box privileges.

SCAB poisons training data through legitimate agent–environment interactions available through a black-box interface. The important shift is the point of influence: a third-party policy can affect the data used for learning even when the attacker cannot directly manipulate the victim’s internals. This makes the training supply chain part of the system’s security boundary.

The reported experiments use only 3% data corruption, reach a peak attack success rate above 90%, and reduce victim returns by 80%. The peak figure describes the strongest reported success rather than a universal success rate. Together, these results demonstrate that limited corruption entering through external agents can have substantial effects on learned behavior, highlighting the practical risk of treating third-party training interactions as inherently trustworthy.
summary.tldr: SCAB demonstrates that third-party policies can introduce effective reinforcement learning backdoors through black-box training interactions.

title: Fox in the Henhouse: Supply-Chain Backdoor Attacks Against Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models have made substantial progress on visual understanding tasks, yet they still perform poorly on high-resolution images. Prior work often attributes this limitation to perceptual constraints, arguing that MLLMs fail to recognize small objects and therefore rely on ”zoom-in" strategies to recover fine details. In contrast, our analysis shows that the dominant failure mode is background interference rather than object size. We study the "zoom-in" operation through a hierarchical decoupling analysis and propose the Hierarchical Decoupling Framework, a training-free method that turns implicit attention into explicit region selection. HiDe first performs Token-wise Attention Decoupling to disentangle question semantics and identify the most informative tokens, then uses their attention patterns to pinpoint the corresponding visual regions. It subsequently applies Layout-Preserving Decoupling to extract these regions from cluttered backgrounds and construct a compact representation that retains key spatial structure while filtering out irrelevant context. HiDe achieves state-of-the-art results on high-resolution benchmarks like Vstar Bench. It boosts Qwen2.5-VL 7B and InternVL3 8B to state of the art performance, reaching 92.1% and 91.6% on Vstar Bench, and even surpasses reinforcement learning based methods. After optimization, HiDe reduces memory usage by 75% compared with the previous training-free approach. Code will be available at https://tennine2077.github.io/HiDe.github.io/.

While zooming is often motivated by difficulty recognizing small objects, the paper's analysis identifies background interference as the dominant failure mode. This shifts the focus toward selecting relevant regions and removing distracting context while preserving useful spatial relationships.

The training-free framework first separates the contributions of question tokens and identifies the most informative ones. Their attention patterns guide the selection of visual regions. A second stage extracts those regions from clutter and builds a compact representation that retains key layout information. In this way, attention becomes an explicit mechanism for choosing what visual evidence the model sees.

HiDe reports state-of-the-art high-resolution benchmark results, including 92.1% for Qwen2.5-VL 7B and 91.6% for InternVL3 8B on Vstar Bench, surpassing reinforcement-learning-based methods there. After optimization, it also reduces memory usage by 75% relative to the previous training-free approach. These results support the paper's emphasis on reducing distracting background while keeping the spatial structure needed for the question.
summary.tldr: HiDe uses question-guided region selection and layout-preserving background removal to improve high-resolution visual reasoning without training.

title: HiDe: Rethinking The Zoom-IN method in High Resolution MLLMs via Hierarchical Decoupling

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) achieve remarkable performance but struggle with complex logical reasoning, particularly in real-world settings. Existing research is largely confined to the closed-world assumption, which posits that all premises required for reasoning are explicitly provided. However, real-world tasks frequently exhibit open-world characteristics, where the provided information is insufficient to infer a conclusion due to missing premises or implicit commonsense knowledge. To address this, we propose OpenIKLR, an Open-world Incomplete-Knowledge-aware Logical Reasoning framework that integrates symbolic logic solvers with LLMs. OpenIKLR first translates natural language into symbolic representations to pinpoint reasoning gaps via a logical solver. It then iteratively generates a minimal set of necessary missing premises using LLMs. To ensure these added premises are both logically sound and factually accurate, we introduce a dual-verification: logic verification via the solver and fact verification via the LLMs. Experiments show that OpenIKLR consistently outperforms existing logical reasoning and RAG baselines across multiple backbones and real-world datasets. The code is available at https://github.com/OpenIKLR/OpenIKLR.

paragraphs: Logical reasoning benchmarks often assume that every premise needed for a conclusion has already been supplied. Real-world questions can omit relevant facts or leave commonsense assumptions implicit. OpenIKLR addresses this open-world setting by treating missing knowledge as something to identify and verify explicitly during reasoning.

The framework first translates natural-language information into symbolic form. A logical solver then locates gaps that prevent a conclusion from following. The language model iteratively proposes a minimal set of necessary missing premises. Proposed additions undergo two checks: the solver verifies their logical role, while language models assess factual accuracy. This separates the question of whether an assumption completes an argument from whether that assumption is factually supported.

Experiments across multiple model backbones and real-world datasets show consistent improvements over the compared logical-reasoning and retrieval-augmented baselines. The results support combining formal gap detection with language-based premise generation and verification. The framework’s contribution is a structured procedure for completing incomplete arguments, with separate logical and factual checks on the added information.
summary.tldr: OpenIKLR combines logical solvers and language models to detect missing premises, propose additions, and check their logic and factual accuracy.

title: Open-World LLM Logical Reasoning

abstract: Data science agents promise to accelerate discovery and insight-generation by turning data into executable analyses and findings. Yet existing data science benchmarks fall short due to fragmented evaluation interfaces that make cross-benchmark comparison difficult, narrow task coverage and a lack of rigorous data grounding. In particular, we show that a substantial portion of tasks in current benchmarks can be solved without using the actual data. To address these limitations, we introduce DSGym, a standardized framework for evaluating and training data science agents in self-contained execution environments. Unlike static benchmarks, DSGym provides a modular architecture that makes it easy to add tasks, agent scaffolds, and tools, positioning it as a live, extensible testbed. We curate DSGym-Tasks, a holistic task suite that standardizes and refines existing benchmarks via quality and shortcut solvability filtering. We further expand coverage with (1) DSBio: expert-derived bioinformatics tasks grounded in literature and (2) DSPredict: challenging prediction tasks spanning domains such as computer vision, molecular prediction, and single-cell perturbation. Beyond evaluation, DSGym enables agent training via execution-verified data synthesis pipeline. As a case study, we build a 2,000-example training set in DSGym that substantially improves a 4B mode on standardized analysis benchmarks. Overall, DSGym enables rigorous end-to-end measurement of whether agents can plan, implement, and validate data analyses in realistic scientific context.

summary.tldr: DSGym standardizes data science agent evaluation and training around executable tasks that require meaningful use of the actual data.

title: DSGym: A Holistic Framework for Evaluating and Training Data Science Agents

abstract: While large audio-language models have advanced open-ended audio understanding, they still fall short of nuanced human-level comprehension. This gap persists largely because current benchmarks, limited by data annotations and evaluation metrics, fail to reliably distinguish between generic and highly detailed model outputs. To this end, this work introduces MECAT, a Multi-Expert Constructed Benchmark for Fine-Grained Audio Understanding Tasks. Generated via a pipeline that integrates analysis from specialized expert models with Chain-of-Thought large language model reasoning, MECAT provides multi-perspective, fine-grained captions and open-set question-answering pairs. The benchmark is complemented by a novel metric: DATE (Discriminative-Enhanced Audio Text Evaluation). This metric penalizes generic terms and rewards detailed descriptions by combining single-sample semantic similarity with cross-sample discriminability. A comprehensive evaluation of state-of-the-art audio models is also presented, providing new insights into their current capabilities and limitations. The code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/xiaomi-research/mecat.

paragraphs: An audio model can produce a broadly plausible description without capturing the details that distinguish one recording from another. Existing annotations and evaluation metrics can struggle to separate those cases. MECAT addresses this measurement problem by creating a benchmark centered on fine-grained audio understanding.

Its construction pipeline combines analyses from specialized expert models with chain-of-thought reasoning by a language model. The resulting material includes detailed captions from multiple perspectives and open-set question-answer pairs. This provides complementary ways to examine what a model understands about an audio sample, beyond whether it can generate a generic description.

The paper pairs the benchmark with DATE, a metric that combines semantic similarity for an individual sample with discriminability across samples. It penalizes generic terms and rewards descriptions that capture distinguishing details. The authors also evaluate state-of-the-art audio models to examine their capabilities and limitations. Together, the dataset and metric make specificity part of the evaluation target, so broadly applicable language is less likely to receive the same credit as a detailed, sample-relevant account.
summary.tldr: MECAT pairs detailed audio tasks with a metric that rewards distinguishing information and penalizes generic descriptions.

title: MECAT: A Multi-Experts Constructed Benchmark for Fine-Grained Audio Understanding Tasks

abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) achieve strong performance on standard, high-quality datasets, but we still do not fully understand how they perform under real-world image distortions. We present VLM-RobustBench, a benchmark spanning 49 augmentation types across noise, blur, weather, digital, and geometric perturbations, evaluated under graded severities (low/mid/high) and binary transforms, yielding 133 corrupted settings. We evaluate 15 VLMs from five families, including proprietary GPT-5.4-mini, on two complementary benchmarks: MMBench (visually grounded) and MMMU-Pro (reasoning-oriented). Our results reveal that visual severity is a weak predictor of difficulty: low-severity spatial perturbations often degrade performance more than visually severe photometric corruptions. In particular, low-severity glass blur reduces MMBench accuracy by about 8 pp on average across models, while the largest drops arise from resampling and geometric distortions (e.g., upsample, elastic transform), reaching up to 34 pp. Overall, our findings suggest current VLMs are semantically strong but spatially fragile, motivating the definition of novel robustness evaluation protocols and training regimes that emphasize resampling and geometric invariance.

paragraphs: VLM-RobustBench examines how vision-language models respond when images are distorted. Strong performance on clean datasets may leave these weaknesses hidden. The benchmark includes 49 augmentation types covering noise, blur, weather, digital changes, and geometric changes, with severity levels and binary transformations producing 133 corrupted settings.

The authors evaluate 15 models from five families on two complementary benchmarks: MMBench for visually grounded tasks and MMMU-Pro for reasoning-oriented tasks. The comparison asks whether a distortion's apparent visual severity predicts how much it disrupts a model. The results show that this relationship is weak: mild spatial changes can cause more damage than visually severe photometric changes.

Low-severity glass blur reduces MMBench accuracy by about eight percentage points on average across models. The largest reported drops, reaching 34 percentage points, come from resampling and geometric distortions such as upsampling and elastic transformations. These findings suggest that current models combine strong semantic abilities with spatial fragility, motivating evaluation and training that pay closer attention to geometric and resampling invariance.
summary.tldr: VLM-RobustBench finds that mild spatial distortions can damage vision-language model performance more than visually severe image corruptions.

title: VLM-RobustBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Robustness of Vision-Language Models

abstract: Layer pruning efficiently reduces Large Language Model (LLM) computational costs but often triggers sudden performance collapse. Existing representation-based analyses struggle to explain this mechanism. We propose studying pruning through decision representation. Focusing on multiple-choice tasks, we introduce two metrics, Decision Margin and Option Frequency, and an Iterative Pruning method to analyze layer-wise decision dynamics. Our findings reveal a sharp decision transition that partitions the network into two stages: a Silent Phase, where the model cannot yet predict the correct answer, and a Decisive Phase, where the correct prediction emerges. We also find that pruning the Decisive Phase has minimal impact, whereas pruning the Silent Phase triggers immediate performance collapse, highlighting its extreme sensitivity to structural changes. Therefore, we conclude that pruning-induced collapse stems from disrupting the Silent Phase, which prevents the critical decision transition from occurring.

paragraphs: Removing layers can lower language-model computation costs, but performance sometimes collapses abruptly. This paper investigates the collapse through decision representations on multiple-choice tasks. It introduces Decision Margin and Option Frequency metrics, together with an iterative pruning procedure, to examine how answer decisions change as information passes through the network.

The analysis identifies a sharp transition between two stages. In the Silent Phase, the model cannot yet predict the correct answer; in the Decisive Phase, the correct prediction emerges. The important finding is that the earlier absence of a correct prediction does not imply that those layers contribute little to reaching the final answer.

In the reported analysis, pruning the Decisive Phase has minimal impact, whereas pruning the Silent Phase causes immediate collapse. The authors conclude that disrupting this sensitive earlier stage prevents the critical decision transition from occurring. Within the studied multiple-choice setting, the results explain why visible answer emergence alone can be misleading when judging which parts of a model can be removed.
summary.tldr: The study links pruning-induced collapse to disrupting a sensitive early phase needed for correct decisions to emerge.

title: Understanding Performance Collapse in Layer-Pruned Large Language Models via Decision Representation Transitions

abstract: Representation learning has driven major advances in natural image analysis by enabling models to acquire high-level semantic features. In microscopy imaging, however, it remains unclear what current representation learning methods really learn. In this work, we conduct a systematic study of representation learning for the two most widely used and broadly available microscopy data types, representing critical scales in biology: cell culture and tissue imaging. We investigate whether, in contrast to natural images, existing models fail to consistently acquire high-level, biologically meaningful features. To this end, we introduce a set of simple yet revealing baselines on curated benchmarks, including untrained models and structural representations of cellular tissue. Our results show that, surprisingly, for a considerable subset of evaluation settings, the baselines are comparable to state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating that many commonly used benchmark metrics are insufficient to assess representation quality and often mask a lack of relevant high-level abstractions. In addition, we investigate how detailed comparisons with these baselines provide ways to interpret the strengths and weaknesses of models for further improvements. Together, our results suggest that progress in representation learning for microscopy requires not only stronger models, but also benchmarks that are more indicative of what is actually learned.

paragraphs: Strong benchmark performance does not necessarily establish that an image model has learned meaningful biological concepts. This paper investigates that distinction in cell culture and tissue microscopy, two widely available imaging settings at different biological scales. The central question is whether existing representation-learning methods consistently capture high-level biological information.

The authors compare current methods with deliberately simple baselines on curated benchmarks. These include models that have not been trained and representations describing cellular tissue structure. Across a considerable subset of evaluation settings, these baselines perform comparably to state-of-the-art methods. That result challenges what the corresponding benchmark scores can establish about the quality of learned representations.

The finding does not imply that every microscopy model fails to learn useful biology. It shows that many commonly used evaluation metrics can conceal the absence of relevant high-level abstractions. Detailed comparisons with simple baselines also help interpret individual models’ strengths and weaknesses. The study therefore argues for improving both learning methods and benchmarks so that reported progress better reflects what models actually learn.
summary.tldr: Simple and untrained baselines rival advanced microscopy models in many evaluated settings, exposing weaknesses in how biological representation quality is measured.

title: Deep Learning for BioImaging: What Are We Really Learning?

abstract: Learning good representations is essential for latent planning with world models. While pretrained visual encoders produce strong semantic visual features, they are not tailored to planning and contain information irrelevant—or even detrimental—to planning. Inspired by the perceptual straightening hypothesis in human visual processing, we introduce temporal straightening to improve representation learning for latent planning. Using a curvature regularizer that encourages locally straightened latent trajectories, we jointly learn an encoder and a predictor of a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) world model. We show that reducing curvature this way makes the Euclidean distance in latent space a better proxy for the geodesic distance and improves the conditioning of the planning objective. We demonstrate empirically that temporal straightening makes gradient-based planning more stable and yields significantly higher success rates across a suite of goal-reaching tasks. Our code is available at https://agenticlearning.ai/temporal-straightening.

paragraphs: A world model can plan using compact internal representations instead of operating directly on images. However, visual features that are good at representing scene meaning may include information that is irrelevant or harmful to planning. This paper proposes shaping the representation around how states evolve over time, so its geometry better supports finding a path to a goal.

The method jointly trains an encoder and predictor in a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture world model. A curvature regularizer encourages nearby portions of latent trajectories to become straighter. The authors show that this makes ordinary Euclidean distance a better approximation to distance along the latent trajectory geometry and improves the conditioning of the planning objective.

Across a suite of goal-reaching tasks, temporal straightening makes gradient-based planning more stable and produces significantly higher success rates. The findings link representation geometry to planning behavior: reducing unnecessary curvature can make the optimization problem easier to navigate. The contribution therefore concerns how a world model organizes its internal states, alongside what those states encode.
summary.tldr: Encouraging straighter latent trajectories improves world-model geometry, stabilizing gradient-based planning and increasing success on evaluated goal-reaching tasks.

title: Temporal Straightening for Latent Planning

abstract: The prefill stage of long-context Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is severely bottlenecked by computational overhead. To mitigate this, recent methods assemble pre-calculated KV caches of retrieved RAG documents (by a user query) and reprocess selected tokens to recover cross-attention between these pre-calculated KV caches. However, we identify a fundamental “crowding-out effect” in current token selection criteria: globally salient but user-query-irrelevant tokens saturate the limited recomputation budget, displacing the tokens truly essential for answering the user query and degrading inference accuracy. We propose ProphetKV, a user-query-driven KV Cache reuse method for RAG scenarios. ProphetKV dynamically prioritizes tokens based on their semantic relevance to the user query and employs a dual-stage recomputation pipeline to fuse layer-wise attention metrics into a high-utility set. By ensuring the recomputation budget is dedicated to bridging the informational gap between retrieved context and the user query, ProphetKV achieves high-fidelity attention recovery with minimal overhead. Our extensive evaluation results show that ProphetKV retains 96%–101% of full-prefill accuracy with only a 20% recomputation ratio, while achieving accuracy improvements of 8.8%–24.9% on RULER and 18.6%–50.9% on LongBench over the state-of-the-art approaches (e.g., CacheBlend, EPIC, and KVShare).

paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented generation can spend substantial computation processing long retrieved documents before answering. Reusing their precomputed key-value caches reduces this work, but some tokens must be recomputed to restore attention interactions. The authors identify a selection problem: tokens that seem important globally can consume the limited budget even when they are irrelevant to the user’s question.

ProphetKV makes the question central to deciding which tokens deserve recomputation. It prioritizes semantic relevance to the query and uses a two-stage pipeline that combines attention measurements across layers. The goal is to spend the available work on connections between the retrieved context and the question, improving attention recovery without recomputing the entire input.

With a 20% recomputation ratio, the method retains 96%–101% of full-prefill accuracy in the reported evaluations. Relative to the evaluated state-of-the-art approaches, accuracy improvements range from 8.8%–24.9% on RULER and 18.6%–50.9% on LongBench. These results show the value of query-aware selection when only part of a cached context can be refreshed.
summary.tldr: ProphetKV prioritizes query-relevant tokens when refreshing reused document caches, retaining near-full-prefill accuracy with 20% recomputation in reported evaluations.

title: ProphetKV: User-Query-Driven Selective Recomputation for Efficient KV Cache Reuse in Retrieval-Augmented Generation

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) face a "loyalty dilemma" when correctness is conditioned on an active world-of-discourse. We identify a systemic failure mode—world misattribution—where models implicitly ground generation in an incompatible regime and drift from the target world. We propose World Entropy Tethering (WET), an inference-time monitor-and-tether: a world-entropy probe flags drift risk on prompt anchors, and a conditional score matching geometry model identifies tethering heads for entropy-gated rescaling. Experiments show: (I) Linear Separability: world labels are linearly decodable from internal states; (II) Geometric Drift: hallucinations are preceded by measurable deviations from the target world region; and (III) Targeted Mitigation: WET improves world consistency and reduces hallucination rates by up to 22.4% without compromising generation quality. Code is available at https://github.com/guess-guess-who-i-am/WET-World-Entropy-Tethering.

paragraphs: A language model’s answer can depend on which world of discourse the prompt establishes. The paper identifies world misattribution as a failure in which generation becomes grounded in an incompatible regime. In this account, some hallucinations arise because the model drifts away from the intended world, rather than simply failing to retrieve a fact.

World Entropy Tethering monitors that risk during inference. A world-entropy probe examines prompt anchors, while a geometry model based on conditional score matching identifies attention heads suitable for tethering. Entropy-gated rescaling then adjusts those heads. The method therefore combines a signal for possible drift with a targeted intervention in the model’s internal computation.

Experiments find that world labels can be decoded linearly from internal states and that measurable departures from the target world’s region precede hallucinations. WET improves world consistency and reduces hallucination rates by up to 22.4% without compromising generation quality in the evaluations. These findings support both the proposed diagnosis of world drift and the usefulness of intervening on it during generation.
summary.tldr: WET detects internal drift from the intended world of discourse and adjusts attention heads, reducing hallucination rates by up to 22.4%.

title: WET: Mitigating World-Conditioned Knowledge Conflicts via World Entropy Tethering

abstract: Amortized causal inference via Prior-data Fitted Networks (PFNs) has emerged as a promising paradigm, enabling zero-shot estimation of causal effects without the need for dataset-specific model tuning. However, the principled effectiveness of unified pre-training across general interventional regimes remains an underexplored question. In this paper, we investigate interventions on subsets of variables within Structural Causal Models (SCMs) and identify a fundamental theoretical limitation of current pre-training approaches. Theoretically, we prove that a single observational SCM induces an exponentially large space of interventional distributions, resulting in a phenomenon we term prior uncoverage. Consequently, this uncoverage yields a mismatch between the learned meta-prior and the true grounding prior, leading to unavoidable posterior inconsistency and estimation bias. To address this, we posit that fine-tuning is a fundamental necessity and propose a target-specific strategy named Point-Wise Interventional Fine-tuning (PWF), enabling the local generalization property. We further scale this approach via Meta-Sampling Fine-tuning (MSF) from a budgeted active learning perspective, thereby achieving uniform generalization on any interventional distribution.
